\subsection{Desire} % *DESIRE
% -----------------------

	What is it? How do we get the righteous version of it?
	
	\begin{description}
	\item[1N 10:17] And it came to pass after I, Nephi, having heard all the words of my father, concerning the things which he saw in a vision, and also the things which he spake by the power of the Holy Ghost, which power he received by faith on the Son of God---and the Son of God was the Messiah who should come---I, Nephi, was desirous also that I might see, and hear, and know of these things, by the power of the Holy Ghost, which is the gift of God unto all those who diligently seek him, as well in times of old as in the time that he should manifest himself unto the children of men.
	\item[1N 11:1] FOR it came to pass after I had desired to know the things that my father had seen, and believing that the Lord was able to make them known unto me, as I sat pondering in mine heart I was caught away in the Spirit of the Lord, yea, into an exceedingly high mountain, which I never had before seen, and upon which I never had before set my foot.
	\item[2N 9:49] Behold, my soul abhorreth sin, and my heart delighteth in righteousness; and I will praise the holy name of my God.
	\item[3N 19:24] And it came to pass that when Jesus had thus prayed unto the Father, he came unto his disciples, and behold, they did still continue, without ceasing, to pray unto him; and they did not multiply many words, for it was given unto them what they should pray, and they were filled with desire.
	\end{description}
	
		\subsubsection{We get what we desire from God}
		
			The principle of Al 29:1--5. Note that this is a desire-based instance of the levels principle, I think.
		
			\begin{description}
			\item[1N 14:7] For the time cometh, saith the Lamb of God, that I will work a great and a marvelous work among the children of men; a work which shall be everlasting, either on the one hand or on the other---either to the convincing of them unto peace and life eternal, or unto the deliverance of them to the hardness of their hearts and the blindness of their minds unto their being brought down into captivity, and also into destruction, both temporally and spiritually, according to the captivity of the devil, of which I have spoken.
			\item[Jac 4:13--14] Behold, my brethren, he that prophesieth, let him prophesy to the understanding of men; for the Spirit speaketh the truth and lieth not. Wherefore, it speaketh of things as they really are, and of things as they really will be; wherefore, these things are manifested unto us plainly, for the salvation of our souls. But behold, we are not witnesses alone in these things; for God also spake them unto prophets of old. 14 But behold, the Jews were a stiffnecked people; and they despised the words of plainness, and killed the prophets, and sought for things that they could not understand. Wherefore, because of their blindness, which blindness came by looking beyond the mark, they must needs fall; for God hath taken away his plainness from them, and delivered unto them many things which they cannot understand, because they desired it. And because they desired it God hath done it, that they may stumble.
			\item[DC 6:8] Verily, verily, I say unto you, even as you desire of me so it shall be unto you; and if you desire, you shall be the means of doing much good in this generation.
			\item[DC 6:20] Behold, thou art Oliver, and I have spoken unto thee because of thy desires; therefore treasure up these words in thy heart. Be faithful and diligent in keeping the commandments of God, and I will encircle thee in the arms of my love.

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Notes}
	% -----

		I must ask: In 1 Kings 3:5-12, Solomon asks for ``an understanding heart'' that he may ``discern between good and bad.'' The Lord has asked him what he wishes to receive, and Solomon asks for the gift of discernment. It's a little different for me because the gift has already been promised to me, but the principle is the same--if I wish to receive it, I must ask.

		It is something I can learn from others: In Ezekiel 44:15-24, the priests who officiate in the temple are instructed to teach the people ``the difference between the holy and profane, and [to] cause them to discern between the unclean and the clean.'' I think the best source of this knowledge for me is the prophets and apostles. They have much more experience in the world than I do, and I can learn from them.

		The gift is received through close companionship with the Holy Ghost: 1 Corinthians 2:14 reads, ``The natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.'' Properly, the passive form of ``discern'' at the end of the verse (in the active voice) means to ``examine a series of particulars in order to search [to select one].'' In other words, with the help of the Spirit of the Lord, I can sift through my experiences and through the things going on around me right now to find those which are spiritually meaningful and important.

		Another important part of this verse is the act of reception. ``Receiveth'' is \textit{dechetai}, which is an active process of reception or taking of that which is offered. I need to actively seek to receive what the Spirit of the Lord is offering me.

		Practice and use improves the gift and capacity, as does spiritual cleansing--see Hebrews 5:14 The translations which I have looked at render \textgreek{τελείων} as ``full grown'' or ``mature,'' and while it has this sense, I don't think it needs to be the only choice here. I think we can choose a different reading, something (rough) like this: ``The firm nourishment belongs to those who are perfect--those who have their organs of sense disciplined through use for the discernment of good and evil.'' This reading brings out the fact that this kind of disciplining of one's faculties is a key step in the process of becoming perfect (perfect in the Matthew 5:48 way). This may happen exclusively in those who are ``mature,'' but it refers to being ``full grown'' in a gospel sense, in a sense related to spirituality. The point is that I should be training my senses now--I can do much to discern good and evil both in others and in myself, and practicing with my own natural capacities will increase my ability. As I do this I am also striving to be cleaner spiritually, which allows me to receive the Holy Ghost, who quickens my judgments (1 Corinthians 2:14).

	1828:
		1. Distribution; the act of dealing out to different persons or places; as the dispensation of water indifferently to all parts of the earth.
		2. The dealing of God to his creatures; the distribution of good and evil, natural or moral, in the divine government.
		3. The granting of a license, or the license itself, to do what is forbidden by laws or canons, or to omit something which is commanded; that is, the dispensing with a law or canon, or the exemption of a particular person from the obligation to comply with its injunctions. The pope has power to dispense with the canons of the church, but has no right to grant dispensations to the injury of a third person.
		4. That which is dispensed or bestowed; a system of principles and rites enjoined; as the Mosaic dispensation; the gospel dispensation; including, the former the Levitical law and rites; the latter the scheme of redemption by Christ.

% -----------------------
\subsection{Divine influence} % *DIVINEINFLUENCE
% -----------------------

	This isn't the best name for this section, but I couldn't think of anything else. The idea is that God really only has one kind of spiritual influence which he uses to interact with us---call it ``spirit'' maybe---but we experience that influence in a bunch of different ways, and so give it a bunch of different names. We might call it power, joy, love, spirit, glory, and so on, but it's all the same influence. It's the same force, but since it can have different effects on us in different circumstances, and we experience those effects differently, we give it different names.
	
	See my notes in the margin at 2N 4:21. An important uniting principle here is that this influence often exhausts us, or our natural strength; we're left feeling enervated, let down almost, when the influence leaves us.
	
	\begin{description}
	\item[DC 95:12] If you keep not my commandments, the love of the Father shall not continue with you, therefore you shall walk in darkness.

\subsection{Doctrine} % *DOCTRINE
% -----------------------

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Doctrine of Christ} % *DOCTRINEOFCHRIST
	% -----
	
		When thinking about the doctrine of Christ, be sure to search the scriptures for other forms, like ``my doctrine.''
	
		A few notes: Christ defines his doctrine in DC 10:67 and 3N 11:30--32, 35, 39 (but the latter half of 3N 11 seems to be the definition; same for 2N 31); In Jn 7:16, he says that his doctrine isn't his, but is of the one who sent him. So the doctrine of Christ is really the doctrine of the Father? Seems to go with Jn 5:19, with Christ doing the things he sees the Father do. See also 3N 11:32, 35, which makes this clear. In Jn 7:17 Christ says that we can test the doctrine to see where it's from. I used to understand that as saying, ``Test the doctrine to see if it's divine and good, or to see if I just made it up.'' I still think that's part of what he's saying, but I think there's another message here for us---with what we know about godhood, and about the roles and responsibilties of the Father and the Son, I think Christ is also saying that he is fulfilling the proper role and that we can know that the doctrine he teaches really does come from the Father and is the one we need to participate in the same plan. That's not as clear as I want it, but I think the idea is there.

\subsection{Economy} % *ECONOMY
% -----------------------

	1828:
		1. Primarily, the management, regulation and government of a family or the concerns of a household.
		2. The management of pecuniary concerns or the expenditure of money. Hence,
		3. A frugal and judicious use of money; that management which expends money to advantage, and incurs no waste; frugality in the necessary expenditure of money. It differs from parsimony, which implies an improper saving of expense. economy includes also a prudent management of all the means by which property is saved or accumulated; a judicious application of time, of labor, and of the instruments of labor.
		4. The disposition or arrangement of any work; as the economy of a poem.
		5. A system of rules, regulations, rites and ceremonies; as the Jewish economy
		6. The regular operation of nature in the generation, nutrition and preservation of animals or plants; as animal economy; vegetable economy
		7. Distribution or due order of things.
		8. Judicious and frugal management of public affairs; as political economy
		9. System of management; general regulation and disposition of the affairs of a state or nation, or of any department of government.

\subsection{Element} % *ELEMENT
% -----------------------

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Native element} % *NATIVEELEMENT
	% -----
	
		This is a topic related to the ultimate fate of the sons of perdition.
		
		\begin{description}
		\item[2N 2:11--16] (In accordance with the discussion with Openshaw, perhaps see this scriptures as a basis for what the ``return to native element'' quotes mean; or these would be like an elaboration. Loss of eternal identity destroys the purposes of God because an undifferentiated stuff can't choose eternal life; it has no agency; since it has no light of Christ, it cannot differentiate between evil and good, and so cannot act in a way that will move it toward or away from eternal life. And something about this, still to be worked out, has to do with eternal identity.) For it must needs be, that there is an opposition in all things. If not so, my first-born in the wilderness, righteousness could not be brought to pass, neither wickedness, neither holiness nor misery, neither good nor bad. Wherefore, all things must needs be a compound in one; wherefore, if it should be one body it must needs remain as dead, having no life neither death, nor corruption nor incorruption, happiness nor misery, neither sense nor insensibility. 12 Wherefore, it must needs have been created for a thing of naught; wherefore there would have been no purpose in the end of its creation. Wherefore, this thing must needs destroy the wisdom of God and his eternal purposes, and also the power, and the mercy, and the justice of God. 12 Wherefore, it must needs have been created for a thing of naught; wherefore there would have been no purpose in the end of its creation. Wherefore, this thing must needs destroy the wisdom of God and his eternal purposes, and also the power, and the mercy, and the justice of God. 13 And if ye shall say there is no law, ye shall also say there is no sin. If ye shall say there is no sin, ye shall also say there is no righteousness. And if there be no righteousness there be no happiness. And if there be no righteousness nor happiness there be no punishment nor misery. And if these things are not there is no God. And if there is no God we are not, neither the earth; for there could have been no creation of things, neither to act nor to be acted upon; wherefore, all things must have vanished away. 14 And now, my sons, I speak unto you these things for your profit and learning; for there is a God, and he hath created all things, both the heavens and the earth, and all things that in them are, both things to act and things to be acted upon. 15 And to bring about his eternal purposes in the end of man, after he had created our first parents, and the beasts of the field and the fowls of the air, and in fine, all things which are created, it must needs be that there was an opposition; even the forbidden fruit in opposition to the tree of life; the one being sweet and the other bitter. 16 Wherefore, the Lord God gave unto man that he should act for himself. Wherefore, man could not act for himself save it should be that he was enticed by the one or the other.
		\item[PPP, \textit{Key}, 38] (He's speaking about air here, as a way of introducing the topic of the Holy Spirit.) The one part, retained and incorporated in the animal system, diffuses life and animation, by supplying the necessary animal heat, \&c., while the other part, not adapted to the system, is discharged from the lungs to mingle with its native element.
		\item[OJBYD 35] In the Evening the President discoursed to a few present upon the subject, that goodness resulted in eternal lives, and wickedness gradually became weaker and Smaller until it was lost in Element.

			\end{compactdesc}

\subsection{Elijah} % *ELIJAH
% -----------------------

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Blessings, power, calling of Elijah}
	% -----
	
		Clearly related to the endowment and to the priesthood; see WJS 197. This is a topic that needs attention I can't give to it right now.
		
		Note also that on 23 June 1842 JS writes a letter to Willard Richards' wife Jennetta in which he says, about Willard, ``never did I have greater intimacy with any man than with him may the blessings of Elijah crown his head forever and ever'' (PWJS 552). Willard was there at the introduction of the endowment a month and a half before, so I think JS is clearly referring to the endowment blessings here and the priesthood.
		
% -----------------------
\subsection{Elijah Able} % *ELIJAHABLE *ABLEELIJAH
% -----------------------

	From PRA-4 2180: ``Bro Elijah Able gave an outline of his history and experiences during a period of forty years. Of his being in Kirtland. Of his appointment an [sic] ordination as a Seventy, and a member of the 3 rd Quorum. He related some of the sayings of the prophet Joseph who told him that those who were called to the Melchisadec Priesthood and had magnified that calling would be sealed up unto eternal life. Spoke of his being appointed by the Prophet to the calling of an Undertaker in Nauvoo. Of his opportunities and conversations with the Patriarch Father Joseph Smith while watching at his bedside during his last sickness. He related one of the themes on which he dwelt at that time and predicted that the saints would go into the wilderness. Br Abel related many other items of interest'' (Appendix 1, minutes of the seventies).

The devil drove us would be the answer; he might say, well, did you not know that I had power over the devil? Yes, but one said I would not give a jackknife for all Nauvoo, and another said, I would not give a pair of mules for the best farm in Hancock county and I was afraid; would the Lord give an endowment to a people who would be frightened away from their duty?

% -----------------------
\subsection{Entice} % *ENTICE
% -----------------------

	1828:
		1. To incite or instigate, by exciting hope or desire; usually in a bad sense; as, to entice one to evil. Hence, to seduce; to lead astray; to induce to sin, by promises or persuasions.
		2. To tempt; to incite; to urge or lead astray.
		3. To incite; to allure; in a good sense.
		
	``Allure'' 1828: % *ALLURE
		To attempt to draw to; to tempt by the offer of some good, real or apparent; to invite by something flattering or acceptable; as, rewards allure men to brave danger. Sometimes used in a bad sense, to allure to evil; but in this sense entice is more common.
		
	``Incite'' 1828: % *INCITE
		1. To move the mind to action by persuasion or motives presented; to stir up; to rouse; to spur on.
		2. To move to action by impulse or influence.
		3. To animate; to encourage.

	\item[2N 26:32] And again, the Lord God hath commanded that men should not murder; that they should not lie; that they should not steal; that they should not take the name of the Lord their God in vain; that they should not envy; that they should not have malice; that they should not contend one with another; that they should not commit whoredoms; and that they should do none of these things; for whoso doeth them shall perish.
	\item[OJBYD 29--30] President Young made a few remarks to some brethren on the subject of Jealousy, which Existed with some men in regard to their filling Offices. He observed that a man might be able to fill the Office of Bishop; and be unfit for a President. Yet the Bishop might feel he was fully qualified for the position of President; the same darkness in his mind which disqualified him \sout{of} for the Office of President; also prevented him from discerning his incapability for wisely filling that office.
	\item[OJBYD 32] Bro Cyrus Wheelock...also had some conversation with the Pres. about the jealous feeling that Exist among men. Pres. remarked [that] many of our feelings would be removed if we were to associate more together; and that course did not remove them immediately, continue to do so, and perhaps it would; any how matters would end right with the faithful
	\end{description}
	
% -----------------------
\subsection{Epistemology of revelation} % *EPISTOFREV *EPISTEMOLOGYOFREVELATION *REVELATIONEPISTEMOLOGY
% -----------------------

	The most important scriptures on this topic, I think, are Al 12:9--11.
	
	See also my notes on the levels principle.
	
	Interesting example to follow is the children-in-the-resurrection idea (see note under ``resurrection''), since it isn't a very clear one and there are old and contemporary views on it.
	
	Some basic points:
	
	\begin{compactitem}
	\item Obedience is essential to receive spiritual perception and knowledge.
	\item There's a hierarchy which determines who can receive legitimate revelation for whom.
		\begin{compactitem}
		\item Some of this at least is due to the observation in DC 46:13--14, where some people people by the Holy Ghost, and others believe their words. The hierarchy isn't just for keeping order; it may just be necessary because some people will only believe on the words of those who bear testimony. There's something here, I think, but I don't think I'm really describing it in the best way.
		\item Another part of this is about general doctrinal matters; see top paragraph of TPJS 24, where JS says that the Lord never ``authorized'' certain people to understand or preach certain things.
		\item Every person is authorized to get revelation to guide himself/herself; see CDBY 54 for two very clear examples of this. So a question with the Holy Ghost arises---will this revelation ever lead us out of the church? Could that happen? Is it possible? I believe it is.
		\end{compactitem} 
	\item People can get manifestations for themselves about many things.
	\item Other things you can only know when you are ordained unto a certain fate; see TPJS 24, top paragraph on that page, about the fate of the devil and his angels and sons of perdition. See Morm 6:22 for a scriptural example.
	\item The epistemology of revelation, at least in part, determines how the church is organized; the organization of the church is a partially an epistemic organization, or organized in a way as to facilitate an epistemic structure for administering God's word to the people on earth.
	\item There are some things we can \textit{only} learn by revelation; it will be important to get clear on what that means exactly.
	\end{compactitem}
	
	Longer discourses on this topic:
	
	\begin{compactitem}
	\item Brigham Young, October 6 1844, CDBY 53--56
	\item Dallin Oaks, the beginning of his talk in general conference on October 6, 2018
	\end{compactitem}
	
	Secondary sources (secondary to the scriptures and JS, BY, and other prophets/apostles):
	
		\begin{compactitem}
		\item John Locke, chapters 18 and 19 of his Essay
		\end{compactitem}

	Some other (longer) thoughts of my own:
	
		\begin{compactitem}
		\item Maybe we should say there is only one critical distinction in the kinds of knowledge: knowledge you learn by experience---not necessarily ``empirical'' in the traditional way of thinking about that, but learning by \textit{living} it. The other kind of knowledge is knowledge you learn by not-living---testimony (in the social-epistemic sense), reading about it, or whatever. The role of the Holy Ghost is to take the latter kind and turn it into the former kind for us, since from the perspective of the gospel the latter kind is the only one that matters.
			\begin{compactitem}
			\item On this see D. Todd Christofferson, October 2015: ``In the Church we not only learn divine doctrine; we also experience its application. As the body of Christ, the members of the Church minister to one another in the reality of day-to-day life. All of us are imperfect; we may offend and be offended. We often test one another with our personal idiosyncrasies. In the body of Christ, we have to go beyond concepts and exalted words and have a real ``hands-on'' experience as we learn to ``live together in love.''''
			\end{compactitem}
		\end{compactitem}

	\begin{description}
	\item[DC 51:9] And let every man deal honestly, and be alike among this people, and receive alike, that ye may be one, even as I have commanded you.
	\item[TPJS 49] We deem it a just principle, and it is one the force of which we believe ought to be duly considered by every individual, that all men are created equal, and that all have the privilege of thinking for themselves upon all matters relative to conscience. Consequently, then, we are not disposed, had we the power, to deprive any one of exercising that free independence of mind which heaven has so graciously bestowed upon the human family as one of its choicest gifts
	\end{description}

\subsection{Eternity} % *ETERNITY
% -----------------------

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Finite eternity}
	% -----

		Here are a few quotes on the idea of eternity having an end, or of eternity being a finite (though very long) duration of time:

		\begin{compactdesc}
		\item[Enos 1:23] And there was nothing save it was...continually reminding them of death, and \textit{the duration of eternity}, and the judgments and power of God, and all these things...would keep them from going down speedily to destruction.
		\item[Mor 8:16--18] (Just an example of from/to all eternity, as referring to the timeless states before and after this life; but also, could God's role change after this eternity?) Wo be unto them that shall pervert the ways of the Lord after this manner, for they shall perish except they repent. Behold, I speak with boldness, having authority from God; and I fear not what man can do; for perfect love casteth out all fear. 17 And I am filled with charity, which is everlasting love; wherefore, all children are alike unto me; wherefore, I love little children with a perfect love; and they are all alike and partakers of salvation. 18 For I know that God is not a partial God, neither a changeable being; but he is unchangeable from all eternity to all eternity.
		\item[DC 39:22] And he that receiveth these things receiveth me; and they shall be gathered unto me in time and in eternity.
		\item[W. W. Phelps, TS 5.24.758] (Originally in a letter to William Smith, written December 25, 1844, published later in the \textit{Times and Seasons}.) Well, now, Brother William, when the house of Israel begin to come into the glorious mysteries of the kingdom, and find that Jesus Christ, whose goings forth, as the prophets said, have been from of old, from eternity: and that eternity, agreeably to the records found in the catacombs of Egypt, has been going on in this system, (not this world) almost \textit{two thousand five hundred and fifty five millions of years}: and to know at the same time, that deists, geologists and others are trying to prove that matter must have existed hundreds of thousands of years; it almost tempts the flesh to fly to God, or muster faith like Enoch to be translated and see and know as we are seen and known!
		\item[Lorenzo Snow] (Lorenzo Snow, quoted by Hyrum Andrus, who gives the source as follows with a note: Lorenzo Snow Papers. Historical Department of the Church. Box 3, folder 6. June 1. 1901. In the report of his reminiscence. President Snow was said to have given the length of an eternity as ``somewhere in the neighborhood of 250.000 years.'' This is at variance with the statement of Elder Phelps written shortly after the death of Joseph Smith, and with President Snow's own statement that the number of years was vast and can scarcely be counted.) I remember once being in the office in Nauvoo where President Joseph Smith and some other brethren got to talking about the length of an Eternity. One of the brethren [Andrus' note: ``no doubt William W. Phelps''] went to work and managed to get the number of years that composed an Eternity...President Smith said that was correct. The number of years was vast and can scarcely be counted. Eternities have a beginning and an end. One eternity commences, and that has an end, and so on --eternities upon eternities.
		\end{compactdesc}

\subsection{Expedient} % *EXPEDIENT
% -----------------------

	An important, if not common, word in the scriptures.
	
	1828:
		1. Literally, hastening; urging forward. Hence, tending to promote the object proposed; fit or suitable for the purpose; proper under the circumstances.
		2. Useful; profitable.
		
	OED:
		Hasty, ‘expeditious', speedy. Also, of a march: Direct. Obs.
		Conducive to advantage in general, or to a definite purpose; fit, proper, or suitable to the circumstances of the case. Const. for, to.
		In depreciative sense, ‘useful' or ‘politic' as opposed to ‘just' or ‘right'. Often absol.
		Studious of ‘expediency'.
		Something that helps forward, or that conduces to an object; a means to an end. Obs. rare.
		A medium or means of reconciliation. Obs.
		A contrivance or device adopted for attaining an end; a resource, ‘shift'.
	
	NT:
		7 times.
			3 uses in Jn, all 3 are \textgreek{sumf'erw}.
			2 uses in 1Co, both are \textgreek{sumf'erw}.
			2 uses in 2Co, both are \textgreek{sumf'erw}. Note that the KJV translation of 2Co 12:1 is wrong.
	BOM:
		62 times.
	DC:
		44 times.

% -----------------------
\subsection{Faith} % *FAITH
% -----------------------

	According to the original Wentworth Letter, the original articles of faith, faith is an ordinance (JSP-H1:500). Andrus's thought about this is that the action accompanying the ordinance of faith is offering a broken heart and a contrite spirit, as in 3N 9:19--20; you could also understand this to be the action for the ordinance of repentance.
	
	In the lectures on faith, faith is described as the motive power of all intelligent beings; seems like we're missing a desire component. The desire component could be hope; see Mor 7:40, no faith without hope. The intellectual component is faith; the desire component is hope; and the component which should characterize our actions, both toward ourselves and others, is charity. Charity shows \textit{how} to put the knowledge and desire into action---how to channel them.
		Though see TPJS 49: ``The fact admitted that certain laws are good, equitable and just, ought to be binding upon the individual who admits this, and lead him to observe in the strictest manner an obedience to those laws.'' The intellectual recognition is here thought sufficient to produce action (obedience).
	
	So faith, hope, and charity are like the basis of the moral psychology for living the gospel. For the gospel to apply to you you have to be ablet to have faith, hope, and charity in these senses. That is, for the gospel to apply to someone human, those things must be there; if any are missing, the application of the gospel may change.
	Faith gives the content of the belief and reasons to think it is true. Such reasons are the well-foundedness of hope. See ``hope'' as well. It's a cycle, though. Faith and hope and charity manifest themselves in a cyclical way in our lives, one after another, over and over again.
	
	Note that Eth 12:32 says a that ``a man must hope, or he cannot receive an inheritance in the place which thou hast prepared.'' Bolsters the idea that hope is necessary, that faith isn't enough of a moving power.
	
	``Faith is things which are hoped for and not seen'' (Eth 12:6). I would gloss it as, faith has to do with things that you don't see, but which you hope for.'' And if hope is well-founded desire, then there must be good reasons for desiring these particular things. But the well-foundedness is reasons for the belief, and that is the intellectual component of faith; so maybe read this line as, ``faith gives the justification for the things that you desire but don't see.''
	There's also a very clear devaluing of the empirical or perceptual experience here---the verse before this says that the people Ether preached to didn't believe because they didn't see. Al 32:21 also mentions this. It's like the BOM is trying to convince us that there are things going on in the world that don't come under our awareness; we can't see them, we have to experience them or come to know them in other ways. But note Eth 12:19, the perceptual witness comes. Maybe eventually we'll get it (the witness in 12:6 doesn't have to be perceptual in every case I think). Then think of Eth 3:19, ``he had faith no longer,'' after he has the perceptual witness. So faith seems to be particularly interested in sincere assent and content that we can't access perceptually.
	I remember that Derek Staples said once that we came to earth to learn to ``walk by faith.'' Other people say that too. I don't know exactly what they mean but maybe it's that we need to practice receiving and accepting and believing these non-perceptual, more spiritual justifications, because those are the ones that we're going to have in the future; we'll have enhanced perceptual capacities, but learning by the Spirit is going to become even more important down the road.
	
	The image I need to get away from having, I think, is of faith as a kind of straining or pushing or forcing yourself to believe, or forcing yourself to will something. I don't think that's the right way to think about it. Think of it instead as the beliefs you have, the content of them, and the reasons or justifications you have for holding those beliefs. That's what faith is about.
	But see Eth 12:19. Think of very strong faith as creating a desire where one wasn't before, or a desire to do something that normally one wouldn't desire to do. There is so much knowledge and the sincere assent is so powerful that a new kind of desire comes into being that wasn't really there anymore. Maybe. A cleaner or purer desire here, maybe; see Al 5:12, but especially Eth 12:4---maybe this is the special kind of hope (well-founded desire) which arises from faith. See quotes at new birth about how we won't desire to sin any longer. That can come from a new faith-born desire and also from the cleansing of our current desires (whatever that means).
	
	Another benefit of thinking of faith as the intellectual component of belief is that it fits really well with the levels principle. See note at levels for 2N 27:23.
	
	Another part of faith, besides the content/reasons thing---the actual assent of our minds, the question of \textit{whether} we actually believe. Very important. Call it ``sincere assent.'' Assent, because we actually believe it; sincere, because it has to be what we really truly believe, deep down, where maybe only God can see. For example I can spend my whole life thinking that Nicholas Cage is a good actor, and can tell people that, join his fan club, write cool blog posts about him, and all that. But deep down I wouldn't really believe it; I'd be living a lie. I'd have the assent part but not the sincere part. 
	Assent doesn't have to be outward either.
	This also should make us careful of looking at people who struggle with belief and taking that to be a moral failing of theirs. It could be---they could choose to believe more---but not everyone can choose to believe. That's a consequence of having a physical brain I think.
		For sincere assent, see DC 52:36; 58:59; 67:3; 80:4; 90:24; Gen 20:5--6; DC 124:15; 
	
	So when you think about faith, make sure you get both parts---the sincere assent part, as well as the intellectual component, the content and reasons for belief. It seems like the latter part is often what we're missing when we talk about faith. Al 12:28--30 has both parts. God set the rules, then needed to send angels to tell men what the rules were and what the truth was (he gave them the intellectual component part of faith); apparently it needed to be kind of impressive, because they beheld ``of his glory''; then they started to act and he made known to them more of the plan, based on their faith (sincere assent). See also Al 32:22--23---in the first place we need to believe, and angels impart the word.
	
	Note that Eth 12:12 looks like it's talking more about faith in true things (sincere assent to true propositions about God and the plan of salvation). But be careful because I don't think it's always being used like this---you have to look at each use individually to see what role it's playing. In Eth 12:12 for example the two mentions of faith might be covering different aspects of what faith actually is.
	
	Faith has to be related to desire in some way---see DC 10:46--50, where desires are granted according to faith, and Al 29:1--5, where desire only is mentioned. Not very clear mysef on this right now.

% -----------------------
\subsection{Familiar} % *FAMILIAR
% -----------------------

	Important for Jac 2:17, for example.
	
	1828:
		1. Pertaining to a family; domestic.
		2. Accustomed by frequent converse; well acquainted with; intimate; close; as a familiar friend or companion.
		3. Affable; not formal or distant; easy in conversation.
		Be thou familiar but by no means vulgar.
		4. Well acquainted with; knowing by frequent use. Be familiar with the scriptures.
		5. Well known; learned or well understood by frequent use. Let the scriptures be familiar to us.
		6. Unceremonious; free; unconstrained; easy. The emperor conversed with the gentleman in the most familiar manner.
		7. Common; frequent and intimate. By familiar intercourse, strong attachments are soon formed.
		8. Easy; unconstrained; not formal. His letters are written in a familiar style.
		
	Also interesting is 2N 26:16, ``familiar spirit.'' % *FAMILIARSPIRIT
	From the OED for that phrase: ``a spirit, often taking the form of an animal, which obeys and assists a witch or other person.'' Related to that phrase is a noun form of ``familiar,'' as ``A spirit, often taking the form of an animal, which obeys and assists a witch or other person.'' The dictionary adds that ``Familiars are particularly associated with early European witchcraft, where they were generally considered to be evil spirits. In the context of shamanism, a familiar is a spirit which assists the shaman in healing and other rituals.''
		Cf. definition 2 from 1828 for the noun form: ``A demon or evil spirit supposed to attend at a call. But in general we say, a `familiar spirit'.''
		This verse in 2N 26 is quoting from Isa 29:4, where the word is \he{'Ob}. From DCH pdf 148: ``ghost---ghost, in contexts of divination, but perh. sometimes medium, necromancer, i.e. one who consults a ghost.''
		Quinn talks about this in \textit{EMMWV} 152--153:
			``Centuries before 1830, the words "familiar spirit" referred only to necromancy (OED 4:54, no. 3). The New York editions of Adam Clarke's commentary in the early 1800s observed, concerning Isaiah 29:4, "The pretenders to the art of necromancy, who were chiefly women, had an art of speaking with a reigned voice...they could make the voice seem to come from beneath the ground" (1811, s.v. Isa. 29:4), and Webster's 1828 unabridged dictionary gave the second definition of "familiar" as a noun: "A demon or evil spirit supposed to attend at a call. But in a general way we say, a familiar spirit" (N. Webster 1828, s.v. "Familiar," emphasis in original). Although the term was often used negatively, a divine [p.153] connotation was also possible within magic: "The same Boissardus writes, that an Illustrious German Count, whom he knew, profest, he had a Familiar Spirit [i.e., guardian angel], whom he affirm'd to be of the Celestial Order, whose Counsel he used in all things he undertook, at home and abroad" (Beaumont 1705, 63, emphasis in original). "Familiar spirit" could also designate elemental spirits such as salamanders (R. Walker 1984, 432). The Book of Mormon's use of Isaiah 29:4 to describe its own coming forth through Smith was consistent with the Smith family's magic parchments of spirit invocation and with early testimony that the otherworldly messenger Moroni introduced the book to Smith by appearing as a spirit three times. Within a magic setting, the Book of Mormon would have proclaimed itself the fulfillment of a biblical prophecy concerning divinely appointed necromancy, or psychomancy---divination through communication with spirits of the dead.''

Behold, in the day of your fast ye find pleasure, and exact all your labours. 4 Behold, ye fast for strife and debate, and to smite with the fist of wickedness: ye shall not fast as ye do this day, to make your voice to be heard on high. 5 Is it such a fast that I have chosen? a day for a man to afflict his soul? is it to bow down his head as a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? wilt thou call this a fast, and an acceptable day to the LORD? 6 Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke? 7 Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh? 8 Then shall thy light break forth as the morning, and thine health shall spring forth speedily: and thy righteousness shall go before thee; the glory of the LORD shall be thy rereward. 9 Then shalt thou call, and the LORD shall answer; thou shalt cry, and he shall say, Here I am. % -----------------------
\subsection{First fruits} % *FIRSTFRUITS
% -----------------------

	In 2N 2:9, referring to Christ, he is the ``firstfruits \textit{unto} God,'' not ``of God'' or ``for God.''
	And being the ``firstfruits'' of anything is being the first mature product of some process. Here the process is the entire current iteration of the plan of salvation, and Christ is the first that is resurrected (and perfected) (2N 2:8), and is therefore the firstfruits of the perfecting and exalting process.

	\item[CDBY 36] We have the honor to be the first fruits of this dispensation, and have to contend with floods of oppression.
	\item[CDBY 37] O ye Elders of Israel, you are the first fruits of the kingdom of God on the earth that is to swallow up all other kingdoms on earth.
	\end{description}

% -----------------------
\subsection{Forgiveness} % *FORGIVENESS
% -----------------------

	Lately I have been thinking about forgiveness and when it comes. The scriptures are fairly clear on this point--I am forgiven as I obey the commandments. ``He that repents and does the commandments of the Lord shall be forgiven'' (DC 1:32), ``And the fulfilling the commandments bringeth remission of sins'' (Moroni 8:25). So, receiving forgiveness for sins is another blessing of keeping the commandments. I've been thinking about this because I've been reflecting on my preparation to take the sacrament every Sunday. In my prayers I have been acting as though forgiveness can come at the moment of taking the sacrament, but I've been wondering if that is actually the case. However, in 3 Nephi 18:10 Christ says, speaking of taking the sacrament, ``this is fulfilling my commandments.'' So there is some scriptural justification for doing what I do. But I would like to know more about this. The knowledge that forgiveness comes as one obeys the commandments is a strong motivation to obey them. For me it's a strong motivation to try and keep them willingly, for the right reasons, with a good attitude. But I want to look into this more. I want to understand more of the process described in Alma 24:10-11, where the people have had their guilt and sins removed by Christ.

	What connection is there between forgiveness/remission of sins and the priesthood?

	The promise of the sacrament prayers is that we will receive the Spirit, that we will ``[always] have his Spirit to be with [us].'' There are three elements here:

	\begin{enumerate}
	\item We take the bread and the water in remembrance of Jesus Christ,
	\item We show to God that we (a) are willing to take upon ourselves the name of his Son, (b) that we are willing to always remember him, and (c) that we are willing to keep his commandments,
	\item This is done that we may always have the Spirit to be with us.
	\end{enumerate}

	Forgiveness of sins doesn't show up anywhere here, even as a promise or as the result of taking the sacrament. I connect the result of taking the sacrament (the promise of the Spirit) more with Moroni 8:25-26 and the visitation of the Holy Ghost. In that visitation, the purpose of the Holy Ghost is to fill us with ``hope and perfect love.'' We need perfect love (charity) because without it we ``cannot inherit'' our place in the mansions of the Father (Ether 12:34). So in this reading the sacrament plays a facilatory role: it helps us receive the Spirit so that we may gain perfect love. In fact, the remission of sins appears here to also play a facilatory role: when we feel it, or understand that we have received it, we feel meekness and lowliness of heart also. Those feelings (``because of'' them) allow the visitation of the Holy Ghost, and he fills us with hope and perfect love. But in order to understand this more I need to answer some more questions: What is the remission of sins? Is it a feeling we receive, or some piece of knowledge, or what? Are ``meekness'' and ``lowliness of heart'' emotions or something else? What are the other possibilities? One could ask the same question about perfect love (charity), hope, and other things which we describe by the vague term ``qualities.'' See TG Remission (of sins) for more here.

	Although both are important the second question seems particularly so because we need to receive the visitation of the Holy Ghost. And this is all pertinent to the priesthood because it is clear we must become something in order to obtain the blessings of the priesthood--going through the motions will not do.

	What is the remission of sins? Is it a feeling we receive, or some piece of knowledge, or what?

	What is the connection between remission of sins and justification?
	
	\begin{description}

And it came to pass that they did so. And after they had done praying unto the Lord we did again travel on our journey towards the tent of our father.

When the son hath done that which is lawful and right, and hath kept all my statutes, and hath done them, he shall surely live. 20 The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him. 21 But if the wicked will turn from all his sins that he hath committed, and keep all my statutes, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live, he shall not die. 22 All his transgressions that he hath committed, they shall not be mentioned unto him: in his righteousness that he hath done he shall live. 23 Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord GOD: and not that he should return from his ways, and live? 24 ¶ But when the righteous turneth away from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity, and doeth according to all the abominations that the wicked man doeth, shall he live? \subsection{Gain} % *GAIN
% -----------------------

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Uses in the NT}
	% -----

		A form of the word \textit{gain} (noun or verb) appears 26 times in the NT. Here's the breakdown.

		\begin{compactdesc}

		\item[\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{kerda'inw}}] 14 times as \textit{gain} (verb). 17 times total. Also translated as win (2) and make (1).

		\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{kerda'inw}} means ``to acquire by effort or investment, \textit{to gain}; [since the avoidance of loss is a gain, can also mean] \textit{spare oneself something, avoid something}.''

		\item[\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>ergas'ia}}] 3 times as \textit{gain} (noun). 6 times total. Also translated as diligence (1), craft (1), and working (1).

		\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>erga'ia}} means ``engagement in some activity or behavior with sustained interest, \textit{practice, pursuit}; manner of activity, \textit{working, function}; business activity, \textit{trade, business}; proceeds of work or activity, \textit{profit, gain}.''

		\item[\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{pleonekt'ew}}] 2 times as \textit{make a gain} (verb + noun). 5 times total. Also translated as defraud (2) and get an advantage (1).

		\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{pleonekt'ew}} means ``to take advantage of, \textit{exploit, outwit, defraud, cheat}.''

		\item[\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{k'erdos}}] 2 times as \textit{gain} (noun). 3 times total. Also translated as lucre (1).

		\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{k'erdos}} means ``that which is gained or earned, \textit{a gain, profit}.''

		\item[\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{porism'os}}] 2 times as \textit{gain} (noun). 2 times total.

		\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{porism'os}} means ``means of gain.''

		\item[\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{diapragmate'uomai}}] 1 time as \textit{gain by trade} (verb).

		\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{diapragmate'uomai}} means ``\textit{gain by trading, earn}.''

		\item[\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{proserg'azomai}}] 1 time as \textit{gain} (verb). 1 time total.

		\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{proserg'azomai}} means ``to earn in addition, \textit{make more}.''

		\item[\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{poi'ew}}] 1 time as \textit{gain} (verb). 568 times total, translated as many English words. This Greek word is translated as \textit{gain} in Lk 19:18.

		\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{poi'ew}} means generally ``to do or make,'' but also has many senses that branch off of those meanings.

		\end{compactdesc}

	% -----
	\subsubsection*{Uses in the BOM}
	% -----

		The word \textit{gain} appears 63 times in the BOM. 35 of these instances are as a verb, and 28 are as a noun.

		\paragraph*{Gain as verb.}The word \textit{gain} appears as a verb 34 times in the BOM.

		\paragraph*{Gain as noun.}The word \textit{gain} appears as a noun 28 times in the BOM. Here's a list with some information about the different uses.

		\begin{compactdesc}
		\item[GET, SEEK, or DESIROUS FOR gain] 24 of 28 uses. 1N 22:23; 2N 26:20, 29; 27:16; Mo 29:40; Al 10:32 (2); 11:20; 30:35a; Hel 6:8, 17 (2); 7:5, 21; 3N 29:7; 4N 1:26; Morm 8:14, 33, 40; Eth 8:22, 23; Eth 9:11; 10:22; 11:15.

		A full 86\% of uses of the noun \textit{gain} in the BOM focus attention on the process and obsession of \textit{getting} it. In this use \textit{gain} must mean something like ``increase of material wealth or social status.'' But it isn't just that; there's a negative connotation here, a focus on that process and obsession, that the BOM views as spiritually harmful or sinful.

		\item[INCREASE in MATERIAL things] 2 of 28 uses. Al 30:35b; 3N 20:19.

		Al 30:35 is included here because that's Alma responding to Korihor. The first use in the verse is what Korihor is accusing, and Alma respond: ``Then why sayest thou that we preach unto this people to get gain, when thou, of thyself, knowest that we receive no gain?'' I don't think that the second use needs to be included in the first group above. Although there is a \textit{get} here earlier, there isn't one directly preceding this occurrence of \textit{gain}. It isn't clear whether Alma is thinking only of an increase in wealth, in a more neutral sense, or whether he also wants to bring attention to the process/obsession with getting it.

		3N 20:19 is a quote from Micah; see the note at \textbf{TG Consecrate $\rightarrow$ BOM Uses}. The Hebrew word translated as \textit{gain} is \textcolor{red}{\<b*E.sa`>}, which in my reader's bible means ``gain; gain made by violence.'' I do not include it in the first group here because it doesn't have the \textit{get} focus and because it's a quote from an OT source.

		\item[GAIN of an individual or group] 2 of 28 uses. 2N 2:2; 2N 33:4.

		These are the only two uses which have a clearly positive connotation in the BOM. Both occur with the verb \textit{consecrate}; I won't go into that here, but see \textbf{TG Consecrate $\rightarrow$ BOM Uses}. God can consecrate our difficulties and challenges (2N 2:2) as well as our spiritual actions (2N 33:4) for the benefit of ourselves as well as others.

		Also, I think that we can draw a link between this meaning of \textit{gain} and the phrase \textit{welfare of soul} which appears 7 times in the BOM (see \textbf{TG Welfare $\rightarrow$ Welfare of the soul}). In 2N 32:9, Nephi says that if we pray before performing something for the Lord, He will consecrate our performance for the \textit{welfare of thy soul}. Just a few verses later, in 33:4, Nephi notes that the Lord will consecrate his own prayers for the \textit{gain} of his people. Similarly, after Enos is forgive of his sins, he begins to feel a desire for the \textit{welfare} of his brothers, and starts to pray for them. We don't get \textit{consecrate} or \textit{gain} in that verse, but the idea of the spiritual \textit{welfare} of someone is what is meant by this positive use of \textit{gain}, I think. It's someone spiritual status--someone's ability to experience a spiritual life and repent, and experience the blessings of the gospel and the Atonement.
		\end{compactdesc}

\subsection{George Laub} % *GEORGELAUB
% -----------------------

	I have two of Laub's journals in my archive. Here's a bit of information. I've requested digitization of the third volume, MS 1983---``A volume containing Laub's later revision of the entries through 1846 is cataloged as MS 1983.''
		George Laub Journal 1: MS 9628
			Summary: Summary of Laub's early life and conversion to the Church in Pennsylvania, his experiences in Nauvoo, and events at the time of the death of Joseph Smith.
			Includes sporadic entries for 1845-1852 concerning Laub's departure from Nauvoo and experiences in crossing the plains, including his stay in Platte County, Missouri, and daily entries for May-August 1852 recording his his journey to Utah.
			Also includes summary entries for 1853-1856 and daily entries for March-April 1857 recording Laub's farming and building activities in Salt Lake City and attendance at church meetings.
			Laub also includes synopses of sermons in Nauvoo given by Joseph Smith, Brigham Young, Hyrum Smith, and Heber C. Kimball, and synopses of sermons in Salt Lake City given by Brigham Young and Heber C. Kimball.
			There is also information concerning Laub's experiences as an adopted son of John D. Lee, the Reformation movement of 1856-1857, and Laub family genealogy.
			A volume containing Laub's later revision of the entries through 1846 is cataloged as MS 1983.
		George Laub Journal 2: MS 20209
			Summary: Account of Laub's activities in Salt Lake City, including attendance at various church meetings and carpentry work done for Brigham Young and Isaac Chase.
			Details events surrounding Mormon preparations for the US army's arrival (Utah War), including grain storage and exploration of mountain refuges. Also records activities of the Utah Militia (Nauvoo Legion), including Laub's own military service in Echo Canyon.
			Volume also includes Laub's synopses of speeches by Brigham Young, Heber C. Kimball, and other Church leaders, including at April conference and at 24th July celebration in Big Cottonwood Canyon.

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Goodness of} % *GODGOODNESS
	% -----
	
		See written notes in large triple at 2N 4:21 for the start of this idea. See 2N 26:7 as well.
			See also ``divine influence.''

		Goodness as the uniting force behind the various manifestations of God? See Al 12:32 for justice; Al 19:6 for light and glory; 2Ch 7:1--3 and 10 for glory, though the connection is loose; For charity, see (a bit circuitous, but...) Mor 7:48 (we pray with all energy and are filled with ``this love'' [charity], so that we can be purified) and 3N 19:25--28 (the people pray, are transfigured and purified, and it looks like they've received charity, if we take the glorified influence of Christ to be a general power that emanates from him)---I know this one is a stretch but these scriptures are nicely connected; Eth 4:11--12; Eth 12:41 talks about the grace abiding in us forever, similar to the word getting in us (so ``word'' would be a very general term for this influence as well, and that fits nicely with Christ as the ``word'' and how he will be in us as the father is in him); see note on ``possessed of it'' at Mor 7:47 for charity and this influence (see also 48; charity is love, so this influence is love, and we're filled with it; see also Mor 8:26, where this filling with chraity is maintained by prayer ``until the end shall come, when all the saints shall dwell with God''---why only until then? Because we'll be in his presence, and will be filled with his influence more easily some other way? In 48, we become the sons of God with this influence; this influence, however we explain it, is closely connected to the new birth and being cleansed---we become new creatures); 1N 11:22 and 25; 1N 17:47 sayas that Nephi is full of the Spirit of God, and the next verse says he's filled with the power of God; 2N 1:26--27 also describes this experience;
		
		Other scriptures important to this topic might be: 3N 7:21--22 (``power and Spirit of God'' is interesting, and in the next verse, the people are ``wrought upon'' by the Spirit---other uses of ``wrought'' like that, or ``work,'' with some other word?); Morm 1:15, where Mormon ``tasted'' and ``knew'' of the ``goodness'' of God; 1N 1:1, Nephi has a similar experience; 1N 2:14; light and truth are all the same?; 2N 26:28 and 33; Jac 3:2 for love/word (especially feasting on love vs. feasting on word); DC 33:16 (power of the Lord's spirit quickens everything; see ``powers''); DC 95:12; Mic 3:8; 
		
		See also goodness as constituting truth (under ``truth'') for more on this idea.

		\item[Isaac Newton] He rules all things, not as the world soul but as the lord of all. And because of his dominion he is called Lord God Pantokrator [i.e. universal ruler]. For god' is a relative word and has reference to servants, and godhood is the lordship of God, not over his own body as is supposed by those for whom God is the world soul, but over servants. The supreme God is an eternal, infinite, and absolutely perfect being; but a being, however perfect, without dominion is not the Lord God. For we do say my God, your God, the God of Israel, the God of Gods, and Lord of Lords, but we do not say my eternal one, your eternal one, the eternal one of Israel, the eternal one of the gods; we do not say my infinite one, or my perfect one. These designations [i.e. eternal, infinite, perfect] do not have reference to servants. The word ``god'' is used far and wide to mean ``lord,'' but every lord is not a god. The lordship of a spiritual being constitutes a god, a true lordship constitutes a true god, a supreme lordship a supreme god, an imaginary lordship an imaginary god. And from true lordship it follows that the true God is living, intelligent, and powerful; from the other perfections, that he is supreme, or supremely perfect. He is eternal and infinite, omnipotent and omniscient, that is, he endures from eternity to eternity, and he is present from infinity to infinity; he rules all things, and he knows all things that happen or can happen. He is not eternity and infinity, but eternal and infinite; he is not duration and space, but he endures and is present. He endures always and is present everywhere, and by existing always and everywhere he constitutes duration and space. Since each and every particle of space is always, and each and every indivisible moment of duration is everywhere, certainly the maker and lord of all things will not be never or nowhere (Isaac Newton, \textit{Principia}, General Scholium, as quoted in \textit{Philosophical Writings}, ed. Andrew Janiak, 90--91).
		\end{description}

	1828:

		1. A religious life; a careful observance of the laws of God and performance of religious duties, proceeding from love and reverence for the divine character and commands; christian obedience.

\subsection{Gold plates} % *GOLDPLATES
% -----------------------

	Joseph kept them covered; there's a possible parallel in Numbers 4:5--16 with the implements of the tabernacle.
	
	Note that the plates are just another externalized source of inspiration, like the Liahona, the divining rod, the seer stone, the Urim and Thummim, and so on. And externalized sources of inspiration lead to revelation---in this case, a long one, the BOM. But note that there were two externalized sources involved here, the seer stone and the plates. They interacted with Joseph to produce the revelation that is the BOM.

	% -----
	\subsubsection{The difference between good/evil and right/wrong}
	% -----
	
		[Below are preliminary notes for a lesson I have thought about teaching on this topic.]
	
		Scriptures that mention right/wrong:
			Al 7:20; 18:5; DC 9:7--9 (this one may have a more good/evil feel); JS-H 1:8, 10, 18 (these verses in JS-H are about which church is right/wrong)
	
		Ask the question: is there a difference between right/wrong on the one hand, and good/evil on the other hand? What I mean is, we make these distinctions all the time about actions, ideas, people, and so on---is the distinction between right and wrong different from the distinction between good and evil?
			Think about that question for a moment. While you're thinking, I want to read two scriptures which bring out the point of the question.
			The first is in 3N 18:20---Christ has just given the sacrament and is now teaching; In verse 20 he says: ``And whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, which is right, believing that ye shall receive, behold it shall be given unto you.''
			Pretty straightforward I think. Now let's go to Moroni 7, a chapter were Mormon hundreds of years later is writing about a lot of different topics. Let's look at the first part of verse 26: ``And after that he came men also were saved by faith in his name; and by faith, they become the sons of God.''
				So Mormon tells us something about faith and how we enter a new relationship with God. Then the verse continues: ``And as surely as Christ liveth he spake these words unto our fathers...'' 
				Now Mormon is about to report some words that Christ delivered while he was visiting Mormon's ancestors. Let's see what he says:
				``Whatsoever thing ye shall ask the Father in my name, which is good, in faith believing that ye shall receive, behold, it shall be done unto you.''
			So notice what we have here: Mormon reports the words that Christ says in 3N 18:20, but makes one small change. What is it?
		So let's return to the question I asked before we read these scriptures: do you think there is a difference between right and wrong on the one hand, and good and evil on the other hand? Why or why not?

% -----------------------
\subsection{Happiness} % *HAPPINESS
% -----------------------

	Properties of happiness:
	
		\begin{description}
		\item[Long lasting] By its nature, happiness is sustainable and long-lasting, as long as we keep doing the things that bring it.
		\end{description}

	Men are that they might have joy (2 Nephi 2:25). Joy is an emotion which we feel; in the strictest sense of the scriptures, happiness is not an emotion, but a state. ``States'' are combinations of mental, physical, spiritual, emotional (etc.) attitudes and characterizations in which we find ourselves. States are the result of actions and beliefs over a fairly long period of time, although in some circumstances it is possible to change rather quickly. States react with existence in order to produce emotions. In scriptural terms, the state of happiness is that state which is capable of interacting with existence in order to produce joy--and more particularly, a fulness of joy. Happiness has a nature (Alma 41:11). This means that not just any actions or choices will produce a state of happiness; happiness is bound or limited to certain actions and certain choices. The way to achieve happiness is to obey the commandments of God (Mosiah 2:41), or, in other words, the commandments form the framework of the nature of happiness. By following the commandments, we set ourselves in the path which leads to a state of happiness and the greatest joy available to us: Alma 27:18 says, ``Now was not this exceeding joy? Behold, this [i.e. This particular kind of joy] is joy which none receiveth save it be the truly penitent and humble seeker of happiness.'' It is not that the act of obeying the commandments in itself produces joy, although feeling joy while exercising obedience is certainly possible. Rather, it is that the act of obeying the commandments, over a long period of time, produces in ourselves a state of happiness which allows us to become the type of person who is capable of experiencing a fulness of joy.

	\begin{description}
	\item[2N 2:10] And because of the intercession for all, all men come unto God; wherefore, they stand in the presence of him, to be judged of him according to the truth and holiness which is in him. Wherefore, the ends of the law which the Holy One hath given, unto the inflicting of the punishment which is affixed, which punishment that is affixed is in opposition to that of the happiness which is affixed, to answer the ends of the atonement---

% -----------------------
\subsection{Happy delusion argument} % *HAPPYDELUSION
% -----------------------

	The Happy Delusion argument is--if living the gospel makes us happier than living any other way, why not live it, whether it's true or not?

	\begin{description}
	\item[CDBY 36] This doctrine is the best for any man to practice, and will do him good.
	\item[JD 24:220] We know that it is of God. But our enemies say it is a delusion; but if this delusion brings peace and joy and happiness and certainty, and all those feelings that fill our soul with inexpressible delight, why, then we are in a better condition than those who are not thus deluded. But we know that we are not deluded.
	\end{description}
	
% -----------------------
\subsection{Heart} % *HEART
% -----------------------

	At least in the BOM, ``heart'' is often used to refer to the seat of desire. See, for example, Mo 5:2, Al 19:33, Al 5:12--13, etc.
		This use of ``heart'' accords with definition \#7 in the 1828, ``The seat of the will; hence, secret purposes, intentions or designs,'' and definitions \#12 and \#13, ``Disposition of mind'' and ``Secret meaning; real intention.''
	And so a change of heart involves a change of desire, among other things.

	\begin{description}
	\item[DC 64:34] (Lots of other good verses in this section about what's in our hearts, I've just put this one only.) Behold, the Lord requireth the heart and a willing mind; and the willing and obedient shall eat the good of the land of Zion in these last days.
	\end{description}

		An important connection is 3N 9:20 and 22, for broken heart/contrite spirit and being like a child. See also 3N 11:37;
		
		Another important connection here: our hearts have to change in order for us to be born again (see Al 5:7, 12--13 for example), and part of that change is letting the Holy Ghost into our hearts to actually do the changing (Mo 5:2). But we can refuse to let the Holy Ghost in by hardening our hearts (2N 33:1--2). So having a \textit{broken} heart destroys the barrier, breaks down the hardness, and allows the Holy Ghost in to change us. See 2N 4:27--32 as well.

% -----------------------
\subsection{Heavenly Mother} % *HEAVENLYMOTHER *MOTHERINHEAVEN
% -----------------------

	See:
		Rudger Clawson (?), ``Our Mother in Heaven,'' MS 72:616--620.

	\begin{description}
	\item[Erastus Snow, JD 19:273--274] Our tabernacles are formed for our spirits, yes, expressly for our spirits. But why were they not all made alike? Why were they not all made just six feet high? and why were they not all, in every respect, all the same length; limbs, likeness, the same; the same length of an arm? You may just as well ask the tailor, ``Why do you make different sized coats and pants?'' And say to the milliner also, ``Why do you make different sizes of dresses and other garments?'' And their answer is, because I have so many different persons to fit, and I make the garment to fit the person. And that is the answer concerning the tabernacles. They are made to fit the spirits. I say, therefore, that God not only includes within himself the male and female principle, the same as man does, but it also includes the two elements which we call spirit and tabernacle, and these are only comparative terms, to illustrate in a crude way the idea of the two principles, the spirit being of finer material, possessing greater intelligence, more fully developed, and organized for greater and more glorious works.
	\end{description}
	
% -----------------------
\subsection{Hebrew and Joseph Smith} % *HEBREW
% -----------------------

	On November 20 1835 Oliver Cowdery returned to Kirtland from New York with some books on languages, including a Hebrew bible, grammar, and lexicon, and a Greek lexicon. See JSP-J1:107, and note 159 on that page, which gives the probable books. The lexicion ``is probably Josiah M. Gibbs, \textit{A Manual Hebrew and English Lexicon Including the Biblical Chaldee},'' 1832. The note says the grammar is probably Moses Stuart's \textit{A Grammar of the Hebrew Language}, fifth edition, 1835. I have PDFs of both of these in the JS folder. I also have a PDF of Seixas's grammar, which is where you see the translation ``empty and desolate'' for \textit{tohu wbohu} in the creation story, which translation JS adopts between the book of Moses revision and the book of Abraham revision (he learned Hebrew in the meantime).
		Oliver Cowdery wrote in a letter to his brother Warren on November 22 1835, ``Dear Brother: I have been prevented from addressing you of late through a multitude of labor, besides I have just returned from N. Y. city, whither I went to purchase a bookbinding establishment and stock, and also a quantity of Hebrew books for the school.''
		
	Important Hebrew words in the Gibbs lexicon JS might have had:
		\he{bohU}: PDF 40---``emptiness, desolation; a desolate place, a waste.''
		\he{ro'+s}: PDF 211--``a head; the best of its kind; a chief, leader; a chief city, metropolis; the highest place, first rank; the top or highest part, as of a mountain, pillar; the first, in number; the beginning; the sum, whole number; a company, multitude, host; a person, individual.''
		\he{r'+syt}: PDF 211---``a beginning; earlier state; earlier time; the first in its kind, a firstling, firstfruits.''
		\he{tohU}: PDF 242---``emptiness, desolation; a desert; metaphorical, vanity; something vain or of no value; as an adverb, in vain.''

	1828:
		1. To make a sound by driving the breath between the tongue and the upper teeth; to give a strong aspiration, resembling the noise made by a serpent and some other animals, or that of water thrown on hot iron. Hissing is an expression of contempt.
		2. To express contempt or disapprobation by hissing.
		3. To whiz, as an arrow or other thing in rapid flight.

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Epistemology of the Holy Ghost}
	% -----

		Scriptures to see: 2Ti 2:25; 

		As I think about it, the epistemology of the Holy Ghost is the study of the various functions of the Holy Ghost that we observe in the world and in ourselves. The ways, means, and purposes of the Holy Ghost.

		From the fact that the spirit has confirmed X to someone, it does not follow that X is true. What follows is that it is important for that person to believe X in order to progress in their current spiritual state. ONE purpose of the spirit is to reveal truths about the plan of salvation; ANOTHER purpose of the spirit is to help us progress, and in accomplishing this second purpose, it may be the case that certain things are confirmed to us and seem to us to be true. But in fact those confirmations may be instances of the spirit accomplishing the second purpose, not the first.

		If a person says that X has been confirmed by the spirit to them, and another says that Y has been confirmed to them, and X and Y are inconsistent, nothing follows about which is true. Both may be false, or one false and the other true, or vice versa. The spirit cannot adjudicate in those types of disputes; that isn't the purpose of the spirit.

		So maybe we start to list the purposes:

		\begin{enumerate}

		\item The Holy Ghost \textit{manifests truths}.

		\item The Holy Ghost \textit{comforts and consoles}.

		\end{enumerate}

		But into which of these two roles does the function I've described above fall? The Holy Ghost confirms some idea \textit{i} to us, but \textit{i} isn't actually true; it's just that believing and holding on to \textit{i} is part of our current spiritual progress.

		We might think that this falls into the first role if we divide the kinds of truths that the Holy Ghost manifests into two groups:

		\begin{description}

		\item[Group 1: Truths about the plan of salvation] Christ is the redeemer; repentance is necessary; we are children of a Heavenly Father; etc.

		\item[Group 2: Truths about values] \textit{i.e. what's good (in terms of our salvation and spiritual progress) for us to believe and do right now} Women should receive the priesthood; women should not receive the priesthood; I should marry my boyfriend; I should not marry my boyfriend; etc.

		\end{description}

		We could also think that the function I described above falls under the role of comforting--the Holy Ghost encourages/exhorts us by confirming these value-judgments to us, so we feel compelled to act.

		I don't know what the answer is, or if this is even the right way to talk about the roles of the Holy Ghost. But I think that the function I described above is very important, and very important to keep in mind as I gain more experience with the spiritual beliefs and confirmations of other people.

	% -----

		\item A portion to dwell in us to give us power (Al 18:34). This power will be physical, mental, spiritual, emotional, whatever adjectives we like.

This was my experience, and this is the feeling of every one who receives the Gospel in an honest heart and contrite spirit.

% -----------------------
\subsection{Hope} % *HOPE
% -----------------------

	Hope is a \textit{well-founded desire}. ``Desire'' there just means desire; ``well-founded'' means that you have a reason for thinking the desire will be fulfilled. See Mor 7:41, for example, which gives the reason for a certain kind of hope: ``through the Atonement of Christ and the power of his resurrection.'' The atonement makes our desires well-founded---our righteous desires, that is. See Eth 12:8, where Christ's work and the atonement is again cited as allowing others to have hope. See also Alma 32:21---when we have faith we hope for things that are true, and it's easiest to have reasons about true things. See also Eth 12:4, where belief in God allows a hope with ``surety,'' and hope comes ``of faith.'' So the intellectual component, the part that actually gives the content of the belief, leads to hope. There has to be content for the belief and there has to be a reason (the well-founded part); see Mor 7:42, ``without faith there cannot be any hope.''
	
	The idea of a well-founded desire as hope makes sense with Morm 5:2, and maybe also Morm 3:12, where you could see some of the relationship between faith and hope in these two verses. See also Job 7:6.
	
	A clear example of hope as well-founded desire is 2N 33:7--9, where Nephi has faith and charity toward certain people, but can't have hope unless people have been reconciled to Christ.
		See also Jac 2:3 in connection with this, where he talks about his ``desire,'' but makes no mention of ``hope'' because the people have not been very righteous.
			Then follow this up with verse 19 of the same chapter.
			
	Other examples of hope as well-founded desire:
		Jac 4:6: Wherefore, we search the prophets, and we have many revelations and the spirit of prophecy; and having all these witnesses we obtain a hope, and our faith becometh unshaken, insomuch that we truly can command in the name of Jesus and the very trees obey us, or the mountains, or the waves of the sea.''
		Jac 4:11: Wherefore, beloved brethren, be reconciled unto him through the atonement of Christ, his Only Begotten Son, and ye may obtain a resurrection, according to the power of the resurrection which is in Christ, and be presented as the first-fruits of Christ unto God, having faith, and obtained a good hope of glory in him before he manifesteth himself in the flesh.
		DC 138:14: All these had departed the mortal life, firm in the hope of a glorious resurrection, through the grace of God the Father and his Only Begotten Son, Jesus Christ.
		Isa 59:9 (the opposite---the wicked can't have hope): Therefore is judgment far from us, neither doth justice overtake us: we wait for light, but behold obscurity; for brightness, but we walk in darkness.

It is like the riches of the world, or the pleasures of the world, or like human life, and all things here; and it is organized perfectly, according to the condition of human man. Lest some may find fault with the term ``human man,'' I will offer an explanation. Are there any beings not liable to change? Yes, there are millions and millions of them in eternity that have passed through the same ordeals that we are passing through. There are myriads and myriads of kingdoms the same as us in this vale of tears. They have not lost their organization, but are sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor, it is raised in Glory. It is sown in weakness, it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body. Those who pass from mortality to immortality will be as we are, only they have passed from death unto life. This is the difference between a human man and those who have passed through the resurrection.

% -----------------------
\subsection{Intelligence} % *INTELLIGENCE
% -----------------------

	\begin{description}
	\item[MA 3.5.461--462] We are surrounded, on every hand, with minds of various descriptions, which evince the faculties of which they are possessed, by the various senses and active powers with which they are furnished. These minds are various, in point of intellectual capacity and acumen, from man downwards through all the animated tribes which traverse the regions of earth, air, and sea. We have the strongest reason to believe, that the distant regions of the material world are also replenished with intellectual beings, of various orders, in which there may be a gradation upwards, in the scale of intellect above that of a man, as diversified as that which we perceive in the descending scale, from man downwards to the immaterial principle which animates a muscle, a snail, or a microscopic animalcula. When we consider the variety of original forms and of intellectual capacities which abounds in our terrestrial system, and that there is an infinite gap in the scale of being between the human mind and the Supreme Intelligence, it appears quite conformable to the magnificent harmony of the universe, and to the wisdom and benevolence of its Almighty Author, to suppose that there are beings within the range of his dominions as far superior to man in the comprehension and extent of mental and corporeal powers, as man is, in these respects, superior to the most despicable insect: and that these beings, in point of number, may exceed all human calculation and comprehension. This idea is corroborated by several intimations contained in the records of revelation, where we have presented to our view a class of intelligences endowed with physical energies, powers of rapid motion, and a grasp of intellect, incomparably superior to those which are possessed by any of the beings which belong to our sublunary system.
	\item[CDBY 76] But before I undertake to explain or give correct views upon this important subject, I would say to all those who are satisfied with all the knowledge they have, and want no more: to you I do not expect to be an apostle this day; but for those who are hungering and thirsting after righteousness, I pray, that they may be filled and satisfied with \textbf{the intelligence of God, even his glory.}
	\end{description}
