	% -----
	\subsubsection{Power of the priesthood (God's power) manifest in technology as knowledge of the natural world grows}
	% -----
	
		It's a bit bananas, but the idea is that as our knowledge of the natural world increases and we become better at manipulating it and controlling it in the ways we want, some of the power of the priesthood which has in the past been set off for certain things---healing is the best example---comes to be manifest in the technology that we have. So we see fewer healings by the power of the priesthood because we have gained a natural power to intervene and heal many bodily problems ourselves. During the time when we didn't have this power of intervention, which is most of human history, priesthood blessings played a more prominent role in healing. But now that we have this power ourselves, priesthood blessing plays a less prominent role.
		
		And so on for other powers of the priesthood. We gradually begin to acquire them naturally, and so exercising the priesthood in order to accomplish the effects of the power isn't as important anymore.
		
		I'm not sure what I think about this idea. Healing is the best example, and maybe the only good one.
	
		\begin{description}
		\item[2N 30:16--18] Wherefore, the things of all nations shall be made known; yea, all things shall be made known unto the children of men. 17 There is nothing which is secret save it shall be revealed; there is no work of darkness save it shall be made manifest in the light; and there is nothing which is sealed upon the earth save it shall be loosed. 18 Wherefore, all things which have been revealed unto the children of men shall at that day be revealed; and Satan shall have power over the hearts of the children of men no more, for a long time. And now, my beloved brethren, I make an end of my sayings.
		\end{description}
		
	%%%%%%%%
	%%%%%%%%
	%%%%%%%%

	I have been reading lately in various places about receiving the fulness of the priesthood. Most of the sources which speak of this directly are not in the scriptures; in fact, the only place where the phrase ``the fulness of the priesthood'' appears is DC 124:28. But the doctrine is taught in the scriptures indirectly, and I prefer to focus on the standard works when trying to understand this.

	According to my thinking so far, there are two facets to receiving the priesthood.

	\begin{compactenum}
	\item Teaching commandments, preaching, calling to repentance
	\item Developing personally and spiritually in order to gain power and become holy
	\end{compactenum}

	There are so many other things to write and discuss; I really don't even know where to start. My thinking has started to go back to the structure of the plan of salvation. The priesthood is related to it, to the way God functions and accomplishes his purposes here on earth. Also, I have begun to be more open to the possibility of women and the priesthood. This is due partly to the things I have read outside of the scriptures but also due to things inside. Anyway, I'm just rambling. Here are the most important pieces of the puzzle that I have found so far, in no particular order:

	\begin{compactitem}
	\item Alma 12
	\item Alma 13
	\item Moroni 7 (esp. 31, 32)
	\item Abraham 1:1-5
	\item 2 Peter 1
	\item DC 20
	\item DC 84
	\item DC 88
	\item DC 107
	\item DC 121
	\item DC 124
	\item DC 132
	\item TPJS 150 (calling/election sure = sealing power in Eph. 1 and 2nd comforter)
	\item TPJS 343 (many called, few chosen)
	\item TPJS 350 (power of Elijah sufficient to make calling and election sure)
	\item HC 5:387-389 (calling/election sure, more sure word of prophecy)
	\item HC 5:401-405 (calling/election sure, more sure word of prophecy)
	\item HC 5: 529-531 (calling/election made sure, more sure word of prophecy, priesthood)
	\end{compactitem}

	All of these passages tell a different part of the story. As I study more, I believe more that gaining the fulness of the priesthood is the ultimate goal in this life. It is apparently the highest blessing that can be given to man on earth, and therefore seems like the thing which I ought to be striving for. I am also convinced that the priesthood is the way through which God accomplishes all his purposes here on the earth. I mean this more broadly than just that he does things through holders of the priesthood; I will try to make this more explicit as I go through Alma 12 and some other scriptures. And that, in fact, is the plan right now--to go through all of these scriptures, distill the lessons and most important parts, and then try to fit them all together.

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Alma 12}
	% -----

		Zeezrom's question in v. 8 is, ``What does this aspect of the resurrection mean?'' Alma does not begin answering that question immediately. Instead, he explains first the process of how one comes to know answers like the one which Zeezrom seeks. Note the similar language: here, ``It is given unto many to know the mysteries of God''; in DC 107, ``The power and authority of the higher, or Melchizedek Priesthood, is to hold the keys of all the spiritual blessings of the church---[namely] to have the privilege of receiving the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven.'' But they don't come immediately--we gain them through this process which Alma is about to describe, which seems similar to the process at the end of DC 121.

		Anyway, the process of gaining these mysteries. There are two possibilities:

		\begin{compactitem}
		\item Hardening heart
		\begin{compactitem}
		\item Receive lesser portion of word
		\item Lesser portion given until knowing nothing concerning mysteries
		\item Taken captive by devil, led by him to destruction
		\item Being captive to the devil in this way is ``the chains of hell''
		\end{compactitem}
		\item Not hardening heart
		\begin{compactitem}
		\item Given greater portion of word
		\item Greater portion given until it is given [to begin] to know the mysteries of God
		\item Continues knowing mysteries until knowing them in full
		\end{compactitem}
		\end{compactitem}

		Note the interplay between the verbs \textit{give} and \textit{receive}. One who hardens his heart receives a lesser portion because he does not spiritual discern the greater portion where someone else with an open heart might; after that, the lesser portion is given to him, meaning the greater portion isn't even available, even if he were spiritually ready. This passage is important because it is a very clear description of the process by which we progress spiritually. I can think of a number of places where we see it.

		\paragraph*{Alma 12:9-11}

		2 Nephi 28:30: ``For behold, thus saith the Lord God: I will give unto the children of men line upon line and precept upon precept, here a little and there a little. And blessed are they that hearken unto my precepts and lend an ear to my counsel, for they shall learn wisdom. For unto him that receiveth I will give more; and them that shall saw we have enough, from them shall be taken away even that which they have.''

		DC 93:28: ``He that keepeth his commandments receiveth truth and light, until he is glorified in truth and knoweth all things.''

		DC 50:24: ``That which is of God is light; and he that receiveth light, and continueth in God, receiveth more light; and that light groweth brighter and brighter until the perfect day.''

		DC 130:19: ``A person gains...knowledge and intelligence in this life through his diligence and obedience.''

		DC 121:45: ``Let thy bowels also be full of charity towards all men, and to the household of faith, and let virtue garnish thy thoughts unceasingly; then shall thy confidence wax strong in the presence of God; and the doctrine of the priesthood shall distil upon thy soul as the dews from heaven.''

		DC 88:33: ``For what doth it profit a man if a gift is bestowed upon him, and he receive not the gift? Behold, he rejoices not in that which is given unto him, neither rejoices in him who is the giver of the gift.''

		All of these verses use distinct words for the object which we receive: \textit{word, truth, light, knowledge, intelligence, doctrine of the priesthood}. I don't know if they are all the same, but the meaning of this is clear: when we receive counsel, instruction, or knowledge from God, we need to obey it. It needs to become part of our lives and form part of the system through which we make decisions. Alma explains this to Zeezrom so he will understand how one can gain knowledge but also so he will understand what kind of a responsibility he will be under after his questions are answered. It is an eternal principle, one on which spiritual progress is based. We get a little knowledge, and we obey it, and we get a little more, and we obey it, and we keep doing this over and over.

		Several of the verses us \textit{receive} to describe our action in obtaining this gift from God. To \textit{receive} something is to take something which is being given or handed to you. DC 88:33 best describes this of the verses above. Receiving is an active process--we have to act in order to receive something--and gospel reception is no different. We must act in order to receive what God is giving us, and we must then act in order to implement that gift (or knowledge or light or intelligence or word) into our lives. Another disturbingly clear place to find this is John 1:5 in the Greek text: \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{ka`i t`o f\char"007Ews >en t\char"007Eh| skot'ia| fa'inei, ka`i <h skot'ia a>ut`o o>u kat'elaben}}. I don't know what else to say; that verse says it all. The myriad meanings of \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{katalamb'anw}} are perfect. The darkness did not: comprehend the light, receive the light, understand the light, take the light for itself, seize the light, make the light its own. We need to \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{katalamb'anw}} what we receive from God.

		And the important thing regarding the priesthood: this is the way we progress. It is the way we grow spiritually. As we change through repentance and obedience, we are eligible to receive more; we receive it by reaching for it (seeking for it, asking for it, being ready to listen when we are in a spiritual environment) and then by obeying it. There is no substitute for this process. Alma 12:11 says that those who harden their hearts receive less and less until they know nothing concerning the mysteries of God (mysteries of God = the knowledge we can gain only by revelation--this includes the very knowledge of God's existence). John 12:35 says, ``Walk while we have the light, lest darkness come upon you.'' But this would be much better translated as a parallel verse for Alma 12:11, because the Greek text uses \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{katalamb'anw}} and \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{skot'ia}}, the very same words used in John 1:5. In other words, the darkness isn't looking to receive or understand the light; it's looking to seize us and make us its own--``And that wicked one cometh and taketh away light and truth, through disobedience, from the children of men, and because of the tradition of their fathers.''

		Returning now to Alma 12...

		\begin{compactitem}
		\item Verses 12-15 describe our situation before God at the point of the resurrection if we have hardened our hearts and rejected the word.
		\item Verses 19-21 ask a question about the first state of man after leaving his state of innocence.
		\item Verses 22-24 (beginning of 24) explain the Fall and what would have happened if Adam had eaten of the fruit. In these verses it seems that the tree of life refers to the resurrection particularly, and not to the love of God or repentance as it appears to in other places (1 Nephi 8, Alma 32).

		A line after the beginning of 24 is extremely important; it marks a turning point in the chapter: ``Nevertheless there was a space granted unto man in which he might repent.''

		Alma has said, in effect, ``This is your state--the situation of Adam is the situation of us all. But, repentance is possible.'' The rest of the chapter explains how.

		\item Verses 25-27 give several more counterfactuals and describe our state further.

		\item In verse 28, we begin to see the priesthood be involved. These next verses are the reasons that I wanted to read this chapter in my study of the priesthood.

		\item Man needed to know of the plan of redemption; he needed to be aware of what was happening to him and what his purpose was.

		\item God sent angels to give knowledge to men. The angels made known the plan of redemption. In accordance with Alma 5:49 and Moroni 7:31, I believe the angels must have had the priesthood. This means that it would have been their responsibility to take this knowledge to the inhabitants of the world. The responsibility comes because of the priesthood. In other words, the priesthood is the means through which God accomplishes his purposes on the earth. It is the means through which the knowledge of the plan of redemption and repentance is disseminated throughout the world. This knowledge is made available according to faith, repentance, and holy works. In other words, returning to the 9-11 of this chapter, we receive more light by showing our faith, repenting, and doing holy works. This is how we open our heart and receive the word.

		\item Verse 31--God gave men commandments so that they would be able to produce faith, repentance, and holy works. Commandments are a necessary part of producing these fruits. ``Now, how could a man repent except he should sin?'' The definition of sin comes in James 4:17: \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{e>id'oti o\char"007E>un kal`on poie\char"007Ein ka`i m`h poio\char"007Eunti, <amart'ia a>ut\char"007Ew| >estin}}. We can't do good in the sense that God wants us to unless he tells us what it is. We have an intuitive sense of that which is good, but actual obedience requires finer instruction on what God expects of us: ``wherefore, they shall come to the knowledge of their Redeemer and the very points of his doctrine, that they may know how to come unto him and be saved.''
		\end{compactitem}

		This chapter gives an outline of the plan of salvation not in terms of events that will happen but in terms of what is actually expected of every one of us. Every person has sinned, and the situation described in this chapter applies to every person. Every person has the ability to gain light and knowledge by obeying the light and knowledge that they have already received; for this reason the light of Christ is given to all, so that they can discern good from evil even though they may not know the exact points of doctrine or the exact commandments. The responsibility of the priesthood is to preach the gospel to the inhabitants of the world. I don't know what else to say about it.

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Alma 13}
	% -----

		I don't really like the chapter division between Alma 12 and 13; they are much better viewed as a single chapter. And, in fact, in the original edition of the Book of Mormon, they were not separate. In fact, there is a chapter division after Alma 13:9, and that seems like a natural breaking point. The first three editions of the Book of Mormon all show this different arrangement, and it makes a lot more sense.

		The key here to understanding the role of the priesthood in the plan of salvation is in Alma 13:1: ``And I would that ye should remember that the Lord God ordained priests after his holy order, which was after the order of his Son, to teach these things unto the people.'' This is what matters. Holders of the priesthood have been called and ordained to teach the plan of salvation, teach the commandments, teach repentance---to give people the knowledge they need for salvation. A priesthood holder cannot force someone to baptism, but he can instruct someone sufficiently that the burden of responsibility has been shifted (Jacob 1:19).

		Verse 2 is a little confusing, but I think by adding some more language I can give a clearer rendering of the idea: ``And those priests were ordained after the order of his Son in such a way that the result would be that the people would know how to look forward to his Son for redemption.'' In its current state the purpose of the verse is a little unclear, but I think this is the idea. God ordained priests in a specific way. The goal of that particular way was that people would know how to look forward to the Son for redemption. Verse 3 then begins to describe the way they were ordained, or the way in which the priesthood comes unto men. This is very important. It is one of the only places in the scriptures that describes the way this works on a general level (the other is Abraham 1:1-5, at least that I can think of).

		It seems that the particular way is that God promises holders of the priesthood blessings (ultimately eternal life) if they magnify their calling and teach the commandments. It's an incentive-based system. But after a person has been transformed by the Atonement (``born again,'' if you prefer), that person will desire to fulfill this mandate without thinking about the reward. They still desire the reward, and think about it and look forward to it, but their love for others grows and they start to do things for different reasons. It begins with an incentive, though---cf. Abraham 1:2: ``And, finding there was greater happiness and peace and rest for me...'' Abraham was first thinking about what was available to him. This is the manner in which we are ordained, because it's the type of creatures we are---we work on these types of incentives. But eventually we begin to change, and our motivations change as well. Verse 3 begins the specifics.

		\begin{itemize}
		\item They were called and prepared on account of (because of) their exceeding faith and good works.
		\item They were called and prepared according to the foreknowledge of God (what exactly does this mean? It may refer to the fact that God knew ahead of time that they would need incentives, but this interpretation is pretty shallow)
		\item ``in the first place'' they were left to choose good or evil---they were allowed to do what they wanted, and they chose good-looking
		\item Since they chose good and exercised faith, they were called with a holy calling (they were called to the priesthood)
		\item Others were once in the same position, left free to choose, but hardened their hearts, rejected the Spirit of God, and lost the opportunity for the blessings which come from holding the priesthood
		\item Those who did not harden their hearts were called and ordained to teach his commandments (Alma 12:28--37)
		\end{itemize}

		This is the general description of how the priesthood comes to men. In my view, there are hints in these verses that the events referred to took place in the pre-mortal existence, but I don't know that this matters very much currently. What matters is that this general pattern plays out in the life of each man in the church. At some point he is on equal standing with those around him, and he can choose what to do. If he chooses good and exercises faith and repentance, he will eventually be called to the priesthood and has a chance to progress in the way described in these verses. If he chooses to harden his heart and reject the Spirit of God, he will lose that opportunity.

		We can see this general process instantiated in the life of Abraham, at least as reported in the first few verses.

		\begin{itemize}
		\item Abraham, already a follower of righteousness, ``finds'' (discovers? Realizes?) that there is greater happiness and peace and rest for him
		\item He desires to possess great knowledge, be a greater follower of righteousness, and to possess a greater knowledge
		\item He desires to be a father of many nations and a prince of peace
		\item He desires to receive instructions and keep the commandments of God
		\item He seeks for the blessings of the fathers and the right to administer them
		\item He becomes a High Priest---a ``rightful heir''--holding the right belonging to the fathers (cf. Alma 13:9, ``thus they become high priests'')
		\end{itemize}

		So:

		\begin{enumerate}
		\item In the first place, we are left to choose good or evil. This is according to the level of knowledge which we have.
		\item We choose good, exercise faith, and repent.
		\item We are called with a holy calling---called to the priesthood.
		\item To magnify our calling, we teach the commandments and preach repentance.
		\item As we magnify our calling, we participate in the process of gaining a greater portion of the word (light and truth) through our diligence and obedience.\item We desire to possess ``greater knowledge'' and to be a ``greater follower of righteousness.''
		\item We continue to the process of gaining more light and truth and the ``doctrine of the priesthood [distils] upon [our souls] as the dews from heaven.''
		\item We gradually receive more and more priesthood until we are able to fulfill the promises in the oath and covenant of having the Father teach us, receiving visitations, communing with the Church of the Firstborn, etc.
		\end{enumerate}

		So the important thing for me at this time is to (1) understand my calling, and (2) magnify it. At this point I understand the calling better---it is the call to bear the knowledge of the plan of salvation, the Atonement, and the ordinances of the priesthood to the world. It is to participate in the work of the Father and to be the means through which he is able to accomplish his purposes on the earth. The principle responsibilities are preaching repentance and teaching the commandments and plan of salvation. But there is more to magnifying the calling than merely doing these things; DC 121:45 makes that clear. I also must change as a person. So, the next question is: what does it mean to magnify one's calling? What types of personal changes must I undergo to carry out the magnification?

		\begin{itemize}
		\item Develop an abhorrence of sin (Alma 13:12). This comes by faith, repentance, righteous works, and then the processes of justification and sanctification.
		\item The beginning of that process is ``bringing forth fruit meet for repentance'' (Alma 13:13). ``Meet'' means ``proper or suitable,'' so this means that I need to produce actions suitable for the process of repentance. Some actions I could produce are not suitable for repentance. What makes the difference? Many guidelines in the scriptures.
		\item I must humble myself before the Lord. I think this is the key phrase which integrates the two halves of the calling to the priesthood---preaching/service to others (magnifying the calling) and developing better attributes (becoming clean). He uses this phrase twice, in verses 13 and 28. In the first we are to humble ourselves and then bring forth fruit meet for repentance. This is the beginning of the magnifying-the-calling track. In verse 28 we are to humble ourselves and then call on his holy name and watch and pray continually---and this leads to all of the qualities we develop, the other track. Of course, they aren't actually separate, but it helps to separate them conceptually in order to see what we need to do. In fact, by calling on his holy name and watching and praying continually, we come to develop divine qualities and then have faith, hope, and charity (v. 29). I think this verse makes it clear that faith, hope, and charity are actions,or are characteristics of the actions which we perform. It isn't like a ball, something that you receive and can just carry around. They must be things that we can do.
		\end{itemize}

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Degenerate priesthood} % *DEGENERATEPRIESTHOOD
	% -----

		There may be ``orders'' of the priesthood which are not true orders, but which are ``types'' of the true order. The types of the true order would still lead people to do good and be righteous, and receive blessings, but wouldn't be the real thing; see Al 13:16. That verse may be saying, there are ordinances, and whether these come from the actual order or from a type of the order, they still help the people do the same thing.

		This is in line with thinking that God is inspiring many people to do his work throughout the earth all the time, whether or not they actually receive the real priesthood and ordinances.
		
		\begin{description}
		\item[Morm 1:19] And it came to pass that there were sorceries, and witchcrafts, and magics; and the power of the evil one was wrought upon all the face of the land, even unto the fulfilling of all the words of Abinadi, and also Samuel the Lamanite.
		\item[Morm 2:10] And it came to pass that the Nephites began to repent of their iniquity, and began to cry even as had been prophesied by Samuel the prophet; for behold no man could keep that which was his own, for the thieves, and the robbers, and the murderers, and the magic art, and the witchcraft which was in the land.
		\end{description}

Are you old enough to know what you are about? If so, preach and labor for the building up of the city of Zion; concentrate yourmeans and influence there, and not scatter abroad. % -----------------------
\subsection{Principle of sufficient reason} % *PRINCIPLEOFSUFFICIENTREASON *PSR
% -----------------------

	Are there reasons and explanations for why the plan of salvation is the way it is, why God has done what he's done, and so on?
	
	\begin{compactdesc}
	\item[CDBY 2789] He has given His son, according to His good pleasure, to redeem the earth, and all intelligent beings thereon, and all inanimate matter, if there is any such thing; to redeem the whole earth and all pertaining to it, and it is His good pleasure to do it. The reasons why He did it are plain and obvious, though we may not say anything about them to-day; yet there are reasons for all this, and that that we may call eternal philosophy, God's philosophy, the philosophy of angels--- natural philosophy, reasonable philosophy, that that commends itself to the human mind, to the intelligence that man possesses, will explain it. If men understood the religion that we believe in they would receive it; it naturally commends itself to the conscience of every just and righteous person, and none such would refuse it if they understood it.
	\end{compactdesc}

If I were to attempt that, the Lord would remove me out of my place, and so He will any other man who attempts to lead the children of men astray from the oracles of God and from their duty...
	\item[Exo 3] (Clear example of a prophet getting called to do a specific work.)
	\item[Exo 18] (The role of a prophet in making the law of the Lord known to people.)
	\item[Num 11:24--29] 24 And Moses went out, and told the people the words of the LORD, and gathered the seventy men of the elders of the people, and set them round about the tabernacle. 25 And the LORD came down in a cloud, and spake unto him, and took of the spirit that was upon him, and gave it unto the seventy elders: and it came to pass, that, when the spirit rested upon them, they prophesied, and did not cease. 26 But there remained two of the men in the camp, the name of the one was Eldad, and the name of the other Medad: and the spirit rested upon them; and they were of them that were written, but went not out unto the tabernacle: and they prophesied in the camp. 27 And there ran a young man, and told Moses, and said, Eldad and Medad do prophesy in the camp. 28 And Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of Moses, one of his young men, answered and said, My lord Moses, forbid them. 29 And Moses said unto him, Enviest thou for my sake? would God that all the LORD's people were prophets, and that the LORD would put his spirit upon them!

And the LORD heard it. 3 (Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth.) 4 And the LORD spake suddenly unto Moses, and unto Aaron, and unto Miriam, Come out ye three unto the tabernacle of the congregation. And they three came out. 5 And the LORD came down in the pillar of the cloud, and stood in the door of the tabernacle, and called Aaron and Miriam: and they both came forth. 6 And he said, Hear now my words: If there be a prophet among you, I the LORD will make myself known unto him in a vision, and will speak unto him in a dream. 7 My servant Moses is not so, who is faithful in all mine house. 8 With him will I speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches; and the similitude of the LORD shall he behold: wherefore then were ye not afraid to speak against my servant Moses? 9 And the anger of the LORD was kindled against them; and he departed.

	\item[1Sam 10] Note how Saul is changed by the Spirit (new birth); he is able to prophecy as well.
	\item[1Sam 12] The role of a prophet in calling people to repent; talks about the Lord's ``anointed.''

David's brothers all meet Samuel but none of them are chosen---it has to be David, and it's clear that the Lord is doing the choosing here. He is guiding Samuel to select David, and as soon as David is anointed, the Spirit falls on him. This is great example of this pattern in the OT.
	\item[1Sam 19:18--24] When Saul is trying to kill David, every person he sends to try to retrieve him ends up being touched by the spirit to prophesy.

You cannot appoint a man at our head; but if you do want any other man or men to lead you, take them and we will go our way to build up the kingdom in all the world...I again repeat, no man can stand at our head, except God reveals it from the heavens.
	\item[CDBY 54] There never was a prophet on the earth that dictated to the people, but he dictated their temporal affairs as well as spiritual.

Sidney Rigdon cannot hold the keys without Joseph, if he had held the keys with Joseph and been faithful he would have been with us. If the Twelve do not apostatize they carry the keys of this kingdom wherever they go.

Then follow me and I will lead you into the kingdom and if I do not then I'll give my soul for yours. All I want you to do is to obey my council and do what I tell you.

\subsection{Psychology} % *PSYCHOLOGY
% -----------------------

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Psychology of the scriptures}
	% -----
	
		How do the mind and cognition work, according to the scriptures?
		
			% Old Testament
			\begin{description}
			\item[1Ch 29:18] O LORD God of Abraham, Isaac, and of Israel, our fathers, keep this for ever in the imagination of the thoughts of the heart of thy people, and prepare their heart unto thee:
			\item[1Ch 6:30] Then hear thou from heaven thy dwelling place, and forgive, and render unto every man according unto all his ways, whose heart thou knowest; (for thou only knowest the hearts of the children of men:)
			\item[3N 19:32--33] (Enhanced understanding through the Holy Ghost; our cognition changes with it. Also, there's a kind of understanding which is attributed to the ``heart'' here; for working out the psychology of the Book of Mormon, we'll have to figure out what the difference is between mind and heart.) And tongue cannot speak the words which he prayed, neither can be written by man the words which he prayed. 33 And the multitude did hear and do bear record; and their hearts were open and they did understand in their hearts the words which he prayed.
			\item[CDBY 31] We are a good-feeling set of men, because of the Spirit which is in us. What produces it? The impulse of the heart.
			\end{description}
			
			% Book of Mormon
			\begin{compactdesc}
			\item[3N 28:9] And again, ye shall not have pain while ye shall dwell in the flesh, neither sorrow save it be for the sins of the world; and all this will I do because of the thing which ye have desired of me, for ye have desired that ye might bring the souls of men unto me, while the world shall stand.
			\end{compactdesc}
		
	% -----
	\subsubsection{Psychology and the Spirit}
	% -----
	
		\begin{description}
		\item[CDBY 31] We are a good-feeling set of men, because of the Spirit which is in us. What produces it? The impulse of the heart.
		\end{description}

% -----------------------
\subsection{Punishment} % *PUNISHMENT
% -----------------------

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Does God punish us?}
	% -----
	
		Lately I've not been wanting to allow that God actually causes afflictions to come upon people. But I don't think the scriptures really agree with that position, at least not always.
		
		Here are a few scriptures about this, including some that talk about God using wicked or pagan people to violently remind his chosen people of their covenants.
	
		\begin{description}
		\item[Hel 12:3] And thus we see that except the Lord doth chasten his people with many afflictions, yea, except he doth visit them with death and with terror, and with famine and with all manner of pestilence, they will not remember him.
		\item[Hel 13] (A lot of verses in this chapter are relevant to this topic.)
		\item[Hel 15:3] Yea, wo unto this people who are called the people of Nephi except they shall repent, when they shall see all these signs and wonders which shall be showed unto them; for behold, they have been a chosen people of the Lord; yea, the people of Nephi hath he loved, and also hath he chastened		them; yea, in the days of their iniquities hath he chastened them because he loveth them.
		\item[3N 9:2--12] Wo, wo, wo unto this people; wo unto the inhabitants of the whole earth except they shall repent; for the devil laugheth, and his angels rejoice, because of the slain of the fair sons and daughters of my people; and it is because of their iniquity and abominations that they are fallen! 3 Behold, that great city Zarahemla have I burned with fire, and the inhabitants thereof. 4 And behold, that great city Moroni have I caused to be sunk in the depths of the sea, and the inhabitants thereof to be drowned. 5 And behold, that great city Moronihah have I covered with earth, and the inhabitants thereof, to hide their iniquities and their abominations from before my face, that the blood of the prophets and the saints shall not come any more unto me against them. 6 And behold, the city of Gilgal have I caused to be sunk, and the inhabitants thereof to be buried up in the depths of the earth; 7 Yea, and the city of Onihah and the inhabitants thereof, and the city of Mocum and the inhabitants thereof, and the city of Jerusalem and the inhabitants thereof; and waters have I caused to come up in the stead thereof, to hide their wickedness and abominations from before my face, that the blood of the prophets and the saints shall not come up any more unto me against them. 8 And behold, the city of Gadiandi, and the city of Gadiomnah, and the city of Jacob, and the city of Gimgimno, all these have I caused to be sunk, and made hills and valleys in the places thereof; and the inhabitants thereof have I buried up in the depths of the earth, to hide their wickedness and abominations from before my face, that the blood of the prophets and the saints should not come up any more unto me against them. 9 And behold, that great city Jacobugath, which was inhabited by the people of king Jacob, have I caused to be burned with fire because of their sins and their wickedness, which was above all the wickedness of the whole earth, because of their secret murders and combinations; for it was they that did destroy the peace of my people and the government of the land; therefore I did cause them to be burned, to destroy them from before my face, that the blood of the prophets and the saints should not come up unto me any more against them. 10 And behold, the city of Laman, and the city of Josh, and the city of Gad, and the city of Kishkumen, have I caused to be burned with fire, and the inhabitants thereof, because of their wickedness in casting out the prophets, and stoning those whom I did send to declare unto them concerning their wickedness and their abominations. 11 And because they did cast them all out, that there were none righteous among them, I did send down fire and destroy them, that their wickedness and abominations might be hid from before my face, that the blood of the prophets and the saints whom I sent among them might not cry unto me from the ground against them. 12 And many great destructions have I caused to come upon this land, and upon this people, because of their wickedness and their abominations.
		\item[1Ch 5:23--26] And the children of the half tribe of Manasseh dwelt in the land: they increased from Bashan unto Baal-hermon and Senir, and unto mount Hermon. 24 And these were the heads of the house of their fathers, even Epher, and Ishi, and Eliel, and Azriel, and Jeremiah, and Hodaviah, and Jahdiel, mighty men of valour, famous men, and heads of the house of their fathers. 25 And they transgressed against the God of their fathers, and went a whoring after the gods of the people of the land, whom God destroyed before them. 26 And the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria, and he carried them away, even the Reubenites, and the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh, and brought them unto Halah, and Habor, and Hara, and to the river Gozan, unto this day.
		\item[1Ch 10:13--14] So Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the LORD, even against the word of the LORD, which he kept not, and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it; 14 And enquired not of the LORD: therefore he slew him, and turned the kingdom unto David the son of Jesse.
		\item[TPJS 13] they [prophets and seers] saw every mountain laid low and every valley exalted when the Lord was taking vengeance upon the wicked...
		\end{description}

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Guilt as punishment (psychological punishment)}
	% -----
	
		\begin{description}
		\item[2N 9:16] And assuredly, as the Lord liveth, for the Lord God hath spoken it, and it is his eternal word, which cannot pass away, that they who are righteous shall be righteous still, and they who are filthy shall be filthy still; wherefore, they who are filthy are the devil and his angels; and they shall go away into everlasting fire, prepared for them; and their torment is as a lake of fire and brimstone, whose flame ascendeth up forever and ever and has no end.
		\item[2N 9:19] O the greatness of the mercy of our God, the Holy One of Israel! For he delivereth his saints from that awful monster the devil, and death, and hell, and that lake of fire and brimstone, which is endless torment.
		\item[2N 9:46] Prepare your souls for that glorious day when justice shall be administered unto the righteous, even the day of judgment, that ye may not shrink with awful fear; that ye may not remember your awful guilt in perfectness, and be constrained to exclaim: Holy, holy are thy judgments, O Lord God Almighty---but I know my guilt; I transgressed thy law, and my transgressions are mine; and the devil hath obtained me, that I am a prey to his awful misery.
		\item[Al 36:7--16] And behold, he spake unto us, as it were the voice of thunder, and the whole earth did tremble beneath our feet; and we all fell to the earth, for the fear of the Lord came upon us. 8 But behold, the voice said unto me: Arise. And I arose and stood up, and beheld the angel. 9 And he said unto me: If thou wilt of thyself be destroyed, seek no more to destroy the church of God. 10 And it came to pass that I fell to the earth; and it was for the space of three days and three nights that I could not open my mouth, neither had I the use of my limbs. 11 And the angel spake more things unto me, which were heard by my brethren, but I did not hear them; for when I heard the words---If thou wilt be destroyed of thyself, seek no more to destroy the church of God---I was struck with such great fear and amazement lest perhaps I should be destroyed, that I fell to the earth and I did hear no more. 12 But I was racked with eternal torment, for my soul was harrowed up to the greatest degree and racked with all my sins. 13 Yea, I did remember all my sins and iniquities, for which I was tormented with the pains of hell; yea, I saw that I had rebelled against my God, and that I had not kept his holy commandments. 14 Yea, and I had murdered many of his children, or rather led them away unto destruction; yea, and in fine so great had been my iniquities, that the very thought of coming into the presence of my God did rack my soul with inexpressible horror. 15 Oh, thought I, that I could be banished and become extinct both soul and body, that I might not be brought to stand in the presence of my God, to be judged of my deeds. 16 And now, for three days and for three nights was I racked, even with the pains of a damned soul.
		\item[Morm 9:1--5] AND now, I speak also concerning those who do not believe in Christ. 2 Behold, will ye believe in the day of your visitation---behold, when the Lord shall come, yea, even that great day when the earth shall be rolled together as a scroll, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, yea, in that great day when ye shall be brought to stand before the Lamb of God---then will ye say that there is no God? 3 Then will ye longer deny the Christ, or can ye behold the Lamb of God? Do ye suppose that ye shall dwell with him under a consciousness of your guilt? Do ye suppose that ye could be happy to dwell with that holy Being, when your souls are racked with a consciousness of guilt that ye have ever abused his laws? 4 Behold, I say unto you that ye would be more miserable to dwell with a holy and just God, under a consciousness of your filthiness before him, than ye would to dwell with the damned souls in hell. 5 For behold, when ye shall be brought to see your nakedness before God, and also the glory of God, and the holiness of Jesus Christ, it will kindle a flame of unquenchable fire upon you.
		\end{description}
		
% -----------------------
\subsection{Purify/purification} % *PURIFY *PURIFICATION *PURE
% -----------------------

	\begin{description}
	\item[Mor 7:48] Wherefore, my beloved brethren, pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart, that ye may be filled with this love, which he hath bestowed upon all who are true followers of his Son, Jesus Christ; that ye may become the sons of God; that when he shall appear we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is; that we may have this hope; that we may be purified even as he is pure. Amen.

	\subsubsection{Word is quick}
	% -----
	
		Original passage is Heb 4:12: ``For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.''
			``Quick'' here is \textgreek{ζῶν}, ``living.'' Almost every modern translation of Heb 4:12 gives this word as ``living.''

% -----------------------
\subsection{Quicken} % *QUICKEN
% -----------------------

	1828:
		1. Primarily, to make alive; to vivify; to revive or resuscitate, as from death or an inanimate state. Romans 4:17.
			Hence flocks and herds, and men and beasts and fowls, with breath are quicken'd and attract their souls.
		2. To make alive in a spiritual sense; to communicate a principle of grace to.
			You hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins. Ephesians 2:1.
		3. To hasten; to accelerate; as, to quicken motion, speed or flight.
		4. To sharpen; to give keener perception to; to stimulate; to incite; as, to quicken the appetite or taste; to quicken desires.
		5. To revive; to cheer; to reinvigorate; to refresh by new supplies of comfort or grace. Psalms 119:25.

Tooby and Cosmides (1992), Ehrenreich and McIntosh (1995), and Pinker (2002) document how widespread, influential, and deeply entrenched such attitudes are, not only among scientists but also in politics and ordinary life. There were originally good reasons for such attitudes. Degler (1991) shows that in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, it was widely assumed (even by Darwin, Humboldt, and the distinguished early twentieth-century linguist Otto Jespersen) that races and ethnicities are sharply distinguished in intelligence and moral capacities?with northern Europeans naturally at the peak of both. % -----------------------
\subsection{Rameumptom} % *RAMEUMPTOM
% -----------------------

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Onomasticon}
	% -----

		The name RAMEUMPTOM is defined in the Book of Mormon as ``the holy stand'' (Alma 31:21, 23) and is described as ``a place of standing, which was high above the head'' (Alma 31:13).

		The first element of the name is most likely related to HEBREW ram, ``to be high, to be exalted,'' and rama, ``eminence, high place,'' the same root that appears in the biblical geographic name RAMAH, ``hill'' (cf. Book of Mormon RAMAH). RAMEUMPTOM could be a noun chain with rame as a masculine construct plural, meaning ``the elevations of.'' The -umptom would then be a nomen rectum, possibly from HEBREW `omed , ``place, position, location,'' with either a pronominal suffix, analogous to the 3rd person plural possessive pronoun -am,[2] or with the nominalizing ending –lm.[3] The latter ending is probably to be preferred because of the analog form in Arabic, `umdan ``standing.'' Given these two HEBREW lexemes, ram and `omed, the meaning of RAMEUMPTOM would then be ``the heights/ elevations of (their) stand'' (RFS), a definition that accords well with the interpretation that the Book of Mormon writers provided.

% -----------------------

	This idea is that the gospel is as real as you want it to be. It doesn't actually become real when we want it to be; it's real all the time. But it's only active in our life if we want it to be, and we can have it as active as we want. We only experience it as real if we want to, and we can experience it as real as we want to.

And behold, it was prepared to show unto our fathers the course which they should travel in the wilderness. 40 And it did work for them according to their faith in God; therefore, if they had faith to believe that God could cause that those spindles should point the way they should go, behold, it was done; therefore they had this miracle, and also many other miracles wrought by the power of God, day by day. 41 Nevertheless, because those miracles were worked by small means it did show unto them marvelous works. \subsection{Rebaptism} % *REBAPTISM
% -----------------------

	All forms of it.
	
		\subsubsection{After excommunication}
		
		\subsubsection{At the beginning of the restoration}
		
		\subsubsection{In the early days of the restored church}
		
			People were re-baptized regularly, to mark out a renewed covenant with the Lord. Take this record, for example, from MHBY50 66, recording events from August 7, 1847, just a couple weeks after the Saints arrived in the Salt Lake valley:
			
				\begin{quote}
				Between nine and ten p.m. the council met and recommended that all the camp be rebaptized and that...[many individuals to officiate]...be clerks to attend to the rebaptisms, and to commence at 6 o'clock in the morning. 289 persons were rebaptized, and renewed their covenant to serve the Lord.
				\end{quote}
				
			The members of the quorum of the twelve were also rebaptized a day earlier---here's WWJ 3:249:
			
				\begin{quote}
				I had not been on the bed but a short time before Br Kimball called upon me \& informed me that the Twelve were going soon to the water to be Baptized for the remission of their sins to set an example to the Church As they would be called upon on Sunday morning to be baptized by the Twelve [all?] those that wished. We considerd this A duty \& privlege as we come into a glorious valley to locate \& build a temple \& build up Zion we felt like renewing our Convenant before the Lord and each other. We soon repaired to the water \& President Brigham Young went down into the water \& Baptized all his Brethren the Twelve that were with him by burying them in the water. He also confirmed us in the Church \& sealed upon us our apostleship \& all the keys, powers \& Blessings belonging to that office. Br Heber C. Kimball Baptized \& Confirmed President Bringham Young. The following are the names of those present on this occasion: B Young H C Kimball O. Pratt W. Richards W. Woodruff G. A. Smith \& A Lyman.
				\end{quote}
				
			MHBY50 says, for that date (page 65),
			
				\begin{quote}
				At night I was rebaptized by Elder Kimball and then baptized Elders Kimball, Richards, Pratt, Woodruff, Smith, Lyman, and Benson, who were confirmed at the waters edge, to set an example to the Church, and recommended that all who desire to be Latter-day Saints should be rebaptized and reconfirmed.
				\end{quote}
				
			See Ogden Kraut's book(let) on rebaptism.
			
			See also:
				JSR 316, where Newel K. Whitney reports that he and his wife were (re)-``Baptised for remission of sins'' (JSR 316, from 27 August 1842, six days after they were sealed)

\subsection{Reconcilation} % *RECONCILE *RECONCILIATION
% -----------------------

	Reconciling ourselves to the will of God (2N 10:24).
	
	A couple definitions from the 1828---
		\#1: To conciliate anew; to call back into union and friendship the affections which have been alienated; to restore to friendship or favor after estrangement.
		\#3: To make consistent or congruous; to bring to agreement or suitableness.
	I think both apply to a scripture like 2N 10:24. Note the importance of definition \#1, of bringing \textit{back} into union---it's a \textit{re}-conciling, meaning we were once ``conciliated'' with God and now must return to that state.
	
	\begin{description}
	\item[2N 25:23] For we labor diligently to write, to persuade our children, and also our brethren, to believe in Christ, and to be reconciled to God; for we know that it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do.
	\item[2N 33:7--9] I have charity for my people, and great faith in Christ that I shall meet many souls spotless at his judgment-seat. 8 I have charity for the Jew---I say Jew, because I mean them from whence I came. 9 I also have charity for the Gentiles. But behold, for none of these can I hope except they shall be reconciled unto Christ, and enter into the narrow gate, and walk in the strait path which leads to life, and continue in the path until the end of the day of probation.
	\item[Jac 4:11] Wherefore, beloved brethren, be reconciled unto him through the atonement of Christ, his Only Begotten Son, and ye may obtain a resurrection, according to the power of the resurrection which is in Christ, and be presented as the first-fruits of Christ unto God, having faith, and obtained a good hope of glory in him before he manifesteth himself in the flesh.
	\item[Eze 45:20] (Interesting to compare the old way of reconciling a house or a person with the new one.) And so thou shalt do the seventh day of the month for every one that erreth, and for him that is simple: so shall ye reconcile the house.

% -----------------------
\subsection{Redemption} % *REDEMPTION
% -----------------------

	The ``redemption'' is spoken of in two ways---first, as our coming back into the presence of God to live with him eternally (Morm 7:7); and second, as coming back into the presence of God at the moment of judgment (Morm 9:12--13). This latter redemption is being redeemed from temporal death (``an endless sleep,'' Morm 9:13); the former is being redeemed from spiritual death (Al 12:16--17).
	
	So when you think of the redemption, you always have to think, what is the person being redeemed \textit{from}? And there are multiple things to be redeemed from in the plan of salvation, so there are multiple redemptions.
	
	\begin{description}
	\item[DC 77:12] (Something weird here with redeeming and power.) We are to understand that as God made the world in six days, and on the seventh day he finished his work, and sanctified it, and also formed man out of the dust of the earth, even so, in the beginning of the seventh thousand years will the Lord God sanctify the earth, and complete the salvation of man, and judge all things, and shall redeem all things, except that which he hath not put into his power, when he shall have sealed all things, unto the end of all things; and the sounding of the trumpets of the seven angels are the preparing and finishing of his work, in the beginning of the seventh thousand years---the preparing of the way before the time of his coming.
	\item[DC 88:14] Now, verily I say unto you, that through the redemption which is made for you is brought to pass the resurrection from the dead.
	\item[Job 33:24--30] Then he is gracious unto him, and saith, Deliver him from going down to the pit: I have found a ransom. 25 His flesh shall be fresher than a child's: he shall return to the days of his youth: 26 He shall pray unto God, and he will be favourable unto him: and he shall see his face with joy: for he will render unto man his righteousness. 27 He looketh upon men, and if any say, I have sinned, and perverted that which was right, and it profited me not; 28 He will deliver his soul from going into the pit, and his life shall see the light. 29 Lo, all these things worketh God oftentimes with man, 30 To bring back his soul from the pit, to be enlightened with the light of the living.
	\end{description}

See Morm 9:12--13; there are multiple redemptions that we can talk about, and at least one of them, the redemption from temporal death, is pretty much the same (or is the same) as the resurrection.

% -----------------------
\subsection{Remission} % *REMISSION
% -----------------------

	Remission of sins is forgiveness of sins.

	\begin{description}
	\item[DC 1:31--33] For I the Lord cannot look upon sin with the least degree of allowance; 32 Nevertheless, he that repents and does the commandments of the Lord shall be forgiven; 33 And he that repents not, from him shall be taken even the light which he has received; for my Spirit shall not always strive with man, saith the Lord of Hosts.
	\item[George Cannon, JD 20:289] There was a time when God required of his people the sacrifice of animals. They brought their animals and they were offered up as sacrifices, and they obtained the remission of sins by that method.
	\end{description}

	I am familiar with a number of scriptures that discuss receiving a \textit{remission} of sins. This is very closely related to \textit{forgiveness}---in fact, given what follows below, especially in the uses of \textit{remission} in the NT, I think that remission and forgiveness of sins are the same thing. Though I'm familiar with these scriptures, I've wondered about what the remission actually is--is it something that we actually \textit{receive}? Something that is actually \textit{given} to us? What is the experience of receiving a remission of sins like?

	And then the other day I had the thought--what if we equated the remission of sin with the baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost? We have more information about when and why the latter is received; if it were the same as the remission of sin, we would also have more information about that. I don't know if this is correct, but it definitely produces some interesting readings of the scriptures. 

	Actually, now that I've started looking at the scriptures, this one practically gives this equivalence:

	\begin{quote}
	For the gate by which ye should enter is repentance and baptism by water; and then cometh a remission of your sins by fire and by the Holy Ghost (2N 31:17).
	\end{quote}

	They are not equated, but a remission of sins comes \textit{by means of} the baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost. Here are some other examples of that relationship: a cleansing comes by means of soap; a punch comes by means of a fist; rain comes by means of water-filled clouds; etc. One entity is causally responsible for the emergence of a second. So I would say that the baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost is causally responsible for producing in us a remission of sins. So wherever you get a remission of sin, you'll find the baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost causing it.

	% -----
	\subsubsection{BOM Uses}
	% -----

		Here's a look at \textit{remission} in the BOM:

		\begin{description}

		\item[2N 25:26] A remission of sin has a \textit{source}. We must \textit{look to} that source in order to receive a remission.

		\item[2N 31:17] The baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost brings a remission of sin.

		\item[Enos 1:2] A remission of sin is \textit{received} by an individual. It can sometimes take great struggle to receive it. It is also likely that the way in which we receive it--that is, the process we experience in order to receive it--is something that will be unique to us. It may not come in the same way as it does to other people.

		\item[Mo 3:13] A remission of sin requires a belief in Christ. This verse also indicates that it is something received by an individual.

		\item[Mo 4:3] This verse is an excellent example of what is described in 2N 31:17. The remission of sin arrives by means of the Holy Ghost. It is received by individuals. I want to say that the experience of this cleansing, effected by the Holy Ghost, is the experience of receiving a remission of one's sins. In other words, the ``remission of sin'' is the name given to the phenomenon of a person being cleansed by the Holy Ghost, the baptism of fire. Is it also the moment of forgiveness? Is it the same as being forgiven (or receiving a forgiveness), or is it different? I don't know that yet. 

		Another important part of this verse is actually in the verse previous: the people \textit{view themselves in their own carnal state}. Having this experience is probably an important part of the process of repentance and change. It may not be as drastic as this. Perhaps experiences like this one, viewing ourselves in this way, lead us to be able to make the sacrifice of 3N 9:20, a broken heart and a contrite spirit.

		\item[Mo 4:11-12] The remission of sin can be \textit{retained} by following certain steps. There are definite things we can do to retain it. Does this mean that we always retain the feelings which we have upon receiving the baptism of the Holy Ghost? I don't think so. This use of \textit{remission} may extend the concept a little farther--on the eternal balance sheet, the sins are still gone; it doesn't mean that we experience the baptism of fire over and over. Think of DC 82:7 here as well--retaining the remission keeps those former sins from coming back and counting against us? 

		But our weekly experience with the sacrament may be a moment in which we can strive to have the same type of cleaning experience with the Holy Ghost.

		Also in these verses, and in the earlier verse in Mo 4, a remission of sin has a tendency to produce great joy in a person.

		\item[Mo 4:20] In order to receive a remission of sin, we must ask for it--we must call on the name of the Lord, and even beg for it.

		\item[Mo 4:26] More important information about retaining the remission of sin. I would say that the majority of Mo 4 is a set of instructions on how to retain the remission of sin. Verse 26 wraps up a very important question about the way we are to relate to other people, especially those who have fewer material things than us. Recognizing the proper relationship, and acting on it properly, are important in retaining a remission of sin.

		\item[Mo 15:11] Similar to 2N 25:26, we look forward to a remission of our sins; it is something that we desire, and wish to receive.

		\item[Al 4:14] More important parts of the process of retaining a remission of sin. Similar to Mo 4:26.

		\item[Al 7:6] We look \textit{forward} for a remission of sin, and we do that with everlasting faith. It may be that the remission of sin does not come when we want it to; it may not come right when we ask, and we may not have an experience like that of the people who were listening to King Benjamin. But it will come--the scriptures make this clear. ``Has [the Lord] suffered that ye have begged [for a remission of sin] in vain? Nay; he has poured out his Spirit upon you, and has caused that your hearts should be filled with joy...'' (Mo 4:20). 

		The verb \textit{look} appears with \textit{remission} 7 times in the BOM. 6 of those uses also have the word \textit{forward}: we are looking \textit{forward}, not backward, for the remission of our sins. The only use which doesn't have forward is 2N 25:26, but by relation to Al 13:16, it's clear that 2N 25:26 is also looking \textit{forward}. The word \textit{forwardness} appears twice in the scriptures, both in 2Co; the second use is \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{projum'ia}}, which means ``exceptional interest in being of service, \textit{willingness}, \textit{readiness}, \textit{good will}'' (870). I think that idea is along the lines of what the BOM has in mind here with these uses of \textit{forward}--it's a very active \textit{looking} which involves action and mindfulness, keeping the commandments of the Lord.

		\item[Al 12:34] By repenting and not hardening our heart, we have ``claim on mercy'' \textit{through} (interesting word there) Jesus Christ. This claim leads to, or perhaps culminates in, a remission of sin. That seems right; see Al 38:8. 

		\item[Al 13:16] The source of the remission of our sins is Jesus Christ; see 2N 25:26 as well.

		\item[Al 30:16] Korihor claims that the remission of sin is a purely psychological phenomenon, influenced by culture; there is no real remission of sin. He's right in a way--a remission of sin is in part a psychological thing, but there is something in the world that makes a difference. Maybe it's the external component of repentance? See that under TG Repentance. I'm still unclear about that.

		\item[Al 38:8] This verse is important. Alma asks Christ himself for \textit{mercy}; because he has repented, he has a prior \textit{claim} on mercy. See Al 12:34 above. He repented and so had a claim on mercy. He then asked for mercy and received a remission of his sins. The remission comes in the form of a very powerful visitation and conversion experience, described in Al 36. This verse, 38:8, gives a clear example of what Alma is talking about in 12:34. This powerful visitation is the baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost, spoken of in 2N 31:17.

		\item[Hel 14:13] Faith in Jesus Christ leads to repentance; repentance allows us to receive a remission of our sins, through the merits of Christ. See Al 12:34.

		\item[3N 1:23] Baptism (for the purpose of repentance) leads to the remission of sins for many people. Only an individual can receive a remission of sin, I think; but many people can receive it together. Maybe this verse is describing something like what is in the beginning of Mo 4 and 5.

		\item[3N 7:16, 23] Prophets testify of the importance of receiving a remission of our sin. The importance can't just be that it makes us feel good; it qualifies us for eternal life (or is a step on the way to qualification). It isn't just about feeling good or being happy; it's about eternal life.

		\item[3N 7:25] Baptism is a ``witness and a testimony'' before God and other people that we have repented and received a remission of sin. This verse may give some flexibility in understanding the order in which these events are to occur. Reading just from 2N 13 and 17, for example, the order would look like this:

		\begin{center}
		Faith $\rightarrow$ Repentance $\rightarrow$ Baptism by water $\rightarrow$ Baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost/remission of sin
		\end{center}

		But from 3N 7:25 we can see that it's possible to receive a remission of sins before baptism, just through repentance, and that one of the functions of baptism is to serve as a formal witness to others that the remission has been received. This flexibility is important. The following quote seems to both support and contradict this:

		\begin{quote}
		\item ``Ah!'' says one, ``Cannot I come to the foot of the cross and, through the atoning blood of Jesus, have my sins washed away without baptism?'' I doubt not that hundreds, in various nations and generations, who have been in ignorance of the true Gospel, and far removed from those who had authority to administer its ordinances, have had their sins blotted out. God has looked in mercy upon them, and on account of their sincerity has witnessed unto them that he accepted the broken spirits and contrite hearts which they offered unto him. I cannot doubt this; but wherever the Gospel of Jesus Christ is preached in its fullness, none can obtain the remission of sins only in the way that God has pointed out, and that is by baptism by one having the authority from God to administer that ordinance (JD 15:115).
		\end{quote}

		What's probably true here is that, when we know the true way of the gospel, we cannot continue following the path of Jesus Christ unless we are baptized, regardless of whether we have already received a remission of our sins. See Acts 10 and the story of Cornelius; I would say that's what's going on in that story.

		\item[3N 12:2] The baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost and the remission of sins are spoken of as separate here, in a way similar to 2N 31:17. I think 2N 31:17 helps us to understand what Christ means here--that the remission of sins comes through that visitation and cleansing of the Holy Ghost.

		\item[3N 30:2] Receiving a remission is one of the steps that we need to take in order to follow Christ. It's interesting that \textit{being filled with the Holy Ghost} is spoken of \textit{after} the remission of sins here; compare Mo 4:12: \textit{And behold, I say unto you that if ye do this ye shall always rejoice, and be filled with the love of God, and always retain a remission of your sins; and ye shall grow in the knowledge of the glory of him that created you, or in the knowledge of that which is just and true.} 3N 30:2 reminds me of that verse. Those who are seeking it are filled with the love of God in Mo 4:12, and the Holy Ghost in 3N 30:2. It could be that being filled with the Holy Ghost is part of the reason why we are able to \textit{grow in the knowledge of the glory of him that created us}.

		\item[Mor 3:3] Again, those who are called to preach the gospel preach the remission of sin; see 3N 7:16, 23.

		\item[Mor 8:11] Trying to get a handle on the meanings of \textit{unto} and \textit{to} in this verse is a totally different project, which hopefully I will be able to do sometime. Here is my gloss of the second part of this verse:

		``Behold, baptism is a part of the process of repentance--specifically, it's part of the requirement to fulfill the commandments, which we do in order to receive a remission of sins.''

		This interpretation of the verse is influenced by Mor 8:25-26. See below.

		\item[Mor 8:25-26] Verse 25 is the influence for my interpretation of Mor 8:11 above. When 8:11 is put that way, verses 11 and 25 say very much the same thing.

		It may be that 8:26 gives a reason to reject the understanding I've been pushing of the remission of sins as the baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost--some visitation of the Spirit. I've said, and the scriptures also say, that the remission of sins comes by the baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost (2N 31:17). But if we ignored that, Mor 8:26 makes it look as though the remission of sins can come without any fanfare or even perhaps any awareness on our part, because the Holy Ghost visits later (though, if we knew this scripture, and were feeling meekness and lowliness of heart, we might reason that we had received a remission of sin).

		But I don't think that we really need to change anything in order to accommodate this verse. We know that the baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost effects the remission of sins in us. Once we've received that, we begin to become more meek and lowly of heart. These Christlike characteristics allow the Holy Ghost to visit us more frequently and bring a different kind of fruit: he fills us with hope and perfect love. His mission here isn't to witness to us that we have been forgiven, or received a remission; it's to inspire us, purify us, and make us even more like Jesus Christ (see Mor 7:48).

		3N 30:2 actually goes along with this as well--the visitation of the Holy Ghost in that verse need not be the one associated with the remission of sins, but it could be this second visitation from Mor 8:26. This all may look back to Mo 4:12 as well.

		One observation from this verse, then, is that the remission of sins is an extremely important part not only of our early spiritual progress, but of our continuing spiritual progress and purification and sanctification. Thus the importance of Mo 4:12 in retaining a remission of sin.

		One last thing--given what I've said above, there's an ambiguity in interpreting 3N 9:20. Which of the following is the proper interpretation of ``the Lamanites...at the time of their conversion, were baptized with fire and with the Holy Ghost, and they knew it not''?

		\begin{compactenum}
		\item This baptism came to them but they did not realize anything had come. They felt nothing.
		\item This baptism came to them and they felt the Holy Ghost. They were aware that they were feeling it. However, they did not realize that the particular experience they were having just happened to be the baptism of fire and of the Holy Ghost.
		\item ``Time'' ought to be understood very loosely here, not as one particular occasion but as an extended period. The Lamanites were converted gradually, and as they were, more and more frequent visitations of the Holy Ghost cleansed them.
		\end{compactenum}

		Not sure which is best right now. Not sure that it matters either, because all three could happen to me, and all have the same result in the end.

		\item[Mor 10:33] Both this verse and the one before it lay down a way to be perfected in Christ. It is very general but there are many important principles here. The \textit{unto} right before ``remission'' probably means ``for,'' at least as I'm thinking about it right now. It looks like this verse is saying that the Atonement is a part of the plan of salvation in order to make possible the remission of sins.

		\end{description}

		\paragraph*{Summary of BOM uses of \textit{remission}.}Here's a bit of a summary of what the BOM say about a remission of sin:

			\begin{compactitem}
			\item The remission of sin has a source, and the source is Jesus Christ and the Atonement.
			\item The remission of sin comes by means of the baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost.
			\item An individual receives a remission of sin; it may only come with great difficulty, but will arrive in a way unique to that person.
			\item A remission of sin can be retained by following certain steps.
			\item We have to ask, even \textit{beg}, to receive a remission of sin.
			\item We are instructed to look \textit{forward} to a remission of sin. We may not be able to choose the time and place that it comes, or the way in which it comes, but we are promised that it will come.
			\item A remission of sin is both a psychological (internal) and external phenomenon.
			\item Prophets testify of the importance of receiving a remission of sin.
			\item Remission of sin can come before or after the baptism of water.
			\item Fulfilling the commandments is an important part of receiving the remission of sin.
			\item One of the reasons for the Atonement is to make possible the remission of sin.
			\end{compactitem}

	% -----
	\subsubsection{NT Uses}
	% -----

		Here's a list of the KJV NT uses of ``remission.''

		\begin{description}

		\item[Mt 26:28] \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>'afesis}}. 

		\item[Mk 1:4] \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>'afesis}}.

		\item[Lk 1:77] \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>'afesis}}.

		\item[Lk 3:3] \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>'afesis}}.

		\item[Lk 24:47] \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>'afesis}}.

		\item[Acts 2:38] \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>'afesis}}.

		\item[Acts 10:43] \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>'afesis}}.

		\item[Rom 3:25] \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{p'aresis}}. There is an interesting difference in translations of this verse. \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{p'aresis}} means ``deliberate disregard, \textit{passing over, letting go unpunished}'' (776a). To me this does not seem the same as forgiveness. Translations vary:

		\begin{description}
		\item[NIV] God presented him as a sacrifice of atonement, through faith in his blood. He did this to demonstrate his justice, because in his forbearance he had left the sins committed beforehand unpunished
		\item[NRSV] whom God put forward as a sacrifice of atonement by his blood, effective through faith. He did this to show his righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over the sins previously committed;
		\item[NASB] whom God displayed publicly as a propitiation in His blood through faith. \textit{This was} to demonstrate His righteousness, because in the forbearance of God He passed over the sins previously committed;
		\item[NAB] whom God set forth as an expiation, through faith, by his blood, to prove his righteousness because of the forgiveness of sins previously committed,
		\end{description}

		Very interesting that the NAB uses \textit{forgiveness}. The other translators take a different view. The Middle Liddell says that \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{p'aresis}} means ``a letting go, remission,'' and cites the NT.

		This is the only use of \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{p'aresis}} in the Greek NT.

		\item[Heb 9:22] \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>'afesis}}.

		\item[Heb 10:18] \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>'afesis}}.

		\end{description}

		\paragraph*{Summary of NT uses of \textit{remission}.}\textit{Remission} appears in the KJV NT 10 times; nine of these are \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>'afesis}}, and the other is \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{p'aresis}}.

			The definition for \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>'afesis}} is ``the act of freeing and liberating from something that confines, \textit{release}; the act of freeing from an obligation, built, or punishment, \textit{pardon, cancellation}'' (155a).

			Here are the other uses of \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>'afesis}}:

			\begin{description}

			\item[Mk 3:29] \textbf{forgiveness}.

			\item[Lk 4:18] \textbf{deliverance}, \textbf{at liberty} (part of an idiom which means \textit{to set free the oppressed}).

			\item[Acts 5:31] \textbf{forgiveness}.

			\item[Acts 13:38] \textbf{forgiveness}.

			\item[Acts 26:18] \textbf{forgiveness}.

			\item[Eph 1:7] \textbf{forgiveness}.

			\item[Col 1:14] \textbf{forgiveness}.

			\end{description}

			So when talking about remission of sin, and forgiveness of sin, the key Greek word is \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>'afesis}}.

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Things to do to retain a remission of sin}
	% -----

		We can retain a remission of our sins and walk \textit{guiltless} (Mo 4:26) before God. The scriptures teach us how to do this. It is possible. What an amazing thing to discover and know.

		See Mo 4:11-12, 26; Al 4:14.

		Note that the JD does not contain even a single occurrence of the idea of \textit{retaining} a remission of sins; it just wasn't spoken of in that way during that time. The BOM clearly talks about that, though.

\subsection{Remorse of conscience} % *REMORSECONSCIENCE *REMORSEOFCONSCIENCE
% -----------------------

	\begin{description}
	\item[TPJS 49--50] All regularly organized and well established governments have certain laws by which, more or less, the innocent are protected and the guilty punished. The fact admitted that certain laws are good, equitable and just, ought to be binding upon the individual who admits this, and lead him to observe in the strictest manner an obedience to those laws. These laws when violated, or broken by the individual, must, in justice, convict his mind with a double force, if possible, of the extent and magnitude of his crime; because he could have no plea of ignorance to produce; and his act of transgression was openly committed against light and knowledge. But the individual who may be ignorant and imperceptibly transgresses or violates laws, though the voice of the country requires that he should suffer, yet he will never feel that remorse of conscience that the other will, and that keen, cutting reflection will never rise in his breast that otherwise would, had he done the deed, or committed the offense in full conviction that he was breaking the law of his country, and having previously acknowledged the same to be just.
	\end{description}
