% -----------------------
\subsection{Repentance} % *REPENTANCE
% -----------------------

	Repentance is the most general principle of progression for intelligences (minds). See Mor 8:25--26 as a general description of this process, especially interpreting terms like ``baptism'' in the broadest way possible (according to Al 32:16, for example).
		Repentance is comprised of several subtypes, including at (1) atoning for sin and (2) learning. But both those things---and I expect this to be true for other subtypes as well---are just different ways of describing repentance in different circumstances.
		Some of the laws of repentance, or the laws of progression for minds:
			that by keeping the commandments we receive a remission of sin (DC 76:52, Mor 8:25, DC 1:32);

	% -----
	\subsubsection{General views on repentance}
	% -----

		According to the original articles of faith in the Wentworth Letter, repentance is an ordinance (JSP-H1 500). See 3N 9:19--20 for a possible action that accompanies the ordinance of repentance: a broken heart and a contrite spirit. That's what Andrus thinks anyway, and I like it. In verse 19 and the OT, it's easy to interpret the scriptures as saying that the people offered sacrifice as part of their repentance process; we do the same now, to fulfill that ordinance, but the sacrifice comes from within ourselves.

		Repentance is the process of (1) receiving and retaining a remission of sin, and (2) becoming pure and holy.

		It may be that sometimes the word \textit{repentance} is used in the scriptures to denote different things. It can denote the overarching umbrella concept, which I discuss below in the aspects section; it may also refer to something more limited, as DC 1:32 shows (it separates repentance from keeping the commandments).

		Something else to keep in mind--there are at least three different ways of thinking about or viewing repentance. I don't know how well these correspond to the senses of the word in the scriptures, but there may be some matching up in some cases.

		\begin{compactenum}
		\item Repentance is an \textit{act} that I do when I commit a serious sin.
		\item Repentance is an \textit{act} that I do regularly, not just for serious sins.
		\item Repentance is a \textit{way of life}.
		\end{compactenum}

		I'm not quite sure how to describe (3) more than that yet. The word in the scriptures that goes with (3) is \textit{penitent}. It is used only in the BOM, and only once outside of Alma. A \textit{penitent} person is one for whom repentance is a way of life--they are constantly seeking to gain more light and knowledge, and more of God's presence in their earthly life. A powerful scripture here is Al 27:17-18:

		\begin{quote}
		Now the joy of Ammon was so great even that he was full; yea, he was swallowed up in the joy of his God, even to the exhausting of his strength; and he fell again to the earth. Now was not this exceeding joy? Behold, this is joy which none receiveth save it be the truly penitent and humble seeker of happiness.
		\end{quote}

		That is the type of life we want, and the type of repentance we want to have.

		How about this? I would say that repentance is \textit{the process of receiving and retaining a remission of sin}. If we go with that, it doesn't really make sense to say something like, ``I need to repent of that sin.'' You need to ask God for mercy with respect to that sin, maybe, but you're engaged in repentance all the time; potentially every act we engage in can be an act of repentance, for we are always in the process of trying to gain and keep a remission of sin. Since fulfilling the commandments is an aspect of repentance, we are always in the act of repentance.
		
		\begin{description}
		\item[Ps 51] This whole chapter has a lot about repentance, very beautiful.
		\end{description}

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Aspects of the repentance process}
	% -----

		It seems like repentance is a very broad, overarching concept. We may not be able to break it down into a chronological series of \textit{steps} that must be taken, but there are at least some \textit{parts} that we can identify and expound on.

		\begin{description}
		\item[Fulfilling the commandments] See my gloss of Mor 8:11 in the TG Remission section above. Also see DC 1:32, DC 58:42-43, 
		\item[Asking for mercy] Is this the individual act of repentance? Another way of using the word? See Al 12:34, 38:8,
		\item[Other people] Specifically, the way in which we conceptualize our relationship and duties to others, and then act on them; see Mo 4:26,
		\item[Relationship to faith] See Hel 5:41, where repentance seems to precede faith;
		\end{description}

	% -----
	\subsubsection{``Balancing the eternal scales'' view of repentance}
	% -----

		There seems to be an internal and an external component to repentance. Some scriptures that may refer to the external component: Al 12:34; Al 42:18-21 (and possibly others; 18, 19, and 20 talk about internal, while 21 seems to switch to external?), 

		distinction: balance-the-scale thinking vs. progression thinking--ways of thinking about our obedience and repentance. In the former, we are always trying to make up for something, or cover a debt, or something like that; in the latter, we are always moving forward?
		
		Note Job 11:6, even with repentance we're still getting a better deal than we deserve.
		
		\begin{description}
		\item[Mor 8:22--24] For behold that all little children are alive in Christ, and also all they that are without the law. For the power of redemption cometh on all them that have no law; wherefore, he that is not condemned, or he that is under no condemnation, cannot repent; and unto such baptism availeth nothing--23 But it is mockery before God, denying the mercies of Christ, and the power of his Holy Spirit, and putting trust in dead works. 24 Behold, my son, this thing ought not to be; for repentance is unto them that are under condemnation and under the curse of a broken law.
		\end{description}

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Up until when is it possible to repent?}
	% -----
	
		The scriptures call the time period during which we can repent the ``day of salvation'' (Al 34:31) or the ``day of grace'' (Morm 2:15). This day has a natural end, after which we can't repent (Al 34:33), but we can also cause the end of the day artificially early through our wickedness (Morm 2:15).

	% -----
	\subsubsection{NT Uses}
	% -----

		Every occurrence in the KJV of \textit{repent} or \textit{repentance} is a form of the word \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{metano'ew}} (the verb) or \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{met'anoia}} (the noun), \textbf{except for} the uses which appear on the following list.

		Note that Lk 5:32 is the same as Mt 9:13 and Mk 2:17, but has the \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{met'anoian}} there.

		\begin{description}

		\item[Mt 9:13] In Greek, this passage ends, \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{o>u g`ar >\char"007Ehljon kal'esai dika'ious >all'a <amartwlo'us}}. There is no occurrence of any word that could mean \textit{repentance}. The word isn't in italics in the KJV, so it must have been in the manuscripts, and was later discovered to be an incorrect addition. See note above for Lk 5:32. 

		\item[Mt 21:29] The Greek word here is \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{metam'elomai}}, which means to change one's mind. This does seem to be an old use of the word \textit{repent}.

		\item[Mt 21:32] \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{metam'elomai}} here. 

		\item[Mt 27:3] The Greek is \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{metam'elomai}} here as well; the gloss in my Bible is ``to be sorry.''

		\item[Mk 2:17] Same situation as Mt 9:13. See note above for Lk 5:32.

		\item[Rom 11:29] The Greek here is \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>ametam'elhta g`ar t`a qar'ismata ka`i <h kl\char"007Ehsis to\char"007Eu jeo\char"007Eu}}. The word translated as \textit{repentance} in the KJV is \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>ametam'elhta}}, which means \textit{irrevocable}; this word is a form of \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{metam'elomai}}, which appears in a few verses above, combined with \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{a}}-privative.

		\item[2Co 7:8] Two uses here, both \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{metam'elomai}}. Note that the next verse \textit{does} have \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{met'anoia}}.

		\item[2Co 7:10] This verse contains two uses of \textit{repent}: ``repentance'' and '' be repented of.'' \textbf{The first is \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{met'anoia}}; the second is \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>ametam'elhton}}.}

		\item[Heb 7:21] \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{metam'elomai}} here. 

		\end{description}

		\paragraph*{Summary of NT uses of \textit{repent}:}

		\begin{itemize}

		\item The words \textit{repent} and \textit{repentance} occur a total of 66 times in the NT. 

		\item Every occurrence of \textit{repent} or \textit{repentance} in the KJV NT is \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{metano'ew}} or \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{met'anoia}}, respectively, \textbf{with 10 exceptions that fall into one of two groups}:

		\begin{description}
		\item[Group 1] \textbf{Mt 9:13; Mk 2:17.} These verses appear to be modeled after Lk 5:32, but do not include the word \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{met'anoia}}.
		\item[Group 2a] \textbf{Mt 21:29, 32; 27:3; 2Co 7:8 (2); Heb 7:21.} These are a form of the verb \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{metam'elomai}}.
		\item[Group 2b] \textbf{Rom 11:29; 2Co 7:10b.} These are a form of the adjective \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>ametam'elhtos}}.
		\end{description}

		\item The word \textit{repent} does not appear in any form in the gospel of John; neither do the Greek words \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{metano'ew}} or \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{met'anoia}}.

		\end{itemize}

		For reference, the definition of \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{metam'elomai}} is ``to have regrets about something, in the sense that one wishes it could be undone, \textit{be very sorry, regret}; to change one's mind about something, without focus on regret, \textit{change one's mind, have second thoughts}.

		The definition of \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>ametam'elhtos}} is ``not to be regretted, without regret; feeling no remorse, having no regret.''.

		Additional reference:

		\begin{compactitem}
		\item \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{metano'ew}} appears 34 times in the Greek text. In the KJV it is translated as \textit{repent} every time. 
		\item \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{met'anoia}} appears 22 times in the Greek text. In the KJV it is translated as \textit{repentance} every time.
		\item \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>ametam'elhtos}} appears 2 times in the Greek text. Both translations in the KJV use a form of the word \textit{repent}.
		\end{compactitem}

	% -----
	\subsubsection{OT Uses}
	% -----

		A few notes first, since I'm not going to go all the way yet:

		\begin{itemize}

		\item The first two uses of \textit{repent} are in Gen 6:6 and 6:7. In the LXX the words are \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>enjum'eomai}} and \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{jum'ow}}, respectively; different words. The first means \textit{to lay to heart, to ponder}; the second, \textit{to be angry} (it's a passive form in Gen 6:7). So God is wondering why he made man? Or just reflecting on it? 

		The Hebrew, on the other hand, has the same word in both verses. It's the Niphal form of \textcolor{red}{\<n.hm>}, which means generally \textit{to be sorry, console oneself}, and perhaps more particularly here \textit{be sorry, rue, suffer grief}. See BDB 636-37.

		\end{itemize}

\subsection{Replenish} % *REPLENISH
% -----------------------

	In ``multiply and replenish the earth,'' the Hebrew means ``fill,'' so there isn't the sense of RE-plenishing, or over doing it over again after it's been done in the past. On the ``fill'' idea, see DC 29:23--24 (especially 24) and 1N 17:36.

\subsection{Requisite} % *REQUISITE
% -----------------------

	1828:
		Required by the nature of things or by circumstances; necessary; so needful that it cannot be dispensed with.

% -----------------------
\subsection{Resurrection} % *RESURRECTION
% -----------------------

	The resurrection restores us to the physical presence of God, overcoming the temporal death which comes upon us because of the Fall.

	\begin{description}
	\item[2N 2:8] Wherefore, how great the importance to make these things known unto the inhabitants of the earth, that they may know that there is no flesh that can dwell in the presence of God, save it be through the merits, and mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah, who layeth down his life according to the flesh, and taketh it again by the power of the Spirit, that he may bring to pass the resurrection of the dead, being the first that should rise.
	\item[2N 9:4] For I know that ye have searched much, many of you, to know of things to come; wherefore I know that ye know that our flesh must waste away and die; nevertheless, in our bodies we shall see God.
	\item[2N 9:11--13] And because of the way of deliverance of our God, the Holy One of Israel, this death, of which I have spoken, which is the temporal, shall deliver up its dead; which death is the grave. 12 And this death of which I have spoken, which is the spiritual death, shall deliver up its dead; which spiritual death is hell; wherefore, death and hell must deliver up their dead, and hell must deliver up its captive spirits, and the grave must deliver up its captive bodies, and the bodies and the spirits of men will be restored one to the other; and it is by the power of the resurrection of the Holy One of Israel. 13 O how great the plan of our God! 	% -----
	\subsubsection{Universality of the resurrection}
	% -----
	
		One way to reconcile BY's comment at CDBY 637--638 below, about not everyone getting a resurrection, with scriptures like Hel 14:16--17, might be to think of Christ's resurrection as bringing everyone back into the presence of God---but not necessarily giving everyone a resurrected body. Everyone returns to God's presence, but not everyone gets another body. There's nothing in Al 40 which goes against this, at least from a quick review of it, and same for Al 41 and 42. But Al 11:41--45 makes it clear that everyone will come back into the presence of God, \textit{and} that everyone will get a body. So if we wanted to reconcile these verses with what BY says we'd have to say that some people are an exception to the ``all'' in Al 11:44 or something. And of course in that quote from BY he's only giving his opinion; I haven't seen that idea anywhere else. There's a way of reading DC 88:26--32 in which not everyone gets a body, too. Those verses are only explicit about ``bodies'' when talking about the celestial kingdom. This connects back to Al 11:45, ``the whole becoming spiritual,'' and the ``spiritual bodies'' mentioned in 88:27. Hyrum Andrus takes these verses to mean that the physical body has a spiritual nature---it's quickened by the Spirit for immortal glory. That may not be the only way to see it, you might see it as actually referring to a spirit and not a physical body. See 1Co 15:44.

I say unto you that this mortal body is raised to an immortal body, that is from death, even from the first death unto life, that they can die no more; their spirits uniting with their bodies, never to be divided; thus the whole becoming spiritual and immortal, that they can no more see corruption.

% -----------------------
\subsection{Round (eternal)} % *ROUND *ETERNALROUND
% -----------------------

	From the 1828 dictionary, under the noun ``round'':

	\begin{enumerate}
	\item A circle; a circular thing, or a circle in motion.
	\item Action or performance in a circle, or passing through a series of hands or things and coming to the point of beginning; or the time of such action.
	\item Rotation in office; succession in vicissitude.
	\item A rundle; the step of a ladder.
	\end{enumerate}
	
	(Compare OED definition 13, ``A cylindrical part of an implement or other manufactured object,'' and 13a, ``A rung of a ladder.'')

	I love definition \#4. A ``rundle'' is just the rung of a ladder. The Lord's course isn't the ladder, but an eternal rung? Or an eternal climbing-up of the ladder, rung by rung, to higher heights? But also in play are the circular ideas of him repeating the same course of action eternity after eternity to perfect more spirits; see the diagram from Orson Hyde that I mention below.

	The other definition of ``rundle'' from the 1828 dictionary is, ``Something put round an axis; a peritrochium; as a cylinder with a rundle about it.'' This is maybe not so related to the eternal round part, but it makes me think of Orson Hyde's diagram of the kingdom of God on page 168 of Words. The OED for ``peritrochium'' is ``A wheel, as part of the mechanical power called the wheel and axle.'' It tells you to ``Cf. axis in peritrochio,'' and that definition says, ``The axle of a wheel...wheel and axis, axis in peritrochio: the Wheel-and-Axle, one of the mechanical powers.'' It's one of the simple machines? I don't know the history here, but it brings up some very interesting images for the gospel.
	
	Uses of ``eternal round'':
		\begin{description}
		\item[1N 10:19] For he that diligently seeketh shall find; and the mysteries of God shall be unfolded unto them, by the power of the Holy Ghost, as well in these times as in times of old, and as well in times of old as in times to come; wherefore, the course of the Lord is one eternal round.
		\item[Al 7:20] I perceive that it has been made known unto you, by the testimony of his word, that he cannot walk in crooked paths; neither doth he vary from that which he hath said; neither hath he a shadow of turning from the right to the left, or from that which is right to that which is wrong; therefore, his course is one eternal round.
		\item[Al 37:12] And it may suffice if I only say they are preserved for a wise purpose, which purpose is known unto God; for he doth counsel in wisdom over all his works, and his paths are straight, and his course is one eternal round.
		\item[DC 3:2] For God doth not walk in crooked paths, neither doth he turn to the right hand nor to the left, neither doth he vary from that which he hath said, therefore his paths are straight, and his course is one eternal round.
		\item[DC 35:1] LISTEN to the voice of the Lord your God, even Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, whose course is one eternal round, the same today as yesterday, and forever.
		\end{description}
		
	% -----
	\subsubsection{BOM uses}
	% -----
	
		A form of ``round'' appears 92 times in the BOM.
		86 of those times are in the adverbial phrase ``round about,'' like ``I cast my eyes round about and saw Lebron James.''
		The other 6 uses:
			3 are ``eternal round'' in the list above
			1 describes the Liahona, ``a round ball of curious workmanship'' (1N 16:10)
			1 is a quote from the Bible, ``round tires like the moon'' (2N 13:18, Isa 3:18)
			1 describes a war, ``the whole face of this land is one continual round of murder and bloodshed'' (Morm 8:8)

\subsection{Sabbath} % *SABBATH
% -----------------------

	The Sabbath for the Nephites wasn't the day they got together to hear the word of God; see Mo 18:23--25, Al 1:26; and maybe 31:12, about the Zoramites;

	\begin{description}
	\item[DC 59:8--14] Thou shalt offer a sacrifice unto the Lord thy God in righteousness, even that of a broken heart and a contrite spirit. 9 And that thou mayest more fully keep thyself unspotted from the world, thou shalt go to the house of prayer and offer up thy sacraments upon my holy day; 10 For verily this is a day appointed unto you to rest from your labors, and to pay thy devotions unto the Most High; 11 Nevertheless thy vows shall be offered up in righteousness on all days and at all times; 12 But remember that on this, the Lord's day, thou shalt offer thine oblations and thy sacraments unto the Most High, confessing thy sins unto thy brethren, and before the Lord. 13 And on this day thou shalt do none other thing, only let thy food be prepared with singleness of heart that thy fasting may be perfect, or, in other words, that thy joy may be full. 14 Verily, this is fasting and prayer, or in other words, rejoicing and prayer.
	\item[Neh 10:31] And if the people of the land bring ware or any victuals on the sabbath day to sell, that we would not buy it of them on the sabbath, or on the holy day: and that we would leave the seventh year, and the exaction of every debt.
	\item[Neh 13:15--22] In those days saw I in Judah some treading wine presses on the sabbath, and bringing in sheaves, and lading asses; as also wine, grapes, and figs, and all manner of burdens, which they brought into Jerusalem on the sabbath day: and I testified against them in the day wherein they sold victuals. 16 There dwelt men of Tyre also therein, which brought fish, and all manner of ware, and sold on the sabbath unto the children of Judah, and in Jerusalem. 17 Then I contended with the nobles of Judah, and said unto them, What evil thing is this that ye do, and profane the sabbath day? 18 Did not your fathers thus, and did not our God bring all this evil upon us, and upon this city? yet ye bring more wrath upon Israel by profaning the sabbath. 19 And it came to pass, that when the gates of Jerusalem began to be dark before the sabbath, I commanded that the gates should be shut, and charged that they should not be opened till after the sabbath: and some of my servants set I at the gates, that there should no burden be brought in on the sabbath day. 20 So the merchants and sellers of all kind of ware lodged without Jerusalem once or twice. 21 Then I testified against them, and said unto them, Why lodge ye about the wall? if ye do so again, I will lay hands on you. From that time forth came they no more on the sabbath. 22 And I commanded the Levites that they should cleanse themselves, and that they should come and keep the gates, to sanctify the sabbath day. Remember me, O my God, concerning this also, and spare me according to the greatness of thy mercy.
	\item[Ps 92] This psalm is subtitled ``a psalm or song for the sabbath day,'' but it's a bit hard to see the connection.
	\item[Isa 56] A number of mentions of the sabbath and blessings associated with it.
	\item[Isa 58:13--14] If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words: 14 Then shalt thou delight thyself in the LORD; and I will cause thee to ride upon the high places of the earth, and feed thee with the heritage of Jacob thy father: for the mouth of the LORD hath spoken it.
	\item[Eze 20] (``Sabbaths'' mentioned several times in these verses, some nice examples.)
	\end{description}

\subsection{Satan (Devil)} % *SATAN
% -----------------------

	Under ``angels,'' see entry on being angels to a devil.
	
	Called Lucifer in the pre-existence, but gets a new name and becomes Satan.
	
	\begin{description}
	\item[DC 76:25--38]
	\item[Isa 14:4--23] That thou shalt take up this proverb against the king of Babylon, and say, How hath the oppressor ceased! the golden city ceased! 5 The LORD hath broken the staff of the wicked, and the sceptre of the rulers. 6 He who smote the people in wrath with a continual stroke, he that ruled the nations in anger, is persecuted, and none hindereth. 7 The whole earth is at rest, and is quiet: they break forth into singing. 8 Yea, the fir trees rejoice at thee, and the cedars of Lebanon, saying, Since thou art laid down, no feller is come up against us. 9 Hell from beneath is moved for thee to meet thee at thy coming: it stirreth up the dead for thee, even all the chief ones of the earth; it hath raised up from their thrones all the kings of the nations. 10 All they shall speak and say unto thee, Art thou also become weak as we? art thou become like unto us? 11 Thy pomp is brought down to the grave, and the noise of thy viols: the worm is spread under thee, and the worms cover thee. 12 How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! how art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations! 13 For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north: 14 I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the most High. 15 Yet thou shalt be brought down to hell, to the sides of the pit. 16 They that see thee shall narrowly look upon thee, and consider thee, saying, Is this the man that made the earth to tremble, that did shake kingdoms; 17 That made the world as a wilderness, and destroyed the cities thereof; that opened not the house of his prisoners? 18 All the kings of the nations, even all of them, lie in glory, every one in his own house. 19 But thou art cast out of thy grave like an abominable branch, and as the raiment of those that are slain, thrust through with a sword, that go down to the stones of the pit; as a carcase trodden under feet. 20 Thou shalt not be joined with them in burial, because thou hast destroyed thy land, and slain thy people: the seed of evildoers shall never be renowned. 21 Prepare slaughter for his children for the iniquity of their fathers; that they do not rise, nor possess the land, nor fill the face of the world with cities. 22 For I will rise up against them, saith the LORD of hosts, and cut off from Babylon the name, and remnant, and son, and nephew, saith the LORD. 23 I will also make it a possession for the bittern, and pools of water: and I will sweep it with the besom of destruction, saith the LORD of hosts.
	\end{description}

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Ultimate fate}
	% -----
	
		\begin{description}
		\item[TPJS 24] Say to the brothers Hulet and to all others, that the Lord never authorized them to say that the devil, his angels, or the sons of perdition, should ever be restored; for their state of destiny was not revealed to man, is not revealed, nor ever shall be revealed, save to those who are made partakers thereof: consequently those who teach this doctrine have not received it of the Spirit of the Lord. Truly Brother Oliver declared it to be the doctrine of devils. We, therefore, command that this doctrine be taught no more in Zion. We sanction the decision of the Bishop and his council, in relation to this doctrine being a bar to communion.
		\end{description}

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Children of the devil}
	% -----

		Just as we can become the children of Christ, so we can become the children of the devil.

		\begin{description}
		\item[Eph 2:3] Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others.
		\item[1N 14:3] And that great pit, which hath been digged for them by that great and abominable church, which was founded by the devil and his children, that he might lead away the souls of men down to hell---yea, that great pit which hath been digged for the destruction of men shall be filled by those who digged it, unto their utter destruction, saith the Lamb of God; not the destruction of the soul, save it be the casting of it into that hell which hath no end.
		\item[2N 9:46] Prepare your souls for that glorious day when justice shall be administered unto the righteous, even the day of judgment, that ye may not shrink with awful fear; that ye may not remember your awful guilt in perfectness, and be constrained to exclaim: Holy, holy are thy judgments, O Lord God Almighty---but I know my guilt; I transgressed thy law, and my transgressions are mine; and the devil hath obtained me, that I am a prey to his awful misery.
		\item[Al 10:28] And now it came to pass that when Amulek had spoken these words the people cried out against him, saying: Now we know that this man is a child of the devil, for he hath lied unto us; for he hath spoken against our law. And now he says that he has not spoken against it.
		\item[Al 11:23] Now Amulek said: O thou child of hell, why tempt ye me? Knowest thou that the righteous yieldeth to no such temptations?
		\item[Al 41:4] And if their works are evil they shall be restored unto them for evil. Therefore, all things shall be restored to their proper order, every thing to its natural frame---mortality raised to immortality, corruption to incorruption---raised to endless happiness to inherit the kingdom of God, or to endless misery to inherit the kingdom of the devil, the one on one hand, the other on the other---
		\item[DC 76:32] (In verse 26 Satan is called ``Perdition,'' so if we're the sons of perdition, it's like having a negative rebirth.) They are they who are the sons of perdition, of whom I say that it had been better for them never to have been born;
		\end{description}
		
	% -----
	\subsubsection{Satan seals us}
	% -----
	
		\begin{description}
		\item[2N 9:46] Prepare your souls for that glorious day when justice shall be administered unto the righteous, even the day of judgment, that ye may not shrink with awful fear; that ye may not remember your awful guilt in perfectness, and be constrained to exclaim: Holy, holy are thy judgments, O Lord God Almighty---but I know my guilt; I transgressed thy law, and my transgressions are mine; and the devil hath obtained me, that I am a prey to his awful misery.
		\item[Al 34:34--35] Ye cannot say, when ye are brought to that awful crisis, that I will repent, that I will return to my God. Nay, ye cannot say this; for that same spirit which doth possess your bodies at the time that ye go out of this life, that same spirit will have power to possess your body in that eternal world. 35 For behold, if ye have procrastinated the day of your repentance even until death, behold, ye have become subjected to the spirit of the devil, and he doth seal you his; therefore, the Spirit of the Lord hath withdrawn from you, and hath no place in you, and the devil hath all power over you; and this is the final state of the wicked.
		\end{description}
		
	% -----
	\subsubsection{Satan's fall}
	% -----
	
		\begin{description}
		\item[CDBY 441] Why not quarrel about Christ coming instead of the Father? When the Father appointed Jesus Christ, the Firstborn, to come and redeem the earth, there was contention got up. The second brother, Lucifer, the son of the morning, wanted the honor to come and redeem the earth. But Christ was the appointed one. It was His right by appointment and birthright. But the war and contention became so hot and the influence of Lucifer was so great that he got one-third of the hosts in heaven to join his standard, and when he was hurled down to hell like lightning from heaven, one-third was cast down with him. Where is he and those that were cast down? With those spirits that accompanied him. They are here on this earth and they have blinded the children of men and [are] still seeking to overthrow the kingdom of God. He is a thorn in the flesh of the children of God. But this is all right, and we should be contented with what God sees fit to grant unto us and be contented with our lot. If the Devil had been contented and acted in his place, he would not have been thrust down to hell. Any man who seeks to do a thing that he cannot do, and should not do, it casts him into hell and makes a hell for him when men ask for things that do not belong to him and it makes him unhappy.
		\item[CDBY 1494] Prest. Young remarked that he did not want to give endowments, only to old people, as they would not be likely to apostatize; but then if we were to carry out that, we should not ordain anyone, only those who would not apostatize; as we would not baptize anyone, only those who would not apostatize. And to carry the thing still further, we expect all who are faithful to take the place of Adam's in worlds to be created; then if there were no apostates, what would we do for devils? As we have to get our devils from this earth, for the worlds that are to be created.
		\end{description}

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Powers and priesthoods} % *SATANPOWERS
	% -----
	
		We know that Satan has power over us only when we allow him to; does \textit{all} his power come this way? Think of the Skousen account of God's power; does Satan get his power the same way? If the elements obey God at all times (Hel 12:7--8), it seems significant that we, a congregation of many elements, higher-order beings, are (the only ones?) able to disobey and allow Satan to have power. Pure speculation, but maybe Satan's power only arises when there's high-level conscious choice.

		\begin{description}
		\item[1N 13:29] And after these plain and precious things were taken away it goeth forth unto all the nations of the Gentiles; and after it goeth forth unto all the nations of the Gentiles, yea, even across the many waters which thou hast seen with the Gentiles which have gone forth out of captivity, thou seest---because of the many plain and precious things which have been taken out of the book, which were plain unto the understanding of the children of men, according to the plainness which is in the Lamb of God---because of these things which are taken away out of the gospel of the Lamb, an exceedingly great many do stumble, yea, insomuch that Satan hath great power over them.
		\item[1N 14:3--7] And that great pit, which hath been digged for them by that great and abominable church, which was founded by the devil and his children, that he might lead away the souls of men down to hell---yea, that great pit which hath been digged for the destruction of men shall be filled by those who digged it, unto their utter destruction, saith the Lamb of God; not the destruction of the soul, save it be the casting of it into that hell which hath no end. 4 For behold, this is according to the captivity of the devil, and also according to the justice of God, upon all those who will work wickedness and abomination before him. 5 And it came to pass that the angel spake unto me, Nephi, saying: Thou hast beheld that if the Gentiles repent it shall be well with them; and thou also knowest concerning the covenants of the Lord unto the house of Israel; and thou also hast heard that whoso repenteth not must perish. 6 Therefore, wo be unto the Gentiles if it so be that they harden their hearts against the Lamb of God. 7 For the time cometh, saith the Lamb of God, that I will work a great and a marvelous work among the children of men; a work which shall be everlasting, either on the one hand or on the other---either to the convincing of them unto peace and life eternal, or unto the deliverance of them to the hardness of their hearts and the blindness of their minds unto their being brought down into captivity, and also into destruction, both temporally and spiritually, according to the captivity of the devil, of which I have spoken.
		\item[1N 14:9--12] And it came to pass that he said unto me: Look, and behold that great and abominable church, which is the mother of abominations, whose founder is the devil. 10 And he said unto me: Behold there are save two churches only; the one is the church of the Lamb of God, and the other is the church of the devil; wherefore, whoso belongeth not to the church of the Lamb of God belongeth to that great church, which is the mother of abominations; and she is the whore of all the earth. 11 And it came to pass that I looked and beheld the whore of all the earth, and she sat upon many waters; and she had dominion over all the earth, among all nations, kindreds, tongues, and people. 12 And it came to pass that I beheld the church of the Lamb of God, and its numbers were few, because of the wickedness and abominations of the whore who sat upon many waters; nevertheless, I beheld that the church of the Lamb, who were the saints of God, were also upon all the face of the earth; and their dominions upon the face of the earth were small, because of the wickedness of the great whore whom I saw.

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Why did he do what he did?}
	% -----

		Alicia hit upon an important insight this morning (2/23/2014) when we were reading DC 76. We've been reading the DC by going through the Smith and Sjodahl commentary, which includes the text of the scriptures as well as commentary. The thought she had arose out of a remark in the commentary about how Satan rebelled against God in order to go out and carry out his plan--and that he is still out in the world today, trying to carry out that very same plan. His primary purpose isn't to destroy God's plan---his primary purpose is to carry out his own plan, and destroying God's plan is something that he does along the way to that primary goal.

		This has helped us understand his actions in the Garden of Eden. We often talk as though Satan did not understand God's plan, and didn't realize that by tempting Adam and Eve he would actually cause something to happen that God wanted to happen. Satan inadvertently furthered God's purposes through his actions, because he did not understand the mechanics of what needed to happen.

		I think that's a bit hard to believe, because we know that Satan was in the highest councils which were considering the question of man's salvation and working out a plan. It seems reasonable that he would have understood God's plan, and Christ's role in it. If he did understand it, why did he do what he did in the Garden? The insight Alicia had is that, even then, he was not just trying to destroy God's plan--he was trying to further his own plan. At that point, the only way he could prove to God that the Christ-centered plan would fail was to get Adam and Eve away from God's presence, so that when they were tempted and sinned later, God could see that a plan based on the Atonement was not going to work. Satan tempted Adam and Eve in the Garden to try to use the results as proof that his plan was superior to the one that had been chosen. This makes far more sense than what we normally say about this, and it also helps me to understand Satan's strategies against us on this earth: he is still trying to carry out his plan, which means that everything he does goes towards taking away our autonomy and agency. Without those things, we cannot choose eternal life; it would have to be forced upon us, as Satan wants.
		
		More ideas here:
			DC 76:28 says he ``sought to take the kingdom of our God and his Christ.''
			See also the first two larger paragraphs of George Laub's journal on WJS 223.

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Metaphor of the Golden Compass} % *GOLDENCOMPASS *ALETHIOMETER
	% -----
	
		God solves an engineering problem: how do I give people spiritual things, over and over, in response to millions of different possible questions, with a way that requires effort on their part? 
		
		And why have scriptures at all? This is not a trivial question; it has to do with the difference between spoken and written words in the gospel.
		
		Points of comparison for golden compass/alethiometer comparison:
			We have to ASK in order to know things (DC 6:11).
		
		Note that the Liahona is kind of like the alethiometer; see 1N 16:10, 16, 26--30. Note that they don't just get guided by the ball; they learn about the ways of the Lord by what is written on it. I can't believe I didn't think of this before. It's perfect.
			Another very interesting thing is that Nephi still gets direct revelation and learns great things from the Lord directly, without the intermediary of the Liahona. See 1N 18:3, for example. So maybe we need the scriptures for some things, but we need to go beyond that as well, beyond what is written to what we learn from living and direct revelation.
			But both are important in the end.
			See 1N 18:12--22 for more about the Liahona.
			2N 5:12 calls it the ``compass,'' and so does Al 37:38.
			
		View the Liahona, and specifically the words that appear on it in 1N 16:29, as a model for truth as goodness. Believing and obeying what you receive, then receiving more---``truth'' is kind of irrelevant almost. The Liahona is the model for truth as goodness, because heed to the words brings us closer to God----line upon line is truth as goodness. Levels principle is truth as goodness. It has to be a reflection of that, because it's clear that not only does the Spirit just NOT give us the truth, it CANNOT, because we are not prepared to receive it, or just not capable of receiving it, in accordance with all the levels. We're not able to receive it because we aren't on the right levels in many different ways.
		And note the parallel to the development of scientific knowledge---that is the model to understand how we receive line upon line, precept on precept. Ancient theories were not even close to being true but they got you a little distance; then theories got better and better as they gathered more observations, developed better concepts, got more precise measurements, and so on. Use the development of scientific knowledge as a model for how line upon line/precept on precept works, and how truth as goodness works. Truth-pragmatism in science, we get closer and closer; truth-goodness in the gospel, we get closer and closer to Heavenly Father. 
			And notice that a very important step in the development of scientific knowledge was throwing off outside authority, like ecclesiastical authority, to follow the conclusions wherever they went. The same is true for us in religion, and for the same reason we have to learn to live by every word that proceeds forth from the mouth of God. We have to throw off the outside forces as well, just as science had to in the course of its development.
			
		See ``urim and thummim'' as well.
		
		Note DC 28, the story of Hyrum Page's seerstone---there is a hierarchy of rules of epistemology of revelation---someone is appointed to receive revelations for everyone, and that is a very foundational rule.
		
		\begin{description}
		\item[Al 12:1] NOW Alma, seeing that the words of Amulek had silenced Zeezrom, for he beheld that Amulek had caught him in his lying and deceiving to destroy him, and seeing that he began to tremble under a consciousness of his guilt, he opened his mouth and began to speak unto him, and to establish the words of Amulek, and to explain things beyond, or to unfold the scriptures beyond that which Amulek had done.
		\item[1N 19:22--23] Now it came to pass that I, Nephi, did teach my brethren these things; and it came to pass that I did read many things to them, which were engraven upon the plates of brass, that they might know concerning the doings of the Lord in other lands, among people of old. 23 And I did read many things unto them which were written in the books of Moses; but that I might more fully persuade them to believe in the Lord their Redeemer I did read unto them that which was written by the prophet Isaiah; for I did liken all scriptures unto us, that it might be for our profit and learning.
		\end{description}

% -----------------------
\subsection{Search} % *SEARCH
% -----------------------

	This usage is interesting: ``they will not search knowledge'' (2N 32:7), with an object directly after ``search'' and no preposition. Nephi does use this construction in other places, and given his other uses and the definitions in the 1828, it seems clear that we are searching THROUGH knowledge like we'd search THROUGH a house for something, looking through it or reviewing it with some purpose in mind. Not sure exactly what this means. Yale makes no change here.
	
	1828
		1. To look over or through for the purpose of finding something; to explore; to examine by inspection; as, to search the house for a book; to search the wood for a thief.
			Send though men, that they may search the land of Canaan. Numbers 13:2.
		2. To inquire; to seek for.
			Enough is left besides to search and know. Milton.
		3. To probe; to seek the knowledge of by feeling with instrument; as to search a wound.
		4. To examine; to try. Psalms 139:23S

\subsection{Second Comforter} % *SECONDCOMFORTER
% -----------------------

	% -----
	\subsubsection{Scriptural Uses}
	% -----

		The word \textit{comforter} appears only four times in the NT. All four occurrences are translations of the Greek word \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{par'aklhtos}}.

		\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{par'aklhtos}} itself only appears five total times. The four translations as \textit{comforter} are at: Jn 14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7. The fifth time this word is translated as \textit{advocate}, and that's in 1Jn 2:1.

		\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{par'aklhtos}} is translated in the following ways in these other translations:

		\begin{compactdesc}
		\item[NIV] advocate (all five times)
		\item[RSV] counselor (first four), advocate
		\item[NASB] helper (first four), advocate
		\item[NLT] advocate (all five)
		\end{compactdesc}

		The translations clearly agree on the use of \textit{advocate} in 1Jn 2:1. That verse is speaking about Jesus Christ; here is the whole thing:

		\begin{quote}
		\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{tekn'ia mou, ta\char"007Euta gr'afw <um\char"007Ein m`h <am'arthte. ka`i >e'an tis <am'arth|, par'aklhton >'eqomen pr`os t`on pat'era >Ihso\char"007Eun Qrist`on d'ikaion}}
		\end{quote}

		This translation of \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{par'aklhtos}} as \textit{advocate} in this verse squares with the other uses of \textit{advocate} in the restoration scriptures:

		\begin{compactdesc}
		\item[Mor 7:28] For he [Christ] hath answered the ends of the law, and he claimeth all those who have faith in him; and they who have faith in him will cleave unto every good thing; wherefore he advocateth the cause of the children of men; and he dwelleth eternally in the heavens
		\item[DC 29:5] Lift up your hearts and be glad, for I am in your midst, and am your advocate with the Father; and it is his good will to give you the kingdom
		\item[DC 32:3] And Ziba Peterson also shall go with them; and I myself will go with them and be in their midst; and I am their advocate with the Father, and nothing shall prevail against them
		\item[DC 45:3] Listen to him who is the advocate with the Father, who is pleading your cause before him
		\item[DC 62:1] Behold, and hearken, O ye elders of my church, saith the Lord your God, even Jesus Christ, your advocate, who knoweth the weakness of man and how to succor them who are tempted
		\item[DC 110:4] I am the first and the last; I am he who liveth, I am he who was slain; I am your advocate with the Father
		\end{compactdesc}

		(\textit{Advocate} also appears in JS-H note 7, but only as the title of the periodical, \textit{Messenger and Advocate}.) So every use of the word \textit{advocate} in the scriptures refers to Jesus Christ and his role as mediator between us and God.

		Of the translations that I quoted above, two (NIV and NLT) translated \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{par'aklhtos}} as \textit{advocate} in all four other cases in the NT as well. One uses ``counselor'' (RSV); another uses ``helper'' (NASB); and the KJV uses ``comforter.'' Is there any source we can look to explain either (1) the provenance of these translation choices, or (2) the differences among them? I'm especially interested in knowing how the KJV came to translate \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{par'aklhtos}} as \textit{comforter}. Remember, that word only appears as a translation of \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{par'aklhtos}} in the NT; it doesn't appear as the translation of any other Greek word.

		Here is a quote from the lexicon, along with the definition, of \textgreek{par'aklhtos}:

		% \begin{quote}
		% ...Latin writers commonly rendered \textgreek{par'aklhtos}, in its NT occurrences, with ``advocatus''...in the few places where the word is found in pre-Christian and extra-Christian literature as well it has for the most part a more general sense: \textbf{one who appears in another's behalf, \textit{mediator, intercessor, helper}}...the passive idea of \textgreek{parakekl\cf hsjai} retreated into the background, and the active idea of \textgreek{parakale\cf in} took its place...the Greek interpreters of John's gospel understood it [\textgreek{par'aklhtos}] in the active sense, [as equal to] \textgreek{parakal\cf wn} or \textgreek{parakl'htwr}...in our literature, the active sense \textit{helper, intercessor} is suitable in all occurrences of the word...In 1Jn 2:1 Christ is designated as \textgreek{par'aklhtos}...the same title is implied for Christ by the \textgreek{>'allos par'aklhtos} of Jn 14:16. It is only the Holy Spirit that is expressly called \textgreek{par'aklhtos} (=\textit{Helper}) in the Fourth Gospel: 14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7.
		% \end{quote}

		% And, for reference, here are the definitions of \textgreek{parakal'ew}:

		\begin{compactenum}
		\item to ask to come and be present where the speaker is, \textit{call to one's side}
		\item to urge strongly, \textit{appeal to, urge, exhort, encourage}
		\item to make a strong request for something, \textit{request, implore, entreat}
		\item to instill someone with courage or cheer, \textit{comfort, encourage, cheer up}
		\end{compactenum}

		Things to look at: 
			definition of paraklhtos in lexicon
			all OT translations of comforter, plus the other words that those Hebrew words are translated as
			LXX appearances/definitions of paraklhtos? 
			uses of ``comfort'' in the NT?
			uses of parakalew and paraklhsis in the NT? What is the relationship between those two words and paraklhtos?
			start a new section to discuss how this all influences Joseph Smith's uses? I should search for his, maybe complete the restoration section for ``comforter.''

\subsection{Seeing} % *SEEING *VISUALPERCEPTION
% -----------------------

	In accordance with levels principle, truth-as-goodness, and so on, I will say that seeing is the most basic epistemic state, and that when the scriptures use ``know,'' they mostly have seeing for yourself in mind. This helps with DC 46, the two groups of people and how they believe, and with prophets seeing the ministry of Christ. They know because they SEE.
	
	So something to explore here as well is that skepticism is a rejection of the law of Christ---seeing the sun and saying you don't, as JS said about the sons of perdition, is a vicious form of skepticism. This idea needs more work.
	
	Another important thing---SEEING is what leads to surety; this is why scriptures about faith, like Al 32:21, talk about seeing. Seeing leads to surety; seeing is perfect knowledge, I would say.
	
	Something important going on here with the three witnesses and spiritual ``seeing'' as well.
	
	See ``seer'' also, or uses of that word.

	\begin{description}
	\item[DC 124:94] (Talking about Hyrum.) And from this time forth I appoint unto him that he may be a prophet, and a seer, and a revelator unto my church, as well as my servant Joseph;
	\item[DC 124:125] I give unto you my servant Joseph to be a presiding elder over all my church, to be a translator, a revelator, a seer, and prophet.
	\item[TPJS 12--13] Wherefore, we again say, search the revelations of God; study the prophecies, and rejoice that God grants unto the world Seers and Prophets. They are they who saw the mysteries of godliness; they saw the flood before it came; they saw angels ascending and descending upon a ladder that reached from earth to heaven; they saw the stone cut out of the mountain, which filled the whole earth; they saw the Son of God come from the regions of bliss and dwell with men on earth; they saw the deliverer come out of Zion, and turn away ungodliness from Jacob; they saw the glory of the Lord when he showed the transfiguration of the earth on the mount; they saw every mountain laid low and every valley exalted when the Lord was taking vengeance upon the wicked; they saw truth spring out of the earth, and righteousness look down from heaven in the last days, before the Lord came the second time to gather his elect; they saw the end of wickedness on earth, and the Sabbath of creation crowned with peace; they saw the end of the glorious thousand years, when Satan was loosed for a little season; they saw the day of judgment when all men received according to their works, and they saw the heaven and the earth flee away to make room for the city of God, when the righteous receive an inheritance in eternity. And, fellow sojourners upon earth, it is your privilege to purify yourselves and come up to the same glory, and see for yourselves, and know for yourselves. Ask, and it shall be given you; seek and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.
	\end{description}

\subsection{Sidney Rigdon} % *SIDNEYRIGDON
% -----------------------

	\begin{description}
	\item[TPJS 30--31] Brother Sidney is a man whom I love, but he is not capable of that pure and steadfast love for those who are his benefactors that should characterize a President of the Church of Christ. This, with some other little things, such as a selfishness and independence of mind, which too often manifested destroy the confidence of those who would lay down their lives for him---these are his faults. But notwithstanding these things, he is a very great and good man; a man of great power of words, and can gain the friendship of his hearers very quickly. He is a man whom God will uphold, if he will continue faithful to his calling. O God, grant that he may, for the Lord's sake. Amen. And again, blessed be Brother Sidney: notwithstanding he shall be high and lifted up, yet he shall bow down under the yoke like unto an ass that croucheth beneath his burden, that learneth his master's will by the stroke of the rod; thus saith the Lord: yet, the Lord will have mercy on him, and he shall bring forth much fruit, even as the vine of the choice grape, when her clusters are ripe, before the time of the gleaning of the vintage; and the Lord shall make his heart merry as with sweet wine, because of Him who putteth forth His hand, and lifteth him up out of deep mire, and pointeth him out the way, and guideth his feet when he stumbles, and humbleth him in his pride. Blessed are his generations: nevertheless one shall hunt after them as a man hunteth after an ass that has strayed in the wilderness, and straightway findeth him and bringeth him into the fold. Thus shall the Lord watch over his generation, that they may be saved. Even so, Amen.
	\end{description}

This is sin; but that that promotes life, happiness, peace, joy and the well-being of intelligence---no matter what the degree is---that that promotes happiness, builds up, refines and makes better, is as good religion as we can ask for.
	\item[Brigham Young, JD 14:98] This is a very singular world that we live in; yet were it not for the spirit of error and confusion that everywhere prevails I think we should call it a very fine, excellent world. The annoyances, difficulties, errors, perplexities, sorrows, and troubles of this life, from first to last, are in consequence of sin being in the world. For me to say it is not right for sin to be in the world, or if we, as intelligent beings, come to the conclusion that sin entered the world by chance, through some mistake, and it was contrary to the design of him who created us, we should err.

Behold, I say unto you, that I do know that Christ shall come among the children of men, to take upon him the transgressions of his people, and that he shall atone for the sins of the world; for the Lord God hath spoken it.
		\item[DC 138:32] (Note that JF.S makes ``transgression'' here to be knowingly rejecting the prophets---at least that's what it seems. There are two other uses of ``transgression'' in this section; interesting to look at those in light of his possible meaning here of knowingly going against the laws of God. The other two uses are in 37 and 59.) Thus was the gospel preached to those who had died in their sins, without a knowledge of the truth, or in transgression, having rejected the prophets.
		\item[Lev 16:16] And he shall make an atonement for the holy place, because of the uncleanness of the children of Israel, and because of their transgressions in all their sins: and so shall he do for the tabernacle of the congregation, that remaineth among them in the midst of their uncleanness.
		\item[Lev 16:21] And Aaron shall lay both his hands upon the head of the live goat, and confess over him all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions in all their sins, putting them upon the head of the goat, and shall send him away by the hand of a fit man into the wilderness:

% -----------------------
\subsection{Single} % *SINGLE
% -----------------------

	Mostly interested in the sense of this word from DC 88:67--68, ``if your eye be single to my glory'' and ``sanctify yourselves that your minds become single to God.''
	
	1828:
		8. Pure; simple; incorrupt; unbiased; having clear vision of divine truth. 
	
	Mt 6:22 says, ``The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.''
		``light'' here is not \textgreek{φώς}, it's \textgreek{λύχνος}. And ``single'' is \textgreek{ἁπλοῦς}.
			\textgreek{λύχνος}: 23892. The word means ``lamp'' and the sense here seems to be that the light is the source of the light of the body, or perhaps the means through which that light is communicated outward. % *λύχνος *luxnos *luqnos
				Note the very interesting use in Rev 21:23, where the Lamb is the \textgreek{λύχνος} for the heavenly city, and they have no need of the sun or moon for light.
			\textgreek{ἁπλοῦς}: 7258. ``pert. to being motivated by singleness of purpose so as to be open and aboveboard, single, without guile, sincere, straightforward i.e. without a hidden agenda.'' % *ἁπλοῦς *haplous
				This word appears only twice in the NT---Mt 6:22 and Lk 11:34, which is almost identical to the verse in Mt.
			
	Those definitions of \textgreek{ἁπλοῦς} remind me of 2N 31:13: ``Wherefore, my beloved brethren, I know that if ye shall follow the Son, with full purpose of heart, acting no hypocrisy and no deception before God, but with real intent...''

% -----------------------
\subsection{Sleep} % *SLEEP
% -----------------------

	\begin{description}
	\item[JD 16:359] Sleep refreshes us here in this life, and we spend about one-third part of our time in that condition, and it is absolutely necessary to our existence in mortality; for without it we should soon perish and die. But because that is the case here, shall we say that it will be necessary in a future state? I think not. It looks inconsistent to me, and like an imperfection in the great work of the Creator, to suppose that for about one-third part of all future eternity intelligent beings are to forget even their own existence in slumber, knowing nothing that is transpiring around them in the one-third part of the thousands and millions of ages to come. It does not look reasonable.
	\end{description}
	
	% -----
	\subsubsection{Relationship between sleep and death}
	% -----
	
		\begin{description}
		\item[CDBY] It is a grief to me to see my brethren fall. I would rather they would live than to die; nevertheless, those that sleep in peace are better off than those that are with us. Death is but a sleep. You will experience something like it before twenty-four hours have passed away. Every twenty-four hours that you live, you experience precisely in similitude the very thing you experience in death and in the resurrection. When you lay your bodies down to rest, you cannot remember going to sleep. No, because your senses begin to withdraw from everything around you. You sit up all night, and between that time and the mourning you will remember waking many times; but you will never remember going to sleep once. So it will be in the resurrection, you will fall to sleep, by and by, and your mortal faculties cease to operate. You will fall to sleep, and sleep a nap until the morning of the resurrection, when the trumpet blows and you awake out of sleep. You will recollect all about what was before you fell asleep; if you have slept a hundred or a thousand years, it is no difference; it is the same to the body with regard to time. You may feel the effects of not being properly refreshed by sleep, but you may awake as often as you please and you will remember the circumstances you were in when you feel asleep. So it is to our bodies sleeping in the gravel, there is no difference.
		\end{description}
