\subsection{Sorrow} % *SORROW
% -----------------------

	% -----
	\subsubsection*{Godly sorrow}
	% -----
	
		\begin{description}
		\item[Morm 2:8--15] But behold, the land was filled with robbers and with Lamanites; and notwithstanding the great destruction which hung over my people, they did not repent of their evil doings; therefore there was blood and carnage spread throughout all the face of the land, both on the part of the Nephites and also on the part of the Lamanites; and it was one complete revolution throughout all the face of the land. 9 And now, the Lamanites had a king, and his name was Aaron; and he came against us with an army of forty and four thousand. And behold, I withstood him with forty and two thousand. And it came to pass that I beat him with my army that he fled before me. And behold, all this was done, and three hundred and thirty years had passed away. 10 And it came to pass that the Nephites began to repent of their iniquity, and began to cry even as had been prophesied by Samuel the prophet; for behold no man could keep that which was his own, for the thieves, and the robbers, and the murderers, and the magic art, and the witchcraft which was in the land. 11 Thus there began to be a mourning and a lamentation in all the land because of these things, and more especially among the people of Nephi. 12 And it came to pass that when I, Mormon, saw their lamentation and their mourning and their sorrow before the Lord, my heart did begin to rejoice within me, knowing the mercies and the long-suffering of the Lord, therefore supposing that he would be merciful unto them that they would again become a righteous people. 13 But behold this my joy was vain, for their sorrowing was not unto repentance, because of the goodness of God; but it was rather the sorrowing of the damned, because the Lord would not always suffer them to take happiness in sin. 14 And they did not come unto Jesus with broken hearts and contrite spirits, but they did curse God, and wish to die. Nevertheless they would struggle with the sword for their lives. 15 And it came to pass that my sorrow did return unto me again, and I saw that the day of grace was passed with them, both temporally and spiritually; for I saw thousands of them hewn down in open rebellion against their God, and heaped up as dung upon the face of the land. And thus three hundred and forty and four years had passed away.
		\item[Mor 9:25] (Godly sorrow doesn't weigh us down to death.) My son, be faithful in Christ; and may not the things which I have written grieve thee, to weigh thee down unto death; but may Christ lift thee up, and may his sufferings and death, and the showing his body unto our fathers, and his mercy and long-suffering, and the hope of his glory and of eternal life, rest in your mind forever.
		\item[Ps 116:3] The sorrows of death compassed me, and the pains of hell gat hold upon me: I found trouble and sorrow.
		\end{description}

		``Godly sorrow'' is the way we describe the sorrow that we are supposed to feel for our sins; this sorrow is supposed to lead us to repentance. The phrase only appears a single time in the scriptures, at 2Co 7:10: ``for godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of.''

		But there is much more to that passage. I hardly even know how to go about trying to unravel what's going on here, but I'll start by giving the definitions of the key words in the verses--there is clearly some wordplay going on between them, and I think it's important to see that. Then I'll give a basic translation but leave the key words untranslated.

		\begin{compactdesc}
		\item[\textcolor{magenta}{\textgreek{lup'ew}}] to cause severe mental or emotional distress, \textit{vex, irritate, offend, insult}; to experience sadness or distress (aorist passive), \textit{become sad, sorrowful, distressed}; (present passive) \textit{be sad, be distressed, grieve}.
		\item[\textcolor{magenta}{\textgreek{lup'h}}] pain of mind or spirit, \textit{grief, sorrow, affliction}.
		\item[\textcolor{blue}{\textgreek{metam'elomai}}] to have regrets about something, in the sense that one wishes it could be undone, \textit{be very sorry, regret}; to change one's mind about something, without focus on regret, \textit{change one's mind, have second thoughts}.
		\item[\textcolor{blue}{\textgreek{>ametam'elhtos}}] not to be regretted, without regret; feeling no remorse, having no regret.
		\item[\textcolor{green}{\textgreek{zhmi'ow}}] to experience the loss of something, with implication of undergoing hardship or suffering, \textit{suffer damage/loss, forfeit, sustain injury} (this verb appears only in the passive; this is the same verb that appears in the ``what does it profit a man if he gains the world but loses his soul'' verses, at Mt 16:26, Mk 8:36, and Lk 9:25).
		\end{compactdesc}

		Here's the translation of the verses:

		\begin{quote}
		for even if I \textcolor{magenta}{\textgreek{>el'uphsa}} you in the letter, I \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{o>u}} \textcolor{blue}{\textgreek{metam'elomai}}; even if I had been sorry [at some point], now I rejoice--for I see that that letter \textcolor{magenta}{\textgreek{>el'uphsen}} you, though it were only for a time. [I rejoice] not because \textcolor{magenta}{\textgreek{>elup'hjhte}} but because \textcolor{magenta}{\textgreek{>elup'hjhte}} \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{e>is met'anoian}}. For \textcolor{magenta}{\textgreek{>elup'hjhte}} \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{kat`a je'on}}, such that you in no way \textcolor{green}{\textgreek{zhmiwj\char"007Ehte}} from us. For \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{<h kat`a je`on}} \textcolor{magenta}{\textgreek{l'uph}} \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{met'anoian e>is swthr'ian}} \textcolor{blue}{\textgreek{>ametam'elhton}} \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>erg'azetai; <h d`e to\char"007Eu k'osmou}} \textcolor{magenta}{\textgreek{l'uph}} \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{j'anaton katerg'azetai}}. For behold, this very thing--\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{t`o kat`a je`on}} \textcolor{magenta}{\textgreek{luphj\char"007Ehnai}}--how much eagerness it \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{kateirg'asato}} in you...
		\end{quote}

		There are so many interesting things going on in this passage; here are just a few.

		\begin{compactitem}

		\item I think that these verses form an important foil for DC 121:39-44. In those verses, we are instructed on how to give correction; I think that these verses in 2Co help us understand how to \textit{take} correction in righteousness. I won't go into more detail here about this; see the article in the Second Corinthians 7 folder, which explains this and agrees with this idea.

		\item There are multiple ways to lose the Holy Ghost, or to drive it away from ourselves. One is through sin (Mo 2:36). Another is through improperly reacting to correction, as these verses describe. A third way is through excessive sorrow, as mentioned in Al 4:15; I think these verses in 2Co can help us understand what's going on there. 

		In Al 4:15, Alma is very upset about the persecutions that he sees. He became ``very sorrowful,'' a phrase that's used only five times in the scriptures (twice in the BOM). But ``the Spirit of the Lord did not fail him.'' Why didn't it fail him? It must be because Alma chose to react to his sorrow in the way described in 2Co 7:11--he let the Holy Ghost entice him to those kinds of fruits, rather than abandoning the Spirit and sorrowing after the manner of the world: without hope.

		\item In connection with Al 4:15, then, I think that we should view the fruits in 2Co 7:11 as actual fruits of the Spirit. They are the result of sorrowing after a godly manner, of allowing the Holy Ghost to work in us to lead us to repentance (this is called the ``goodness of God'' [\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{t`o qrhst'on to\char"007Eu jeo\char"007Eu}}] in Rom 2:4). It may be that the Spirit works these things in us at times, and at other times that we choose to respond in these ways. I don't think it makes much of a difference.

		The fruits listed in 2Co 7:11 are:

		\begin{compactdesc}

		\item[\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{spoud'h}}] swiftness of movement or action, \textit{haste, speed}; earnest commitment in discharge of an obligation of a relationship, \textit{eagerness, earnestness, diligence, willingness, zeal}. 12 times total in Greek NT.

		The second definition is the one we want here. When we are corrected, we can respond \textit{eagerly} and work \textit{diligently} to change our behavior and become more righteous.

		An interesting side-note here is that sometimes we can choose to respond this way without having been overtly corrected or criticized. Sometimes when I hear about the successes of people we know, I feel upset or jealous, or wish to respond by minimizing their accomplishments. But these moments can be seen instead as opportunities to improve and change my own behavior. By responding under the influence of the Spirit, and by trying to allow the Spirit to maintain its influence over me, I can find opportunities to become better where before I just committed immature sins that require repenting anyway.

		Along these lines, here's a long quote from an article in the \textit{Wall Street Journal}, published in late April, 2014, by Jennifer Breheny Wallace. Social media is doing this to people to:

		\begin{quote}
		Facebook now boasts more than a billion users--and it isn't the only one boasting. With posts showing off work promotions you didn't get, fun parties you weren't invited to and exotic vacations you can't afford, Facebook and other social-media websites have become huge generators of modern envy. In the process, they're providing researchers with a unique platform for examining those feelings.

		It isn't always a friendly picture. A study published last August by the journal Plos One, led by researchers at the University of Michigan, found that the more people used Facebook, the less satisfied they were with their lives. In another study last year involving almost 600 Facebook users, German researchers say they witnessed the ``rampant nature of envy'' on social-networking websites.

		So modern envy seems to be bad--but it doesn't have to be. Researchers are finding that, if approached the right way, there can actually be an upside to this deadly sin.

		Psychologists classify envy in two ways: malicious and benign. With benign envy, you are motivated by another person's success and strive to emulate it. With malicious envy, you want to cut the advantaged person down so you look better by comparison. Let's say you feel pangs of envy after your rival at another firm gets promoted. Malicious envy might drive you to undermine his success, but benign envy would inspire you to work harder and get promoted, too.

		Studies show benign envy can be a great motivator. In a 2011 study published in the Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, researchers in the Netherlands conducted a series of experiments with more than 200 university students. Researchers found that when they triggered feelings of benign envy--as opposed to admiration or malicious envy--in the students, it drove them to want to study more and perform better on a test measuring creativity and intelligence. While admiration may feel better, the researchers found, it doesn't motivate performance like the pain and frustration of envy.

		Psychologists and other experts aren't immune to these feelings either. ``There's a man in my field who has made a big name for himself by so brilliantly promoting his work,'' says executive coach Marcia Reynolds. ``Whenever I hear his name, I feel something in the pit of my stomach.'' But instead of dismissing her envy, she reflects on it and asks herself, ``What's holding me back? Can't I play at his level too?''

		``Those painful pangs of envy are there for an evolutionary reason,'' says Texas Christian University researcher Sarah E. Hill, ``alerting us that someone has something of importance to us.'' Building on this theory, Dr. Hill and others conducted a series of experiments, published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, to test whether envy improves attention and memory--the tools needed to copy a rival's steps to success. In one experiment, half of the participants were asked to recall past feelings of envy; the other half weren't. The two groups were then shown mock interviews of fictitious peers. The group primed with envy paid closer attention and better recalled details about the interview subjects. In other words, envy made them more astute. Not only can envy motivate us to reach for higher goals, it may even give us the cognitive push to get there.

		Envy works at the office, too. In a 2010 Harvard Business Review paper, business school professors Tanya Menon and Leigh Thompson examined workplace envy through the lens of hundreds of executives and their organizations over a 10-year period. While the case studies showed that unchecked envy can damage careers and organizations, the authors also found that envy can be put to good use. Your ``envy reflex,'' they write, can point you in the right direction, focusing your time and attention on the areas that are important to you. ``Think of it as data on what you value,'' they add.

		To guard against falling into the malicious-envy trap, the professors suggest taking stock of your own achievements when faced with envy. In an experiment, they asked people to prepare for a task in which they had to evaluate a rival's latest idea. They asked half of the participants to list their own accomplishments or values before the task; the other half weren't asked to do so. The affirmation group was willing to spend 60\% more time learning about the rival's plan than the control group. If employees were encouraged to follow similar thinking, they wrote, ``the impact could be huge.''
		\end{quote}

		I definitely have an envy reflex; I want to respond with eagerness to make my life better and become a disciple of Christ when the reflex is turned on.

		\item[\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>apolog'ia}}] a speech of defense, \textit{defense, reply}; the act of making a defense, \textit{defense}; claim of extenuating circumstances, \textit{excuse}. 8 times total in the Greek NT.

		Certainly an interesting addition to a list of fruits of the Spirit. The lexicon says that this word is used ``generally of eagerness to defend oneself.'' Perhaps it relates to a defense that one gives to oneself, not to another--in examining our actions, we may try to reason with ourselves about which are acceptable and which are not. I don't have more to add here right now; I don't think this is a difficult one for the list. It definitely is a natural reaction, and can be channeled in a good way, I think.

		\item[\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>agan'akthsis}}] \textit{indignation}. This is the only occurrence in the Greek NT.

		The verb that this noun comes from, \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>aganakt'ew}}, appears seven times in the Greek text. It means ``to be indignant against what is assumed to be wrong, \textit{be aroused, indignant, angry}.'' I think this can be taken as indignation against the one who corrects, because perhaps he's being unfair, but it can also be indignation against the wrongness in one's own behavior. You can feel irritation about your own behavior, frustration at your weaknesses.

		\item[\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{f'obos}}] The relevant sense of the word is ``the product of an intimidating/alarming force, \textit{fear, alarm, fright}.'' Appears 47 times in the Greek NT.

		Feeling fear at your own state, perhaps; fear of your state in relation to God, or relation to other people; fear of what you might lose. There may be a difference between the \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{f'obos}} of godly sorrowing, and the \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{f'obos}} of the world's sorrow. You fear different things, for different reasons.

		\item[\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>epip'ojhsis}}] yearning desire for, \textit{longing}. Appears twice in the Greek NT--here, and just earlier, in 2Co 7:7.

		Could be a yearning desire for repentance? A longing for the remission of sin? In Mo 4:20 King Benjamin says that the people have ``begged'' for a remission of their sins. Maybe it's that kind of desire for a remission and forgiveness that we need to have. The Holy Ghost plays a part in this--it can change our desires--see Al 19:33 or Mo 5:2, for example. This is all a cycle. It happens continually, over and over.

		\item[\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{z\char"007Ehlos}}] intense positive interest in something; \textit{zeal, ardor}; intense negative feelings over another's achievements or success, \textit{jealousy, envy}. Appears 16 times in the Greek NT.

		Could be similar to \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>epip'ojhsis}} here; a positive interest in changing, in repenting, in correcting the mistake.

		\item[\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>ekd'ikhsis}}] meting out of justice, \textit{giving of justice}; retaliation for harm done, \textit{vengeance}; penalty inflicted on wrongdoers, \textit{punishment}. Appears 9 times in the Greek NT.

		The lexicon lists 2Co 7:11 under the third sense of this word. I'm inclined to be a bit more charitable, and take the first sense, if possible: ``meting out of justice, \textit{giving of justice}.'' I'm reminded of another thing King Benjamin says, about how our actions will change as we retain the remission of our sins: ``ye will not have a mind to injure one another, but to live peaceably, \textbf{and to render to every man according to that which is his due}'' (Mo 4:13). Very similar to the first sense here.

		\end{compactdesc}

		It may be that Paul uses all of these in a negative way, but I don't think we need to see them that way. We could see them as invitations to do better, to take correction with humility, and as ways to properly react when we are corrected so that we retain the Holy Ghost and repent.

		\item The last point I'll raise is that these verses, in conjunction with Mt 16:26, Mk 8:36, and Lk 9:25, explain what was going on with me on my mission when I was scared that obedience would make me lose the person I was. Here is Lk 9:25--the other two verses are similar enough that they don't need to be quoted:

		\begin{quote}
		\textgreek{t'i g`ar >wfele\char"007Eitai >'anjrwpos kerd'hsas t`on k'osmon <'olon <eaut`on d`e >apol'esas >`h zhmiwje'is?}
		\end{quote}

		There are two important things to point out here. The first is the verb \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{zhmi'ow}}, which appears here as well as in 2Co 7:9, when Paul is talking about how the people ended up not losing anything when he corrected them. The second thing is that \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{<o k'osmos}} appears both here and in 2Co 9:10. In that verse, there is a worldly way of sorrowing; in this, you gain the world. What matters is that while we may gain certain things when we act in a worldly manner, we will ultimately lose what is most important to us. Alma's instructions are pretty clear:

		\begin{quote}
		And now I say unto you, all you that are desirous to follow the voice of the good sheperd, come ye out from the wicked, and be ye separate, and touch not their unclean things...(Al 5:57).
		\end{quote}

		\end{compactitem}

		\paragraph*{\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{kat`a je'on}}}Note that the phrase \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{kat`a je'on}} occurs at Rom 8:27; 2Co 7:10, 11; Eph 4:24; 1Pe 4:6. I think these verses are pretty powerful when you think of the meaning of the \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{kat`a je'on}} in 2Co 7.

% -----------------------
\subsection{Soul} % *SOUL
% -----------------------

	The scriptures talk about the soul in two ways. One is as the combination of the body and spirit (DC 88:15), and the other is just as our spirit (Al 29:16).
	
	% -----
	\subsubsection{Body and spirit}
	% -----
	
		\begin{description}
		\item[1N 14:3] And that great pit, which hath been digged for them by that great and abominable church, which was founded by the devil and his children, that he might lead away the souls of men down to hell---yea, that great pit which hath been digged for the destruction of men shall be filled by those who digged it, unto their utter destruction, saith the Lamb of God; not the destruction of the soul, save it be the casting of it into that hell which hath no end.

\subsection{Sources} % *SOURCES
% -----------------------

	This section is to list the sources I use when I study. If I have particular notes on a source, I'll also include that here.
	
	\begin{description}
	\item[CDBY] Complete Discourses of Brigham Young.
		Here is a list of interesting talks from these volumes:
		% reading: 53 long talk; top 61
		\begin{compactdesc}
		\item[September 9 1843 (28--30)] Gathering; importance of building the temple; importance of giving everything you have to spare for the construction of the temple and not worrying about money; the blessings of sacrifice (he gives a talk later this afternoon, starting on page 30, following up on some of these ideas and making the stakes clear)
		\item[August 7 1844--August 8 1844 (39--45)] On the question of succession to Joseph Smith and who would lead the church; the organization of the church; prophets must be called of God; the people have to decide whether they want to do things as God has organized them; how the church is organized with respect to the priesthood; stresses that Joseph laid the \textit{foundation} for what is to come, and the saints have to build on top of that (important when thinking of BY's later doctrinal innovations); many examples of the people voting in response to one of BY's questions about how they want things to be; mentions Sidney Rigdon many times.
		\item[August 18 1844 (45--48)] should we continue to baptize for the dead? (does not dwell on that question long, but returns to it briefly on August 25 1844, saying that they can continue to be baptized); no one can lead the people away except the 12; pleads with the people to stay in Nauvoo; emphasizes the importance of finishing the temple and getting the endowment, and that you can't get the endowment anywhere else; in this talk he's mainly trying to convince peopel to stay and get the endowment in Nauvoo, waiting for further counsel from the twelve apostles; he finishes with a dream of a fruit tree and dead branches at the top---by cutting them the tree began to grow just fine.
		\item[September 8 1844 (49--53)] Public trial of Sidney Rigdon; those who are for Joseph in one group, and those for Sidney in another, and another for Lyman Wight, etc.; you have to decide whether you're going to stick around and finish the temple or abandon the work that has taken so long to build; reports a conversation with Sidney about a meeting Sidney held in which he ordained people to be prophets, priests, and kings; tries to convince the people of Sidney's evil intentions and his dishonest behavior, including going against Joseph and prophesying that the temple wouldn't be built; he says if you follow Sidney, you'll soon have John C. Bennett back, and the Laws, and other nasty people; 
		\item[October 6 1844 (53--56)] how the church is organized---by revelation; many thoughts on revelation, receiving personal revelation, and the hierarchy of revelation for families, the whole church, and so on. Reconstructing from both the HC account and the one in WWJ, the question seems to be, with Joseph dead, even if the apostles are in charge, do they have a right to receive revelation? BY's argument seems to be---every saint can receive revelation for her own life; therefore, the apostles can receive revelation. But proper revelation only comes to those who have charge over a certain stewardship (such as a person over her own life). And since the stewardship of the apostles is the entire church, it is proper for them to receive revelation for the entire church.
		\item[December 29 1844 (61--62)] how the kingdom is organized, with Christ at the head, followed by prophets and others; a brief bit about pre-earth life; 
		\item[April 6 1845 (76--80)] 
		\item[August 3 1845 (90--96)]
		\end{compactdesc}
	\item[TPJS] Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith. I have a paperback, 1976 but it says first printed in softcover in June 1989. The cover is blue and has a picture of Joseph facing to the right. The final page number is 395. I am pretty sure that this is the edition which most other sources reference; I also own a newer edition, but they kind of messed that one up by changing the pagination.
	\item[WJS] Words of Joseph Smith I quote only from my PDF version. I have tried to make sure that the old quotes I had in previous versions of this document have been changed over to the new pagination from the PDF, but I haven't yet checked for all of them. Going forward I'm quoting only from the PDF though.
	\item[RSR] Rough Stone Rolling.
		\begin{compactdesc}
		\item[]
		\end{compactdesc}
	\item[JSR] The Joseph Smith Revelations: Text and Commentary. Edited by H. Michael Marquardt, Signature Books, 1999.
	\item[OJBYD] The Office Journal of President Brigham Young, 1858--1863, Book D, Collier's Publishing Company, 2006.
	\item[HDDC] Historical Development of the Doctrine and Covenants, which is Robert J. Woodford's 1974 PhD dissertation at BYU.
	\item[EMD] Early Mormon Documents, a five-volume set edited by Dan Vogel.
	\item[MEC] Mormon Endowment Ceremony, in the book \textit{Evolution of the Mormon Temple Ceremony}. 	\item[DLDSTW] Development of LDS Temple Worship, 2011, edited by Devery Anderson.

% -----------------------
\subsection{Space} % *SPACE
% -----------------------

	Interesting word, especially in the scriptures.
	
	% -----
	\subsubsection{BOM uses}
	% -----
	
		Appears 87 times. The great majority of these---84 I think---appear with a duration of time, as in ``for the space of many days'' of ``for the space of two years,'' something like that. So the word just means something like ``period'' or ``duration'' here.
		
		But three verses don't so obviously connect to time:
			\begin{compactdesc}
			\item[Al 12:24] And we see that death comes upon mankind, yea, the death which has been spoken of by Amulek, which is the temporal death; nevertheless there was a \textbf{space} granted unto man in which he might repent; therefore this life became a probationary state; a time to prepare to meet God; a time to prepare for that endless state which has been spoken of by us, which is after the resurrection of the dead.
			\item[Al 40:21] But whether it be at his resurrection or after, I do not say; but this much I say, that there is a \textbf{space} between death and the resurrection of the body, and a state of the soul in happiness or in misery until the time which is appointed of God that the dead shall come forth, and be reunited, both soul and body, and be brought to stand before God, and be judged according to their works.
			\item[Al 42:5] For behold, if Adam had put forth his hand immediately, and partaken of the tree of life, he would have lived forever, according to the word of God, having no \textbf{space} for repentance; yea, and also the word of God would have been void, and the great plan of salvation would have been frustrated.
			\end{compactdesc}
		First of all, they're all in Alma, which is interesting. And they're all actually said by Alma---that's interesting because many of the other uses with time are clearly from the narrator of a story, not a speaker actually saying something within a story.
		Al 40:21 has a very natural interpretation in terms of time, since it's talking about death and the resurrection as moments in time, and the ``space'' here is whatever comes between those points.
		But 12:24 and 42:5 are interesting because they both come in the context of \textit{repentance}. And I wonder if we can take these uses of ``space'' to having an actual spatial meaning---there was a \textit{space}, some spatial dimension or some volume or something, in which we can repent. And that space is this earth, maybe.
		Note DC 88:37 here: ``And there are many kingdoms; for there is no space in the which there is no kingdom; and there is no kingdom in which there is no space, either a greater or a lesser kingdom.'' And every kingdom gets a law (88:38). So this space that we're in right now, this kingdom---the telestial kingdom, maybe, at least according to the temple---is the space for repentance. The temple says, ``We go now with Adam and Eve into the lone and dreary world. Brethren and sisters, this represents the Telestial Kingdom, or the world in which we now live.''
			
% -----------------------
\subsection{Sphere} % *SPHERE
% -----------------------

	\begin{description}
	\item[DC 77:3] They are limited to four individual beasts, which were shown to John, to represent the glory of the classes of beings in their destined order or sphere of creation, in the enjoyment of their eternal felicity.
	\item[DC 93:30] All truth is independent in that sphere in which God has placed it, to act for itself, as all intelligence also; otherwise there is no existence.
	\item[Mos 3:9] And out of the ground made I, the Lord God, to grow every tree, naturally, that is pleasant to the sight of man; and man could behold it. And it became also a living soul. For it was spiritual in the day that I created it; for it remaineth in the sphere in which I, God, created it, yea, even all things which I prepared for the use of man; and man saw that it was good for food. And I, the Lord God, planted the tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and also the tree of knowledge of good and evil.
	\item[JD 1:9] The world of resurrected beings, and the world of spirits, are two distinct spheres, as much so as our own sphere is distinct from that of the spirit world. Where then does the spirit go, on its departure from its earthly tabernacle? It passes to the next sphere of human existence, called the world of spirits, a vail being drawn between us in the flesh, and that world of spirits. Well, says one, is there no more than one place in the spirit world? Yes, there are many places and degrees in that world, as in this. Jesus Christ, when absent from his flesh, did not ascend to the Father, to be crowned, and enthroned in power. Why? Because he had not yet a resurrected body, and had therefore a mission to perform in another sphere. Where then did he go? To the world of spirits, to wicked, sinful spirits, who died in their sins, being swept off by the flood of Noah. The thief on the cross, who died at the same time, also went to the same world, and to the same particular place in the same world, for he was a sinner, and would of course go to the prison of the condemned, there to await the ministry of that Gospel which had failed to reach his ease while on the earth. How many other places Jesus might have visited while in the spirit world is not for me to say, but there was a moment in which the poor, uncultivated, ignorant thief was with him in that world. And as he commenced, though late, to repent while on the earth, we have reason to hope that that moment was improved by our Saviour, in ministering to him that Gospel which he had no opportunity to teach to him, while expiring on the cross. ``This day shalt thou be with me in Paradise,'' said Jesus, or, in other words, this day shalt thou be with me in the next sphere of existence--the world of spirits.
	\item[JD 1:93] We are now, or may be, as perfect in our sphere as God and Angels are in theirs, but the greatest intelligence in existence can continually ascend to greater heights of perfection.
	\item[JD 1:257] All intelligences which exist possess a degree of independence in their own sphere. For instance, the bee can go at will in search of honey, or remain in the hive. It can visit one flower or another, as independent in its own sphere as God is in His. We find a degree of independence in everything which possesses any degree of intelligence; that thinks, moves, or acts: because the very principle of voluntary action implies an independent will to direct such action.
	\item[Brigham Young, JD 2:129--130] It may appear strange to some of you, and it certainly does to the world, to say it is possible for a man or woman to become perfect on this earth. It is written ``Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.'' Again, ``If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body.'' This is perfectly consistent to the person who understands what perfection really is. If the first passage I have quoted is not worded to our understanding, we can alter the phraseology of the sentence, and say, ``Be ye as perfect, as ye can,'' for that is all we can do, though it is written, be ye perfect as your Father who is in heaven is perfect. To be as perfect as we possibly can, according to our knowledge, is to be just as perfect as our Father in heaven is. He cannot be any more perfect than He knows how, any more than we. When we are doing as well as we know how in the sphere and station which we occupy here, we are justified in the justice, righteousness, mercy, and judgment that go before the Lord of heaven and earth. We are as justified as the angels who are before the throne Of God. The sin that will cleave to all the posterity of Adam and Eve is, that they have not done as well as they knew how.
	\item[Parley P. Pratt, \textit{Key}, 33] The great distinguishing difference between one portion of this race and another, consists in the varied grades of intelligence and purity, and also in the variety of spheres occupied by each, in the series of progressive being.
	\end{description}

\subsection{Spoken vs. written word} % *SPOKENWRITTENWORD
% -----------------------

	I've started to notice that there might be a spiritually important difference between the spoken and the written word. There is something special about \textit{studying} the written word---much harder to do with the spoken word---the experience of the spoken word is very different. It's much harder to \textit{study}.
	
	Another important difference could be that the authors of the scriptures are all dead, and this affects the way their testimony is ``enforced'' on us; see CDBY 36, ``Elder Brigham Young arose, and said he felt disposed to add his testimony; be of good cheer. The testimony is not in force while the testator liveth; when he died it was in force; so it is with Joseph.'' Also CDBY 39, ``Did not care who lead the church, one dead prophets testimony is [-] to 10,000 living if God spoke by him.''
	
	Process of trying to understand the spoken word: Mo 2:9; 3N 11:5; 
	
	Another aspect of this is scriptures that say that certain spoken words can't be written---see 3N 17:15--17; but see also 3N 19:32, where tongue can't speak nor can be written Christ's words; but see also 3N 26:16, where certain words are forbidden to be written (also 18, not lawful to be written).
	
	Another aspect is the \textit{word} of God, which has many meanings; but it's \textit{in} us, and is a part of this issue as well (see, for example, 4N 1:30).
	
	See ``voice of God.''
	
	Here are some scriptures and quotes about it.

% -----------------------
\subsection{Suffering} % *SUFFERING
% -----------------------

	The Greek verb \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{p'asqein}} is the most commonly used verb in the NT, I think, to described what Christ did--he suffered. A related word for his \textit{sufferings} is \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{p'ajhma}}.

	Note that Rom 8:17 says that we \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{sump'asqein}} \textit{with} Christ. The particle before this verb is \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{e>'iper}}, and the lexicon gives the meaning here as \textit{if indeed, if after all, since}. So we are joint-heirs \textit{since} or \textit{if indeed} we suffer with him.

		\subsubsection{Uses of \textit{paschein}}

		Here is a summary of the places where the verb \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{p'asqein}} appears.

		\begin{description}

		\item[Mt 16:21] From that time forth began Jesus to shew unto his disciples, how that he must go unto Jerusalem, and suffer many things of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and be raised again the third day.

		\textit{Notes:} \textbf{Object}: many things. \textbf{Agent inflicting suffering}: marked by \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{>ap'o}}.

		Christ appears to be obligated to suffer--includes \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{de\char"007Ei}}.

		\item[Mt 17:12] But I say unto you, That Elias is come already, and they knew him not, but have done unto him whatsoever they listed. Likewise shall also the Son of man suffer of them.

		\textit{Notes:} \textbf{Agent inflicting suffering}: marked by \textcolor{red}{<up'o}.

		Once again, Christ's suffering is inflicted on him by other people. Contrast this with the BOM's use of \textit{anguish}, which is far more \textit{internal} in the BOM. See TG \textit{anguish}.

		\item[Mt 17:15] Lord, have mercy on my son: for he is lunatick, and sore vexed: for ofttimes he falleth into the fire, and oft into the water.

		\textit{Notes:} According to the lexicon, this is the only neutral use of \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{p'asqein}} in the NT. It is preceded by \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{kak\char"007Ews}}, which gives it the negative connotation. Translated as \textit{[he is] sore vexed} here.

		This sense, at least, carries the idea that something is \textit{happening to} the boy; this is actually the sense of \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{p'asqein}}. From the lexicon at \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{p'asqw}}:

		\begin{quote}
		(\textcolor{red}{\textgreek{p}}. expresses the passive idea corresponding to the active idea in \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{poi'ew}}) of everything that befalls a person, whether good or ill. Yet its usage developed in such a way that \textcolor{red}{\textgreek{p}}. came to be used less and less frequently in a good sense, and never thus without some clear indication, at least from the context, that the good sense is meant (785).
		\end{quote}

		So maybe there is something to the point about \textit{anguish} above as well. It's interesting, at least, that all the uses of \textit{anguish} in the BOM are more internal like that. But I still don't have a good way of distinguishing between anguish and suffering, for suffering requires some sort of internal reaction to external stimuli as well.

		\end{description}

Whatever the answer to this question is, I think this verse is important to it.

	% -----
	\subsubsection{My own testimony}
	% -----
	
		I was realizing that I wrote this testimony for a family collection in December 2014, but hadn't included it here. I wanted to put it in now and I'll try to include future written testimonies if I ever create them for something.
		
		This first one I wrote in September 2014 for a little book Meredith put together with the testimonies of all the adults in the family at that time. We received copies of it over Christmas when we were in Belmont, the same Christmas that Matt got home from his mission in Idaho.
		
		\begin{quote}
		
			My faith has grown slowly throughout my life, but I've had a small number of moments in which my understanding and testimony of the gospel seemed to take a great leap forward. These experiences usually occur after I have been thinking, studying, and discussing a particular topic for a long time--they are watersheds that set the course of my belief and my gospel reflection for the subsequent months or years. These moments form the most important part of my testimony, and so I would like to share some of them. I believe the understanding gained from these experiences was given from the Holy Ghost. I don't believe that this guarantees their truth; what I have learned, though, is that it's critical to my spiritual progress that I continue to think in these ways until the Lord reveals otherwise.

			One of the first of these experiences came as I was preparing for my mission. I was attending a mission prep class once per week and doing a few other things. It occurred to me that I had never asked God in prayer whether the LDS church was really the right one to belong to. I decided that it would be important to ask about this before I was a missionary, so I started to pray about it. I prayed regularly for a while, asking God to give me an answer. Nothing came. I wasn't sure why I wasn't receiving anything--it seemed like an important issue to get revelation about before spending two years telling other people that they could receive the same revelation.

			Then one day I realized that the reason God wasn't giving me an answer was that I already had one. I already believed that the LDS church was the true one before I started asking in prayer. Why did I need to ask about something that I already believed? Wouldn't the purpose of any answer just be to help me believe it? I quit praying about it and left on my mission soon after, having learned that God wasn't going to give me something that I already had. This pattern has been repeated many times in my life.

			Another important moment came during a mission meeting over a year later. When I was a missionary, I struggled to understand what I could do to help other people accept the gospel. I loved the people that we met in the streets and visited in their homes, and I became intensely interested in knowing what they needed from me in order to feel love and light from the Lord. This topic came up during a mission meeting as we looked at Alma 26:22: "Yea, he that repenteth and exerciseth faith, and bringeth forth good works, and prayeth continually without ceasing--unto such it is given to know the mysteries of God; yea, unto such it shall be given to reveal things which never have been revealed; yea, and it shall be given unto such to bring thousands of souls to repentance, even as it has been given unto us to bring these our brethren to repentance." After we read this scripture, our mission president asked us what the phrase "the mysteries of God" might be referring to. A missionary from Argentina, Elder Velez, said that he thought this phrase referred to the gift of discernment, and to the power we can have to understand things which are normally a mystery to all except God: the feelings of a person's heart. 

			When Elder Velez made this remark, it was though many disparate events from the months before were suddenly and forcefully connected. I realized that my purpose as a missionary was actually the purpose of a disciple of Christ--I was to seek the gift of discernment to understand what others needed in order for them to receive the measure of the gospel, however small or large, for which they had been prepared. Formerly I had thought that the "mysteries" spoken of in this verse must refer to knowledge of the intricacies of the plan of salvation, but these things are unimportant compared to what is inside other people.

			I have not always kept this purpose in mind, and I have not always used wisely the light which comes from the Lord's discerning gifts. But in that moment I saw a small part of the great love that the Lord has for all His children and for me, and the great responsibility which falls on me to spread that love in the world.

			Several years later, after I was married, I had another experience which has profoundly impacted my testimony and from which I continue to draw inspiration as I think about the gospel. When we were living in Provo, I was once studying the scriptures and came across the following quote from Brigham Young:

			"When God speaks to the people, he does it in a manner to suit their circumstances and capacities. He spoke to the children of Jacob through Moses, as a blind, stiff-necked people, and when Jesus and his Apostles came they talked with the Jews as a benighted, wicked, selfish people. They would not receive the Gospel, though presented to them by the Son of God in all its righteousness, beauty and glory. Should the Lord Almighty send an angel to re-write the Bible, it would in many places be very different from what it now is. And I will even venture to say that if the Book of Mormon were now to be re-written, in many instances it would materially differ from the present translation. According as people are willing to receive the things of God, so the heavens send forth their blessings. If the people are stiff-necked, the Lord can tell them but little" (JD 9:311).

			The thought floored me. How could the translation of the Book of Mormon be different from the one we have now? What does this say about the original record, and what does it say about the translation process? More importantly, what does it say about the process of receiving revelation in general, and the way in which the Lord gives us light and knowledge as we progress? Encountering this remark from Young was a turning point in the way I thought about the gospel. Previous to finding it, I had been working with what I now believe to be a very limited and constrained understanding of the scope of the gospel. If God could change the translation of the Book of Mormon based on the level of obedience and knowledge among a people, then why couldn't he change a great many other things as well? Many doubts I've had, such as the relationship between the gospel and other sources of knowledge, have dissolved away as I have explored this idea. It is always in my mind when my faith comes up against new and challenging questions.

			Excluding the core doctrines of the atonement and salvation, this principle is the most important one that I have ever learned. My faith is not only stronger because of it, but completley different. It has strengthened me and helped me to understand the ways in which God views His children on earth.

			The last experience that I want to share came when we were living in Boston. I was in a feminist philosophy class at Tufts, and had chosen to write a term paper on the relationship between feminism and some aspects of Mormon theology. I had been reading from many different sources and at the time was reading from a philosopher named Georg Hegel. Hegel was a German writing in the early nineteenth century, and his work is difficult and opaque. The parts I was reading were from a passage called the "master-slave dialectic." In that passage, he describes the process through which a person becomes self-conscious, or aware of themselves as a conscious being. He thinks that this can only happen when you encounter another being like yourself--you only become aware of yourself when you become aware of someone else.

			As two beings become aware of each other and themselves, though, Hegel thought that their interaction gets ugly fast. He thought that they soon begin a life-and-death struggle in order to assert themselves and their power over the other. Eventually one of them assumes control over the other and their relationship turns into that between a master, the empowered one, and a slave, the subjugated one. The idea in our feminist class was that something like this master-slave relationship was being played out in the world, on a large scale and in a more abstract way, between men and women. Men are constantly asserting their power over women, subjugating them, keeping them in the position of a slave.

			As I thought about this antagonistic view of the relationship between men and women, I had an instance of great clarity in which I saw that the atonement and eternal marriage were the way out of Hegel's trap. Fear and selfishness push us into a place of hostility toward others, and we set ourselves above them in order to hide our weaknesses and guilt. Repentance through the atonement cleanses us of these poisons, and Christ restores in us our lost purity and righteousness. From this position of innocence we can face other children of God without animosity. We become aware of ourselves as inheritors of eternal life, and we also become aware of our need for another person who can inherit with us. We become aware that we can join in an eternal marriage and end the inimical cycle between us and others once and for all.

			I wish my words could do justice to this experience. In those moments I felt like I understood so much more than that, and it was one of the most beautiful experiences of my life. From this I have gained a new testimony of eternal marriage and Christ's power to heal all of our mortality. I believe that the restored gospel is the way to end our pain and our guilt, and to put an end to enmity in our lives.

			These experiences and the things I learned from them are the foundation of my testimony. I don't know why God has chosen to interact in these particular ways with me, but I am grateful that He has. My beliefs now are very different from those I had when I arrived home from my mission, but the core is the same. I believe that repentance cleanses our hearts and minds, and allows us to receive greater light and knowledge from the Lord. I believe that the commandments are for our benefit. I believe in trying to sustain church leaders and in trying to build the kingdom of God on earth. Ultimately, my testimony is just that we can live with God again and be with our families forever through Christ, the mediator of the new covenant.
			
		\end{quote}

% -----------------------
\subsection{Third part (of those who fell from heaven)} % *THIRDPART *ONETHIRD
% -----------------------

	I think Andrus's argument is wrong; it should be one-third the fration, as in 1/3, and not the third part, as in three parts, not necessarily of equal size. I wrote the following to President Openshaw on 1/6/2016:
	
		\begin{quote}
			I noticed that you mentioned the ``one third'' as spoken of in Revelation, the spirits who didn't keep their first estate and so never received bodies. The way you used the phrase ``one third'' you seemed to take it as referring to a fraction---as in, 33\% of the spirits. I bring this up because I've recently been listening to some lectures that Hyrum Andrus gave in the 90's, and he likes to understand the one third as one-third PART, where it doesn't have anything to do with fractions. The phrase ``third part'' is in Rev 12:4 and other places. For Andrus it shows that there were three parts or divisions among the spirits, and the third one---not a fraction, just the ordinal third---didn't keep their estate. I think that this is the wrong interpretation. The Greek in Revelation is \textgreek{to triton} or \textit{to triton}, and that's the way you mean ``one third'' (fraction) in Greek. So Andrus may have some other justification for his view but to me it seems incorrect.
		\end{quote}
		
	The NIV, RSV, NRSV, NKJV, NASB, and other modern translations just say a ``third'' without the ``part'' thing.
	
	This is something that's a bit frustrating about Andrus---he was extremely skilled at reading the scriptures carefully and being systematic. But he wasn't a very good scholar in another sense, of being thoughtful about issues that could affect his interpretation. 

	\begin{description}
	\item[DC 29:36] And it came to pass that Adam, being tempted of the devil---for, behold, the devil was before Adam, for he rebelled against me, saying, Give me thine honor, which is my power; and also a third part of the hosts of heaven turned he away from me because of their agency;
	\item[CDBY 29] Has the Lord spoken in these last days, and required us to build Him a house? Then why query about it? If He has spoken it is enough. I do not care whether the people gather or not, if they don't want to do so. I do not wish to save the people against their will. I want them to choose whether they will gather and be saved with the righteous, or remain with the wicked and be damned. I would like to have all people bow down to the Lord Jesus Christ; but it is one of the decrees of the Lord that all persons shall act upon their agency, which was the case even with the angels who fell from heaven.
	\item[CDBY 441] Why not quarrel about Christ coming instead of the Father? When the Father appointed Jesus Christ, the Firstborn, to come and redeem the earth, there was contention got up. The second brother, Lucifer, the son of the morning, wanted the honor to come and redeem the earth. But Christ was the appointed one. It was His right by appointment and birthright. But the war and contention became so hot and the influence of Lucifer was so great that he got one-third of the hosts in heaven to join his standard, and when he was hurled down to hell like lightning from heaven, one-third was cast down with him. Where is he and those that were cast down? With those spirits that accompanied him. They are here on this earth and they have blinded the children of men and [are] still seeking to overthrow the kingdom of God. He is a thorn in the flesh of the children of God. But this is all right, and we should be contented with what God sees fit to grant unto us and be contented with our lot. If the Devil had been contented and acted in his place, he would not have been thrust down to hell. Any man who seeks to do a thing that he cannot do, and should not do, it casts him into hell and makes a hell for him when men ask for things that do not belong to him and it makes him unhappy.
	\end{description}

% -----------------------
\subsection{Translation of records} % *TRANSLATIONOFRECORDS
% -----------------------

	More specifically, the translations and translation process of Joseph Smith.
	
	From a gospel perspective, translation is just revelation with some externalized source of light, inspiration, or guidance.
	
	See the title page of the BOM, where Moroni twice says that the book is going to be ``interpreted''--doesn't use the word ``translated.'' Cf. Mosiah 8:13, where Ammon calls the tools used to translate records ``interpreters.'' Mosiah 28:4 as well, where we're told that the tools used by Mosiah are ``for the purpose of interpreting languages.'' There seems to be an interesting difference between the 2013 sense of ``interpret'' and the senses alive in the 1828 dictionary--the first definition given is ``To explain the meaning or words to a person who does not understand them; to expound; to translate unintelligible words into intelligible ones.'' Cf. 2 Nephi 31:3, where the Lord speaks unto men according to their language, unto their (level of?) understanding. All of this should support what's in Alma 12:9-13 or so, and what Brigham Young says when he notes that the translation of the BOM would materially differ in some places. The Lord always takes into account our current level of understanding when he gives us light: ``When God speaks to the people, he does it in a manner to suit their circumstances and capacities. He spoke to the children of Jacob through Moses, as a blind, stiff-necked people, and when Jesus and his Apostles came they talked with the Jews as a benighted, wicked, selfish people. They would not receive the Gospel, though presented to them by the Son of God in all its righteousness, beauty and glory. Should the Lord Almighty send an angel to re-write the Bible, it would in many places be very different from what it now is. And I will even venture to say that if the Book of Mormon were now to be re-written, in many instances it would materially differ from the present translation. According as people are willing to receive the things of God, so the heavens send forth their blessings. If the people are stiff-necked, the Lord can tell them but little'' (JD 9:311).
	
	Think of this translation as interpretation (Eth 3:22--24); then you're subject to all the facets of the levels principle, and BY 9:311 makes sense too.
	
	Activities Joseph Smith engaged in which we might call ``translations'' today (in order to show how different they are):
		\begin{itemize}
		\item Translating the Book of Mormon
		\item Translating the ``parchment'' to produce DC 7, even though it seems there never was a parchment
		\item Translating the Bible again
			Note book of Moses here too
		\item Translating the Book of Abraham
		\end{itemize}
		
	How did JS think of his ``translation'' of these different items?
		Book of Abraham
			He seemed to believe that Abraham and others had actually written the material on the papyri themselves.
				Charles Francis Adams, who visited JS in Nauvoo on May 15, 1844 with Josiah Quincy Jr. From Adams' diary: ``Upon our return from the meal we were introduced into another chamber which had been prepared in the interval, and here we sat down and held a long conference with the prophet upon himself, his doctrines and his projects. He then took us down into his mother's chamber and showed us four Egyptian mummies stripped and then undertook to explain the contents of a chart or manuscript which he said had been taken from the bosom of one of them. The cool impudence of this imposture amused me very much. `This,' said he, `was written by the hand of Abraham and means so and so. If anyone denies it, let him prove the contrary. \textit{I} say it''' (From ``Charles Francis Adams Visits the Mormons in 1844,'' \textit{Proceedings of the Massachusetts Historical Society}, 68, 285).
				Josiah Quincy Jr., from his \textit{Figures of the Past}, 386: ```That is the handwriting of Abraham, the Father of the Faithful,' said the prophet. `This is the autograph of Moses, and these lines were written by his brother Aaron. Here we have the earliest account of the Creation, from which Moses composed the First Book of Genesis''' (see 385, where Quincy talks about JS's bragging about having knowledge of many languages).
					On 387 Quincy writes: ``We were further assured that the prophet was the only mortal who could translate these mysterious writings, and that his power was given by direct inspiration.'' This point may be in favor of the ``special translation'' view, but remember also that even by this time in 1844 *here
			For something like the ``revelatory translation'' view, see JSEP 7, especially note 22. I think the ``mnemonic'' view is similar.
		Book of Mormon
		Bible
			FWR 23, where it is reported that JS uses the word ``translating'' in talking about the version of the Bible he has been working on
				But see FWR 29 for ths use of ``translation'' in copying down the revelations

It seems probable that Oliver Cowdery desired to translate out of curiosity, and the Lord taught him his place by showing him that translating was not the easy thing he had thought it to be. % -----------------------
\subsection{Transfiguration} % *TRANSFIGURATION
% -----------------------

	By this word I mean, when someone's face or body is changed to have a more spiritual nature for a temporary period.
	
	The word occurs twice in the NT, at Mt 17:2 and Mark 9:2. Both occasions are reporting Christ's transfiguration on the mountain, and in both it's a passive form of \textgreek{μεταμορφόω}.
	
	Here is a bit about \textgreek{μεταμορφόω}. % μεταμορφόω*
		NT appearances: Mt 17:2; Mk 9:2; Rom 12:2; 2Co 3:18
		CGEL: 230; BDAG: 639b; PGL 854a;
			Both of these lexicons give two senses of this word---one sense for Mt and Mk, and the other sense for the other two occurrences.
			For Mt and Mk: ``to change in a manner visible to others, \textit{be transfigured}.''
			For the other two: ``to change inwardly in fundamental character or condition, \textit{be changed, be transformed}.''z
			These definitions come from BDAG.
			The emphasis for the first meaning seems to be on altered appearance. 
		There is a different emphasis in at least some of the restoration uses. There are eight occurrences of ``transfigure'' or ``transfiguration'' in the restoration scriptures:
			3N 28:15, 17; Morm 8:33; DC 63:20, 21; 138:45; Mos 1:11, 14.
			The uses in 3N 28 deal with the disciples who were changed. I think it's talking about all twelve, not just the three who were going to remain on the earth and not die.
				Again, though, the emphasis is not on the change of appearance---it's on a change of the physical nature---and not just something like a moral change, as in Rom 12:2---it's on a change of the physical nature which allows one to be in the presence of God, to perceive things differently (to have a different kind of perceptual ability), and so on. It's not about appearance or moral character: it's a change of the physical nature itself, so that perception and cognition work through different mechanisms.
			It may be that you don't get this emphasis in the NT because the two most similar uses are both speaking about Christ, who already had such a great amount of the Spirit that he perceived and cognized differently anyway.
			The uses in the DC: 63:20 and 21 are talking about the earth, but we're also told that the transfiguration will be ``even according to the pattern which was shown unto mine apostles upon the mount.'' So there is something important that happens in the NT account---the DC says ``of which account the fulness ye have not yet received''---that applies even to a being as different as the earth when it is transfigured.
				But nothing here about changed perception or anything else.
				138:45 is just naming the mount of transfiguration.
			The two uses in Mos 1 clearly follow after the uses in the BOM, where there is a changing of the physical nature in order to allow for altered perception and cogntion, as well as to allow one to be in the presence of God/behold his glory/tolerate his presence.
			
	A couple of JS uses of ``transfigure'':
		TPJS 13, ``they [seers and prophets] saw the glory of the Lord when he showed the transfiguration of the earth on the mount.''
			Again, clearly related to the DC 63 uses of the word; it clearly connects the transfiguration of Christ with the DC uses in 63. There is some kind of important connection here.
			DC 63 is ``late August 1831,'' while TPJS 13 is from a year later, August 1832.
		WJS 28, ``The Savior, Moses, \& Elias---gave the Keys to Peter, James \& John on the Mount when they were transfigured before him.''
			So who's transfigured here, according to this quote? Seems like it's talking about Peter, James, and John being transfigured before Christ.
		WJS 141, ``we were eyewitnesses of his majesty and heard the voice of his excellent glory \& what could be more sure? transfigured on the mount''
			This is a tough one. I think it's talking about his calling as prophet, and how he received some kind of witness or proof like the one that Peter, James, and John received. Hard to tell though.
		WJS 177, ``Men will set up stakes and say thus far will we go and no farther, did Abraham when called upon to offer his son, did the Saviour, no, view him fulfiling all rightousness again on the banks of jordon, also on the Mount transfigured before Peter and John there receiving the fulness of preisthood or the law of God.''
			Extremely important quote, though not so much for transfiguration itself---this says that Christ received the fulness of the priesthood during the event on the mount of transfiguration.
			Also extremely important for the priesthood itself---``the fulness of priesthood OR THE LAW OF GOD''!!!!!

% -----------------------
\subsection{Trump} % *TRUMPET
% -----------------------

	There is something significant about the use of \textit{trump} in the scriptures; it's almost like a specific, well-defined power or blessing that can be given to someone in certain circumstances. See, for example, Al 29:1, where Alma wants to ``speak with the trump of God, with a voice to shake the earth.'' Then see Hel 5:26--27: ``And it came to pass that Nephi and Lehi did stand forth and began to speak unto them, saying: Fear not, for behold, it is God that has shown unto you this marvelous thing, in the which is shown unto you that ye cannot lay your hands on us to slay us. And behold, when they had said these words, the earth shook exceedingly, and the walls of the prison did shake as if they were about to tumble to the earth; but behold, they did not fall.'' There you get mention of the power, but not its name, something to do with ``trump.'' That word is in the DC a lot, though.
	
	Another connection to make here is the difference between the spoken and the written word, and DC 84:45, where we learn that the word is Spirit (or spirit, no capital letter, as it is in the original text).

	\subsubsection{Goodness as criterion or constitutive of truth} % *TRUTHGOOD *TRUTHASGOODNESS
	% -----
	
		The key scriptures for this idea are Mor 10:6; Al 32:28, 35; DC 84:45. But there are many other verses which support the idea as well. It's like goodness is a more basic or primary distinction in the gospel than truth or falsity; truth is built out of goodness.
		
		Note that the levels principle is bound up very tightly with this idea.
			See especially, at the levels principle, the note on 2N 33:14--15, with ``seal.''

% -----------------------
\subsection{Turn out fine} % *TURNOUTFINE
% -----------------------

	The idea that, if we're righteous, things will work together for our good and turn out fine in the end.
	
	\begin{description}
	\item[DC 90:24] Search diligently, pray always, and be believing, and all things shall work together for your good, if ye walk uprightly and remember the covenant wherewith ye have covenanted one with another.
	\item[Jer 17:7--8] Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is. 8 For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.
	\item[Jer 24:5--7] (This is a pretty extreme example.) Thus saith the LORD, the God of Israel; Like these good figs, so will I acknowledge them that are carried away captive of Judah, whom I have sent out of this place into the land of the Chaldeans for their good. 6 For I will set mine eyes upon them for good, and I will bring them again to this land: and I will build them, and not pull them down; and I will plant them, and not pluck them up. 7 And I will give them an heart to know me, that I am the LORD: and they shall be my people, and I will be their God: for they shall return unto me with their whole heart.
	\item[TPJS 43] Avoid contentions and vain disputes with men of corrupt minds, who do not desire to know the truth. Remember that "it is a day of warning, and not a day of many words." If they receive not your testimony in one place, flee to another, remembering to cast no reflections, nor throw out any bitter sayings. If you do your duty, it will be just as well with you, as though all men embraced the Gospel.
	\item[CDBY 36] Take care of yourselves, be wise, be humble, and you will prosper. I curse all who degrade themselves with corruption and licentiousness, as many have done. Magnify your calling, keep yourselves pure and innocent, and your path shall be clear as the horizon.
	\end{description}
	
% -----------------------
\subsection{Understanding} % *UNDERSTANDING
% -----------------------

	It's clear that the word in some places at least must refer to the psychological capacity of understanding, or that thinking part of us, like we might see the term in Descartes or Locke or someone like that. 2N 31:3 fits here, and something like DC 88:11 must, since it uses the word in the plural.
	
	Mk 12:33 uses \textgreek{σύνεσις}, ``faculty of perceiving readily with the mind.''
	
	1828:
		1. The faculty of the human mind by which it apprehends the real state of things presented to it, or by which it receives or comprehends the ideas which others express and intend to communicate. The understanding is called also the intellectual faculty. It is the faculty by means of which we obtain a great part of our knowledge. Luke 24:45. Ephesians 1:18.
			By understanding I mean that faculty whereby we are enabled to apprehend the objects of knowledge, generals or particulars, absent or present, and to judge of their truth or falsehood, good or evil.
		2. Knowledge; exact comprehension.
			Right understanding consists in the perception of the visible or probably agreement or disagreement of ideas [this is Lockean].
		3. Intelligence between two or more persons; agreement of minds; union of sentiments. There is a good understanding between the minister and his people.
	
% -----------------------
\subsection{Unfolding} % *UNFOLDING *FOLDING
% -----------------------

	I love the metaphor of revelations and knowledge unfolding; I think of a towel. With just a single (even) fold, half the towel is hidden from view. And even when there are no folds, you still can't ever see all the towel at once (unless you have a mirror or something). If it's just you and the towel, even if it is completely unfolded, you can never see more than half of it at one time. Hence the importance of prophets and apostles, who view the towel from a different vantage point, but also of other people generally, or can step around to the other side and tell us what's over there while we continue to look at the side we're already familiar with.
	Note that the towel looks different from each vantage point as well; it makes a different shape on our retina, and so looks different to us.

% -----------------------
\subsection{Universality of the gospel} % *UNIVERSALITY
% -----------------------

	I don't have a better name for this principle yet. The idea is that God inspires every people to teach his word, even though it isn't always exactly the fulness of the restored gospel. So Plato and Aristotle were inspired, for example, and other great thinkers and philosophers. These people are inspired to create a moral philosophy for an age, and that philosophy becomes the ``gospel'' and the standard for judging the people who lived during that time. I hope at some point to be able to explain this principle better.

\subsection{Urim and Thummim} % *URIMTHUMMIM
% -----------------------

	See Num 27:21 (15--23); Deu 33:8 (part of Moses' last blessing to the Levites); 1Sam 28:6 (Saul is looking for answers from the Lord through it); Neh 7:63--65 (a priest should have it); Al 37:21--26;
	
	See also any mention of the ephod, especially in places like 1Sam 30:7--8, where David uses the ephod to inquire something of the Lord. It's a breastplate, or a piece of armor or clothing for the chest, which is similar to the breastplate/Urim \& Thummim thing that Joseph Smith had.
	
	The term ``Urim and Thummim'' wasn't in use in the earliest days of the church, and mentions of it in DC 10 and 17 were inserted later, I think. See JSR 49--51 for a brief commentary on this point. See also JSP-D1:84, note 320.
		So Urim and Thummim is a good example of how JS's understanding of something grew over time, and they went back and revised things in accordance with their later understanding.
